rows.title: Theater and performance venue classification
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal

Distinguish Group C (theater with proscenium stage) from Group H (assembly without stage), calculate seating area at 0.9 sqm/seat, apply egress width at 7.6 mm/person, and verify compliance with stage minimum dimensions and accessibility standards.

|---

## Core Concept

<ExamTip>
The LEA frequently tests theater vs. assembly classification. The single deciding factor is the presence of a **fixed proscenium stage** — not seating capacity. A 1,200-seat concert hall WITH a fixed proscenium stage is still Group C (Theater), not Group H.
</ExamTip>

Theater and performance venue classification is a **critical LEA trap** per **ERR-DSGN-005**. The distinction hinges on the _presence of a stage_:

- **Group C (Theater with Proscenium Stage):** Traditional theaters, playhouses, and concert halls with a raised stage platform and backstage area. Typical capacities are 50–500 seats.
- **Group H (Large Assembly):** Stadiums, arenas, concert halls without a dedicated stage, amphitheaters, and sports complexes. Typical capacities are 500+ seats; these may have temporary or multi-purpose stages.

This classification difference is significant because Group C uses education/recreation egress standards, while Group H uses assembly egress standards with different occupant load calculations and larger exit aggregate widths. The LEA frequently presents mixed descriptions, requiring students to identify whether a venue is Group C (if a fixed proscenium stage exists) or Group H (if it features flexible staging).

<KeyValues items={[
  {label:"Seating area per person", value:"0.9 sqm"},
  {label:"Minimum proscenium stage", value:"9.0 m × 12.0 m"},
  {label:"Main aisle width (RA 9514)", value:"1.1 m minimum"},
  {label:"Exit width rate", value:"7.6 mm/person"},
  {label:"Max travel distance (unsprinklered)", value:"45 m"},
  {label:"Accessible parking stall", value:"3.7 m × 5.0 m"}
]} />

### Space Program Standards

Below are the standards per **RA 9514** and theater design practice:

**Seating:**

- **Fixed theater seating:** 0.9 sqm per person, which includes seat and aisle allowance.
- **Row spacing (front-to-front):** 850–1,050 mm, with 900 mm being typical for comfort.
- **Aisle width:** **1.1 m minimum** per RA 9514 2019 IRR Division 10 Section 1005.

**Stage (Proscenium Theater):**

- **Minimum proscenium stage:** **9.0 m wide × 12.0 m deep**.
- **Backstage support:** 30–50% of the stage area, including wings, fly loft, and storage.
- **Dressing rooms:** 1 per 10 performers, with a minimum of 3 sqm per room.
- **Technical control:** 1.5–2.0% of total GFA for lighting and sound booths.

**Emergency Egress:**

- **Minimum exits:** 2 exits required from the seating area at any occupancy > 0 per RA 9514 Section 7.1.
- **Exit width aggregate:** Occupancy × 7.6 mm/person per RA 9514 2019 IRR assembly standards.
- **Travel distance:** 60 m if sprinklered or 45 m if unsprinklered.
- **Stairwell:** Maximum riser of 200 mm and minimum tread of 250 mm.

**Occupant Load Calculation:**

- **Seating area:** 0.9 sqm per person, which already accounts for seated occupancy and aisle circulation.
- **Stage/backstage:** Typically 1 per 25 sqm for technical crew.
- **Lobby/support:** 1 per 1.4 sqm per RA 9514 2019 IRR Division 3 Table 10.2.

---

## Key Provisions

### Occupancy Classification (Group C vs. Group H)

| Feature | Group C (Theater) | Group H (Assembly) |
|:------------------- |:----------------------------------------------------- |:---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Stage** | Fixed proscenium stage required | No stage OR multipurpose stage |
| **Typical Capacity** | 50–500 seats | 500–5,000+ seats |
| **Examples** | Playhouse, symphony hall | Arena, stadium, amphitheater |
| **Egress Rule** | 2 exits minimum | 2 exits minimum |
| **Exit Width Rate** | 7.6 mm/person | 7.6 mm/person |

### Seating Layout & Dimensions (RA 9514)

| Parameter | Requirement | Notes |
|:------------------- |:--------------------------------------- |:------------------------------------------------------- |
| Fixed seating area | 0.9 sqm per seat | Includes seat width + circulation |
| Row spacing | 850–1,050 mm | Typically 900 mm |
| Main aisle width | **1.1 m minimum** | Per RA 9514 Section 7.1 |
| Side/emergency aisle | **1.1 m minimum** | Must accommodate two-way traffic |

### Accessibility & Inclusion (BP 344)

- **Accessible seating:** Minimum 1 per 50 seats or 2% of total, whichever is greater.
- **Wheelchair space:** 1.5 m × 2.0 m per space, allowing for companion seating.
- **Accessible parking stall:** **3.7 m × 5.0 m** per BP 344 2024 Revised IRR.
- **Ramp gradient:** **1:20 maximum** per BP 344 2024 Revised IRR Part 2 Section 206.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-004-07-core-concept" type="image" caption="Theater Typology — Proscenium, Thrust, and Arena Stage Configurations" description="Comparison diagram of three theater stage types: proscenium (framed stage, 0.9 sqm/seat), thrust (stage extends into audience), and arena (surrounded). Shows stage minimum dimensions, seating angles, and egress requirements per RA 9514." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

---

## Philippine Practice Context

### Community Theater (Group C, 200 Seats)

- **Seating Area:** 200 seats × 0.9 sqm = **180 sqm**.
- **Stage:** 9.0 m × 12.0 m proscenium.
- **Emergency Egress:** 200 occupants require 1,520 mm aggregate exit width.
- **Parking:** 200 occupants ÷ 50 sqm/stall (assembly standard per PD 1096 Rule XIX Appendix A Table IX) ≈ **4 stalls minimum**.

### Concert Hall (Group C, 500 Seats)

- **Seating Area:** 500 seats × 0.9 sqm = **450 sqm**.
- **Occupant Load:** 500 (seats) + 8 (backstage) + 5 (lobby) = **513 occupants**.
- **Emergency Egress:** 513 occupants × 7.6 mm ≈ **3.9 m aggregate width**.
- **Parking:** 513 occupants ÷ 50 sqm/stall ≈ **10 spaces minimum**.

---

## How It's Tested

**Occupancy Classification Trap (Difficulty 0.7):**
"A concert hall has 1,200 seats and a flexible stage. What occupancy group applies?"

- **Answer:** If it has a fixed proscenium stage, it is **Group C**. If it has a multipurpose or no stage, it is **Group H**.

**Seating Occupancy Pattern (Difficulty 0.7):**
"A 250-seat theater allocates 0.9 sqm per seat. How much floor area is required for the seating area?"

- **Answer:** 250 × 0.9 sqm = **225 sqm minimum**.

**Egress Analysis Pattern (Difficulty 0.9):**
"A 400-seat theater has two 1.0 m wide exit doors. Verify compliance."

| **Answer:** Required width = 400 × 7.6 mm = 3,040 mm (3.04 m). Since 2.0 m is available, it is **NON-COMPLIANT**.

<WikiMistakeCard number={1} title="Group C vs Group H Trap" wrongValue="Use seating capacity alone to classify" correctValue="Check for a fixed proscenium stage — that's the deciding factor" explanation="A 200-seat community theater with a fixed stage is Group C. A 1,200-seat arena with flexible staging is Group H. The LEA often includes stage descriptions to test this distinction." />

<Tip>
**Memory aid for stage minimums:** Think "9 × 12 = 108" — the minimum proscenium stage is 9.0 m wide × 12.0 m deep (108 sqm). For seating: 0.9 sqm per seat is roughly 1 sqm, making mental math fast under exam pressure.
</Tip>

---

**Exam Tip — ERR-DSGN-005:** The presence of a proscenium stage determines Group C vs Group H classification. Stadiums and arenas without fixed stages = Group H, regardless of seating capacity.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-004-07-core-concept" type="image" caption="Theater Seating and Egress — Sightlines, Row Spacing, and Exit Distribution" description="Theater seating plan showing: minimum row spacing (850mm), seat width (500-550mm), sightline angles (max 30° to top of stage), and exit distribution at 7.6 mm/person. Proscenium stage minimum dimensions and BP 344 accessible seating zones shown." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-005-10** (Multi-Purpose Halls) for Group C vs Group H distinction, **LEA-DSGN-008-01** (Fire Egress) for seating egress calculations, and **LEA-DSGN-007-08** (Human Factors) for sightline standards.

## Common Mistakes

---

rows.title: Roofing materials serve three critical functions: weather
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Classify roofing materials (corrugated GI sheets, clay tiles, concrete tiles, asphalt shingles, standing seam metal, green roofs) by slope requirements, weather resistance, fire rating, and service life for Philippine climate conditions.
## Core Concept

Roofing materials serve three critical functions: weather protection, structural support, and thermal regulation. In the Philippines, galvanized corrugated iron (GI) sheets remain the most common residential choice due to cost and availability. These sheets are manufactured per ASTM A653 and come in standard gauges: Gauge 26 = 0.46 mm (0.0181 inches), Gauge 24 = 0.61 mm (0.0239 inches), Gauge 22 = 0.76 mm (0.0299 inches). Gauge 26 (0.46 mm) is the common minimum for residential applications per industry practice, though Gauge 24 (0.61 mm) is increasingly standard. These measurements include the zinc coating per ASTM A653 specification. GI coating weight is specified by G-rating (G90 = 0.90 oz/ft² or Z275 metric equivalent = 275 g/m²), which directly affects corrosion resistance in tropical salt-air environments.

Long-span metal roofing (trapezoidal or corrugated profiles spanning 6-12 meters) reduces support framing costs but requires precise fastening and expansion control in temperature-sensitive applications. Clay and concrete roof tiles provide excellent thermal mass and 50+ year durability but demand stronger roof framing due to weight (approximately 5-6 kN/m²). Asphalt shingles are lightweight and affordable but suffer accelerated degradation in tropical UV and humidity. Built-up roofing (BUR) and single-ply membranes (TPO, PVC, EPDM) serve low-slope or flat roofs and require proper slope (minimum 1/4:12 or 2%) for drainage. Metal standing seam systems offer superior panel-to-panel integration and accommodate building movement through hidden fastening.

Selection criteria include: structural capacity of frame, roof slope, expected service life, maintenance accessibility, thermal properties (k-value for insulation bonded to sheets), and fire rating per NFPA 101.


<ArticleMedia id="media-roofing-material-chart" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison chart of roofing materials: corrugated GI sheets, clay tiles, concrete tiles, asphalt shingles, standing seam metal, and green roofs with slope, weather resistance, fire rating, and service life data"
  caption="Future chart: roofing material comparison — slope requirements, weather resistance, fire rating, and service life"
  suggestedAsset="Material property comparison table with application photos or icons"
  placementIntent="Helps learners select appropriate roofing material for Philippine climate" />

## Key Provisions

| Property | Value | Standard | LEA Relevance |
|----------|-------|----------|---------------|
| GI Gauge 26 thickness | 0.46 mm | ASTM A653, PH Code | Minimum residential specification |
| GI Gauge 24 thickness | 0.61 mm | ASTM A653, PH Code | Common upgrade; ~33% stronger |
| G90 coating weight | 0.90 oz/ft² or 275 g/m² | ASTM A653 | Tropical corrosion resistance |
| Minimum roof slope | 1/4:12 (2%) | Manufacturer standards/NRCA | Common flat roof drainage guideline |
| Clay tile weight | 5-6 kN/m² | ASTM C1167 | Structural design load |
| Standing seam panel span | 6-12 m | Manufacturer | Reduces purlins, increases cost |
| BUR ply count | 3-4 plies + cap sheet | ASTM D6162 | Durability, UV protection |
| Single-ply membrane thickness | 45-60 mils (1.1-1.5 mm) | ASTM D4434 (PVC), D6878 (TPO) | Puncture resistance, longevity |

## Philippine Construction Context

Philippine construction heavily relies on GI corrugated roofing in residential and light commercial sectors due to lower material cost and minimal fabrication complexity. The tropical maritime climate with high salt spray (especially near coastal zones) makes G90 coating essential; G60 (0.60 oz/ft²) results in premature rust. Annual rainfall exceeding 2000 mm in many regions demands fastidious slope design and overlapping sheet length (minimum 150 mm lap for horizontal joints, 200 mm for vertical). Major Philippine brands include DN Steel, SteelAsia (formerly Pag-asa Steel), Union Galvasteel Corporation, and Steelworld Manufacturing, all of which dominate the market with consistent ASTM compliance. Thermal comfort in un-insulated GI roofs drives adoption of reflective coatings (high emissivity finish) to reduce interior temperature rise.


<ArticleMedia id="media-roof-slope-comparison" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison diagram showing roof slope requirements for different roofing materials: GI sheets, clay tiles, concrete tiles, asphalt shingles, standing seam, and green roofs"
  caption="Future chart: roof slope requirements by roofing material type"
  suggestedAsset="Comparison diagram or chart of minimum slopes per material"
  placementIntent="Helps learners match roofing materials to roof slope requirements" />
## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Gauge & Thickness Conversion** — "A roof specification calls for Gauge 24 GI corrugated sheets per ASTM A653. What is the approximate thickness in millimeters?" (Answer: 0.61 mm; tests conversion familiarity and standard knowledge.)

**Pattern 2: Material Selection for Climate** — "For a coastal residential project in Batangas exposed to salt spray, which GI coating specification is required?" (Answer: G90 or Z275; tests understanding of corrosion factors in tropical maritime zones.)

**Pattern 3: Slope Requirement** — "A flat roof design must accommodate a 1000 m² area with a minimum slope for water drainage. What is the minimum slope per NSCP 2015?" (Answer: 1/4:12 or 2%; tests code knowledge for low-slope roofs.)

**Pattern 4: Material Comparison** — "Compare the structural implications of upgrading from Gauge 26 to Gauge 24 GI roofing on rafter spacing. What is the stress reduction factor?" (Answer: Approximately 33% increase in bending capacity; tests understanding of material strength relationships.)

<Tip>Memorize gauge-to-thickness pairs: Gauge 26 = 0.46 mm, Gauge 24 = 0.61 mm, Gauge 22 = 0.76 mm. Remember ASTM A653 G90 = Z275 metric equivleant. In tropical zones, default to G90 unless project budget forces G60.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing gauge numbers with thickness: assuming Gauge 30 is thicker than Gauge 26." correction="Lower gauge numbers indicate thicker material. Gauge 26 (0.46 mm) is standard; Gauge 30 (0.31 mm) is thinner and not used for primary roofing in Philippines." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Selecting G60 coating for coastal salt-air exposure without verification of project lifecycle costs." correction="G90 (275 g/m²) is mandatory for tropical maritime climates. G60 premature rust negates any first-cost savings over 20+ year service life." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Using minimum slope of 1/4:12 for non-draining flat roofs without sump pumps", "Ignoring sheet overlap length (150 mm horizontal, 200 mm vertical) in slope calculations", "Applying asphalt shingle specs to tropical zones without 3-5 year lifecycle planning"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Roofing, Waterproofing, and Insulation: **lea-matl-006-02-core-concept**, **lea-matl-006-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-006-04-core-concept**, **lea-matl-006-05-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Embodied carbon measures greenhouse gas emissions generated
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA ## Learning Goal Define embodied carbon and explain how material extraction, manufacturing, transportation, and installation contribute to a building's total carbon footprint, and identify strategies to reduce embodied carbon through material selection and specification. ## Core Concept Embodied carbon measures greenhouse gas emissions generated during material extraction, processing, manufacturing, transport, and end-of-life disposal. Low-embodied-carbon materials either reduce emissions through efficient processing (recycled steel via electric arc furnace) or substitute high-impact materials with waste products (fly ash replacing Portland cement). The LEA focuses on three strategies: material substitution, recycling processes, and carbon sequestration in organic materials. Recycled steel produced via electric arc furnace (EAF) generates approximately 0.9-1.1 kg CO2e per kg of material versus 1.8-2.0 kg CO2e per kg via blast oxygen furnace (BOF), representing roughly 50 percent lower emissions. Fly ash (Class F or Class C per ASTM C618) replaces 15-30 percent of Portland cement in concrete, reducing embodied carbon by 20-40 percent. Timber sequesters carbon during growth, storing approximately 0.46 kg CO2e per kg in the material itself. ## Key Provisions Recycled Steel (EAF)0.9-1.1ASTM A996 (deformed bars)Reinforcement Portland Cement Concrete0.11-0.15ASTM C150 (Type I/II cement)Structural Concrete with Fly Ash0.08-0.10ASTM C618 (Class F/C)20-40% reduction vs pure cement Timber (Softwood)-0.46 (sequestered)ASTM D245 (stress grading)Carbon sink; net negative when burned Recycled Concrete Aggregate0.04-0.06ASTM C33 (grading limits)Base course; non-structural fill Aluminum (primary)8.24ASTM B221 (extrusions)Cladding; not structural in concrete Ground Granulated Blast Furnace Slag (GGBS)0.06-0.08ASTM C98930-50% cement replacement Class F fly ash is derived from burning anthracite or bituminous coal, contains 50-70 percent silica, and requires 15-25 percent dosage by weight in concrete for pozzolanic reaction. Class C fly ash (from lignite or subbituminous coal) contains 20-40 percent calcium oxide, self-cements as well as reacts pozzolani­cally, and is dosed at 20-35 percent. Ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) is a cooled byproduct of iron smelting meeting ASTM C989, contributing both pozzolanic and cementitious properties at 30-50 percent replacement rates. Recycled aggregates (coarse and fine) must meet ASTM C33 gradation limits and are acceptable for non-structural applications (fill, base course) when absorption and durability are verified. Reclaimed wood from demolished structures is reused as framing timber when no chemical treatment is detected; treated wood reclamation requires specialized processing to avoid contamination. Recycled plastic lumber is manufactured from post-consumer polyethylene or polypropylene, does not meet structural loading standards of ASTM D2105, and is primarily used for non-structural applications (decking, signage, landscaping components). ## Philippine Construction Context The Philippines generates approximately 2.78 million tonnes of coal fly ash annually from power plants in Calaca (Batangas) and Mauban (Quezon) operated under PSALM (Power Sector Assets and Liabilities Management Corporation). Pozzolanic Philippines Inc. operates a classifying plant at Calaca Power Plant, supplying low-ignition fly ash meeting local specifications. Adoption of fly ash concrete reduces both embodied carbon and material costs, aligning with Green Building Code provisions promoting waste utilization. DENR (Department of Environment and Natural Resources) timber harvest restrictions and DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) acceptance of alternative materials have driven increased specification of coco lumber, bamboo, and recycled aggregate in construction. Rice hull ash, a byproduct of rice milling, serves as a secondary pozzolan in some regional specifications, though standardization remains inconsistent across provinces. BERDE (Building for Ecologically Responsive Design Excellence) version 5 allocates 8-9 percent of points to sustainable materials credits, with documented embodied carbon reductions earning certification points. Buildings achieving 15-20 percent reduction in structural embodied carbon may qualify for additional green building tax incentives under RA 9729 (Climate Change Act) provisions. ## How It's Tested LEA candidates must identify material types by embodied carbon value, match pozzolanic materials to ASTM specifications, calculate percentage reductions in concrete embodied carbon when fly ash or GGBS replaces Portland cement, and apply replacement rate limits. Questions typically present a structural design scenario requiring 30 percent cost reduction while maintaining strength; the correct answer involves substituting 25 percent fly ash (within ASTM C618 Class F limits) without compromising concrete compressive strength or durability. A second test approach compares environmental product declarations (EPDs) for equivalent materials: candidates select the option with lowest cradle-to-gate embodied carbon or recognize that recycled steel embodied carbon is roughly half that of primary steel. Calculation questions require converting percentage replacement (25% fly ash) to embodied carbon reduction using provided baseline values (e.g., cement = 0.82 kg CO2e/kg; fly ash = 0.15 kg CO2e/kg; reduction = ~37%). Always verify embodied carbon values from published EPDs or lifecycle assessment databases (ICE, OneClick LCA) rather than assuming values. The actual CO2e per kilogram varies by manufacturing location, process efficiency, and transport distance. When a question provides a baseline embodied carbon for concrete (0.11 kg CO2e/kg), multiply by the percentage cement content and the percentage fly ash replacement to calculate net reduction. ## Common Mistakes When asked to specify recycled steel for low embodied carbon, candidates incorrectly state that all recycled steel has equal emissions. In reality, EAF (electric arc furnace) steel achieves 0.9-1.1 kg CO2e/kg via electrical melting of scrap, while BOF (blast oxygen furnace) primary steel requires 1.8-2.0 kg CO2e/kg using iron ore and coke. Recycled steel via EAF is roughly 50 percent lower carbon and is the preferred specification for low-embodied-carbon projects. Class F fly ash is limited to 15-25 percent dosage by weight in structural concrete per ASTM C618 guidelines; Class C is 20-35 percent. Candidates sometimes specify 40-50 percent fly ash replacement, which may result in slower early strength gain and reduced durability due to incomplete pozzolanic reaction. Always confirm replacement percentage aligns with concrete strength class and early-age strength requirements. Recycled concrete aggregates (RCA) can substitute for virgin aggregates in non-structural fill and base courses when meeting ASTM C33 gradation. However, RCA exhibits higher absorption (3-8%) versus virgin aggregate (0.5-1%), affecting long-term durability and strength. Recycled aggregates are not suitable for primary structural concrete without additional testing and strength verification; candidates must recognize this limitation to avoid over-specifying reuse.
  • Forgetting to multiply cement content (%) by cement embodied carbon (kg CO2e/kg) before calculating reduction
  • Confusing kilograms of material with percentage composition in a concrete mix design
  • Assuming zero embodied carbon for fly ash or slag (they have small positive values, ~0.05-0.15 kg CO2e/kg)
  • Applying the same embodied carbon value to both Class F and Class C fly ash (Class C typically has 10-15% higher emissions due to calcium oxide content)
  • Using embodied carbon values from international databases without accounting for local transport distance and fuel type in the Philippines
    •  ## Related Articles See also within Sustainable and Green Materials: **lea-matl-005-05-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-08-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-09-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-10-core-concept**. > **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Live load (LL)
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define live load in the seismic context as part of the effective seismic weight (W)
- Distinguish between full live load and reduced live load for seismic mass calculation
- Explain why only a portion of live load is included in seismic weight
- State the NSCP percentage of live load used in seismic weight for typical occupancies

Live loads (floor occupancy loads) are the responsibility of the occupant, not the designer. The NSCP specifies minimum live load values for design; the occupant must not exceed them. Partition loads (dead load from non-structural walls) must be added if partitions are present or anticipated. Storage loads can be severe and override standard floor loads if the space will contain stored materials.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-004-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Live Load Values — NSCP Table 202 Minimum Occupancy Loads" description="Reference diagram showing common NSCP live load values organized by occupancy: Residential (1.9 kPa), Office (2.4 kPa), Corridors (3.8 kPa), Assembly fixed seats (2.9 kPa), Assembly no fixed seats (4.8 kPa), Light storage (6.0 kPa), Heavy storage (12.0 kPa), Flat roof (1.0 kPa). Live load reduction rule illustrated with tributary area ≥18.6 m² threshold." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

_Live load_ (LL) is the load exerted by occupancy, equipment, and temporary activities on a floor. It is distinct from dead load (permanent structural weight). The NSCP provides a table of minimum live load values for different occupancy types, measured in kPa (kiloPascals):

| Occupancy Type | Minimum LL (kPa) |
|---|---|
| Residential (apartments, houses) | 1.9 |
| Office | 2.4 |
| Corridors (above 1st floor) | 3.8 |
| Assembly (fixed seating) | 2.9 |
| Assembly (no fixed seating) | 4.8 |
| Construction walkway | 7.0 |
| Storage (light) | 6.0 |
| Storage (heavy) | 12.0 |

These are _minimum_ values. If the occupant uses the space differently (e.g., a residential unit converted to office, an office space used for storage), the higher live load applies.

_Tributary area_ is the floor area that drains into a structural member. The NSCP permits _live load reduction_ (a discount factor) when the tributary area exceeds a threshold (typically 14 m² for standard buildings). The reduction is calculated as:LL(reduced) = L0 × (0.25 + 15 / √(K_LL × A_I)) per NSCP 205.5, where A_I is influence area and K_LL is live load element factor.m². The reduction recognizes that the probability of all floor occupants loading simultaneously is low in large open areas; a percentage of seats will be empty, some desks unmanned. Small areas (< 14 m²) get no reduction because every seat/desk occupant contributes to the total.

_Fixed partition load_ is the dead load of non-structural walls (drywall, insulation, cladding, etc.). If partitions are present or anticipated (e.g., an office floor that might be subdivided later), the code requires a minimum partition load of 1.0 kPa be added to the design. This accounts for the weight of walls that will eventually be installed.

_Live load responsibility_ is a legal and moral one. The NSCP specifies design minimums; the building owner/occupant is responsible for ensuring actual use does not exceed the assumed design live load. If a residential unit is converted to office, the floor was not designed for the higher 2.4 kPa office load and may fail. Violations of this responsibility lead to structural distress, collapse, and legal liability.

## Key Provisions

| Parameter | Value / Rule | LEA Context |
|-----------|--------------|-------------|
| Residential LL | 1.9 kPa | Apartments, single-family homes |
| Office LL | 2.4 kPa | Typical commercial office space |
| Corridors (above 1st floor) | 3.8 kPa | Circulation; higher than floor LL |
| Assembly fixed | 2.9 kPa | Theaters, auditoriums with fixed seating |
| Assembly no fixed seating | 4.8 kPa | Concert halls, dance floors, gathering spaces |
| Construction walkway | 7.2 kPa | Temporary loads during construction |
| Storage light | 6.0 kPa | Books, light materials |
| Storage heavy | 12.0 kPa | Steel, machinery, dense materials; severe |
| Fixed partition | 1.0 kPa minimum | Dead load; add if partitions present/anticipated |
| LL reduction threshold | 14 m² tributary area | Areas > 14 m² may apply reduction formula |
| Economic housing (BP 220) max floor area | 60 m² per unit | Applies to BP 220 projects; NSCP LL still 1.9 kPa regardless of size |

The distinction between occupancy categories is critical. A 2.4 kPa office floor cannot safely accommodate 4.8 kPa assembly loads or 12.0 kPa storage loads. Occupancy changes require structural re-evaluation.

## Philippine Practice Context

In Metro Manila, mixed-use developments often blend residential, office, retail, and parking on a single structure. Design floors must accommodate the highest live load of any intended occupancy on that floor. A typical scenario: ground floor (4.8 kPa assembly for lobbies/shops), floors 2–5 (office 2.4 kPa), floors 6–20 (residential 1.9 kPa with 1.0 kPa partition allowance). Partition load is essential because office-to-residential conversion mid-project is common; designers anticipate this and add 1.0 kPa at design time.

Low-cost housing (60 m² maximum per unit, per Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board guidelines) is designed at residential 1.9 kPa. However, occupants sometimes add improper loads (heavy storage, equipment installations) that exceed this assumption, leading to visible sagging and code violations. The designer specifies the LL assumption; the occupant/owner is bound by it.

Storage facilities (warehouses) in industrial zones require 12.0 kPa if heavy materials might be stacked. A common error: designing a "flexible" warehouse at only 6.0 kPa (light storage) to save cost, then loading it with machinery (12.0 kPa equivalent) once in operation. This violates the occupant's responsibility and risks collapse.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Live load table lookup.** "What is the minimum design live load for an office building in the Philippines?" → 2.4 kPa (from the table).

**Pattern 2: Occupancy mismatch.** "A residential floor is designed for 1.9 kPa LL. The owner later converts it to office storage. Is this compliant?" → No. Office storage exceeds residential load. Structural re-design or use restriction required.

**Pattern 3: Partition load reasoning.** "Why must a 1.0 kPa partition load be included in an office floor design if no partitions are built initially?" → Because partitions will likely be installed later when offices are subdivided. The 1.0 kPa reserves capacity for this predictable change.

**Pattern 4: Tributary area and reduction.** "A column supports a 20 m² tributary area on a residential floor. Can live load reduction be applied?" → Yes, because 20 m² > 14 m² threshold. Calculate the reduction factor.

<Tip>Live load defaults to the table value. Partitions always add 1.0 kPa (if anticipated). Storage can be 2–6× the occupancy LL if heavy materials are present. The occupant's use is the occupant's responsibility—the designer provides the capacity, not the police.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Load Types** (lea-strc-001-02) for the complete live load discussion, **Base Shear** (lea-strc-004-03) for how seismic weight enters the formula, and **Required Strength** (lea-strc-005-01) for how live load factors into combinations.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

rows.title: Code of Ethical Conduct
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

- Explain the architect's primary obligation to public health, safety, and welfare as the foundational ethical duty.
- Identify the prohibition on misrepresenting qualifications, experience, or expertise.
- Describe the affirmative duty to report illegal practice, unlicensed individuals, and professional misconduct.
- Apply public-obligation ethical standards to LEA scenarios involving code violations, misrepresentation, and reporting duties.

The architect's primary obligation to the public transcends individual projects — it encompasses a duty to maintain public health and safety, represent qualifications honestly, and report violations of professional standards that endanger the community.

## Core Concept

The Code of Ethical Conduct establishes that architects carry **civic responsibilities to the public** regardless of whether these arise from good citizenship or professional practice. This foundational obligation precedes client interests and contractual relationships. The architect must advance the safety, health, and well-being of people and communities through competent practice and honest representation.

The obligation has three critical dimensions. First, architects must maintain uncompromising standards for health, safety, and welfare in all work — this is absolute and non-negotiable. Second, architects cannot misrepresent their qualifications, experience, or expertise in any communication. Third, architects must actively report when they encounter illegal practice, unlicensed individuals posing as architects, or professional misconduct that endangers the public.

<LawCallout code="ra9266" section="Section 1-a, 1-c, 1-d, 1-f" title="Public Obligation Under the Code">
Section 1-a requires architects to "advance the safety, health and well-being of the people and the community" and contribute to preservation of architectural heritage. Section 1-c requires compliance with government laws and regulations as a good citizen. Section 1-d prohibits paid advertisements and self-laudatory publicity. Section 1-f prohibits misrepresentation of qualifications unless backed by recognized expertise.
</LawCallout>


<ArticleMedia id="media-eth003-public-obligations" layout="single" variant="contained" type="image" status="placeholder" aspectRatio="16:9" title="Duties to the Public — Obligation Hierarchy" alt="Funnel diagram showing the three critical dimensions of public obligation: (1) maintain uncompromising standards for health/safety/welfare, (2) no misrepresentation of qualifications, (3) affirmative duty to report illegal practice. Each dimension shows the Code section reference and example violations. Callout emphasizes public welfare supersedes all commercial interests." placementIntent="ethics-framework" suggestedSearchQuery="architect duties to public health safety welfare reporting illegal practice Code of Ethics Section 1" suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" />
Section 1-a of the Code establishes the public obligation as the broadest category — it supersedes all commercial interests. An architect cannot prioritize profit, convenience, or client demands if doing so compromises public safety.

Section 1-c requires compliance with government laws and regulations as a good citizen. This creates dual accountability: both to professional standards and to civil law. An architect who becomes aware of building code violations, illegal construction, or unlicensed practitioners must report these matters, even if the client requests silence.

## Key Provisions

| Provision | Source | LEA Relevance |
|-----------|--------|---------------|
| Advance safety, health, well-being | Code §1-a, RA 9266 §3 | Primary public obligation — absolute priority |
| Do not misrepresent qualifications | Code §1-f, RA 9266 §29 | Cannot claim specializations without professional consensus/years of experience |
| Abide by government laws/regulations | Code §1-c | Dual obligation to laws AND professional code |
| No paid advertisements or endorsements | Code §1-d, §1-e | Cannot solicit ads; cannot endorse building materials for compensation |
| Report illegal practice | Implicit in §1-c, §1-a | Affirmative duty when aware of violations |
| Factual materials permitted | Code §1-d | Can present factual aims/standards/progress through literature/work quality |
| Preserve architectural heritage | Code §1-a | Obligation to protect historic examples |

## Philippine Practice Context

Under RA 9266, architects registered in the Philippines assume specific public duties. Architects must report to the Board of Architecture any unlicensed individuals claiming to practice architecture — failure to report constitutes complicity in unauthorized practice. The professional identification card and signature/seal signify that the architect has personally verified compliance with safety and code requirements. In government practice, architects cannot permit non-architects to perform architectural work under the architect's seal; this protects the public from incompetent design.

The Board has emphasized that architects cannot shield themselves behind "following client instructions" when public safety is compromised. An architect who signs sealed plans containing unsafe design bears full responsibility and may face suspension or revocation under RA 9266 §23.

<Warn>
  **Exam Trap:** A common LEA distracter suggests that "following client instructions" or "the client approved the design" absolves the architect of public safety responsibility. This is WRONG. The architect's public obligation under Section 1-a is absolute and non-delegable. The architect cannot hide behind client approval when public safety is compromised. Section 23 makes the architect-of-record fully liable for sealed plans regardless of client instructions.
</Warn>

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Misrepresentation Scenarios**
An architect includes "30 years hospital design experience" when he has 5 years. This violates §1-f because specializations must be "well known facts or sanctioned by professional consensus and years of experience."

**Pattern 2: Safety vs. Profit Conflict**
Client demands cost reduction that compromises building safety. Architect's obligation? Code §1-a and §2-c require the architect to advise the client against proceeding; this overrides commission loss.

**Pattern 3: Reporting Obligation**
Architect discovers unlicensed person preparing architectural drawings. Must report under Code §1-c (abide by laws) and RA 9266 §29 (prohibition on unauthorized practice). Silence makes architect complicit.

**Pattern 4: Paid Endorsements**
Building material manufacturer offers fee for architect to endorse product. Code §1-e prohibits this. Code §4-b allows only "marker discount which shall be credited to the Client" — no commissions.

<ExamTip>
  **LEA Priority:** Questions about "public obligation" almost always test the hierarchy — public safety trumps client profit. The "PSR" mnemonic helps: (P) Public safety above all else, (S) Specializations require credentials, (R) Report violations. When an LEA question involves a conflict between profit and public welfare, public welfare always wins.
</ExamTip>

<Tip>**Memory Aid: "PSR" = Public Safety Reporting.** Remember the three core elements: (P) Public safety above all else, (S) Specializations require credentials, (R) Report violations. When an LEA question involves a conflict between profit and public welfare, public welfare always wins.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
  mistakes={[
    "Thinking paid advertisements are allowed if factual — Code §1-d explicitly prohibits 'paid advertisement' and self-laudatory publicity; only unpaid presentation of work through literature is permitted",
    "Assuming qualification disclaimers work — 'I have experience in...' does not satisfy §1-f; specializations must be 'well-known facts or sanctioned by professional consensus and years of experience'",
    "Confusing client obligation with public obligation — §1-c public duty to laws and professional standards applies even when client requests otherwise",
    "Believing that following client instructions shields architects from public safety responsibility — RA 9266 §23 makes the architect-of-record fully liable for sealed plans",
    "Treating reporting violations as optional — Code §1-c is mandatory; silence about illegal practice is a violation itself",
  ]}
/>

---

## Related Articles

- [RA 9266: Legal Framework](lea-prac-law-001)
- [Prohibited Acts and Penalties](lea-prac-law-003)
- [Grounds for Suspension and Revocation](lea-prac-eth-008)

rows.title: Landscape architecture
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Integrate plants, hardscapes, water features, and spatial organization into outdoor environments, select appropriate plant materials for Philippine tropical conditions, apply zoning strategies for landscape areas, and coordinate hardscape with softscape.

Landscape architecture integrates plants, hardscapes, water features, and spatial organization to create outdoor environments that enhance site functionality, aesthetics, and ecological health.
Understanding plant selection, zoning strategies, and the relationship between hardscape and softscape is essential to comprehensive site planning.

## Core Concept

Landscape architecture is the design and planning of outdoor space.
It bridges architecture, ecology, and urban design by creating places where people interact with nature.
Within site planning, landscape architecture serves multiple functions simultaneously: stormwater management, microclimatic control, habitat creation, visual placemaking, and recreational opportunity.
**Plant Selection for Climate and Resilience:**

In Philippine practice, tropical landscape design must account for:

- High humidity and intense monsoon rainfall
- Salt spray exposure in coastal sites
- Volcanic soil conditions in some regions
- Intense solar radiation year-round
- Flood and typhoon resilience requirements

Native species (trees, shrubs, groundcovers) are preferred because they require minimal irrigation, withstand local pests, and support biodiversity.
Common Philippine tropical species include narra (Pterocarpus indicus), calamansi (Citrus microcarpa), sampaguita (Jasminum sambac), and various bamboo species.
Non-native species may require more maintenance and irrigation, increasing site operating costs.
**Hardscape vs. Softscape:**

- **Softscape:** Plants, soil, water features, mulch. Provides biodiversity, stormwater absorption, shade, microclimate control, and visual warmth.
  Requires maintenance (pruning, watering, fertilization).
- **Hardscape:** Paving, walls, structures, furniture.
  Provides durability, low maintenance, clear spatial definition, and water drainage (when properly sloped).
  Can absorb heat and create urban heat island effect if excessive.

Balanced hardscape-softscape integration is critical.
Excessive hardscape creates hot, sterile sites; excessive softscape becomes unkempt and expensive to maintain.
**Outdoor Rooms and Spatial Organization:**

Landscape design organizes outdoor space into functional zones or "rooms"—gathering spaces, activity zones, buffer areas, and transition spaces.
Each room serves distinct purposes: seating areas for social gathering, play areas for recreation, circulation zones for movement, buffer zones for privacy and noise reduction.
This zoning improves usability, social equity, and environmental performance.

**Open Space Programming (PD 1216, PD 957, and PD 1096):**

For residential subdivisions, PD 1216 defines open space as an area reserved for parks, playgrounds, and recreational use.
Under PD 1216 (amending PD 957), subdivisions with an area of one (1) hectare or more must allocate a percentage of gross area for parks and playgrounds based on density:

- 20 lots or below per hectare: 3.5%
- 21 to 25 lots per hectare: 4.0%
- 65 lots and above per hectare: 9.0%
  At the individual lot level, the National Building Code (Rule VIII) governs the Total Open Space within Lot (TOSL). For example, a 15m × 20m (300 sqm) R-1 lot typically requires an Unpaved Surface Area (USA) of 20% to 30% depending on whether it is an interior or corner lot. This space must be:
- Accessible to all residents
- Programmed for actual use (not merely leftover land)
- Connected by walkways and seating
- Protected from future encroachment

**Stormwater Management Through Landscape:**

Landscape features can slow, filter, and infiltrate stormwater:

- **Bioretention basins:** Rain gardens that absorb water and filter pollutants
- **Permeable paving:** Allows water infiltration instead of runoff
- **Swleas and berms:** Graded landforms that channel water and reduce velocity
- **Tree trenches:** Allows tree roots to access and filter stormwater

This reduces
strain on municipal storm sewers and improves water quality.

**Microclimate Control:**

Strategic planting modifies site climate:

- Trees create shade, reducing air temperature and cooling building interiors
- Vegetation increases humidity in arid zones
- Wind-breaks (shelter belts) reduce wind speed for comfort and energy savings
- Water features create cooling through evaporation
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-04-core-concept" type="image" caption="Landscape Design — Planting, Hardscape, and Spatial Organization" description="Landscape plan showing: plant material selection (Philippine tropical species), hardscape zones (walkways, plazas, patios), water features, spatial organization (open, semi-private, private), and zoning strategy for different outdoor use areas." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

|
Element | Typical Application | Design Consideration | Source |
|---------|---|---|---|
| Native Trees | Shade, structure, wildlife |
Species suited to local climate and soil | DENR/BFP Guidelines |
| Understory Shrubs | Privacy, separation, color |
Non-invasive, pest-resistant species | Horticultural Standards |
| Groundcovers | Bank stabilization, erosion control | Deep-rooted, drought-tolerant species |
Soil & Water Conservation |
| Permeable Paving | Hardscape with infiltration | Slope minimum 2% for drainage |
Stormwater Best Practices |
| Bioretention Basins | Stormwater absorption | 1–1.5m depth, underdrain for poor soils |
EPA Stormwater Manual |
| Seating Areas | Social gathering |
Sized per actual density/programming | PD 1216 / PD 957 |
| Pedestrian Connectivity |
Movement and access | Continuous, accessible pathways (BP 344) | Accessibility Standards |
**Open Space Allocation Summary:**

- Subdivisions (1 ha+): 3.5% to 9% for Parks/Playgrounds (PD 1216)
- Individual Lots: TOSL/USA varies by NBC Rule VIII (e.g., 20-30% for R-1)
- General Practice: Non-sleaable area often totals ~30% but is density-dependent

**Native Species Examples (Philippine Context):**

- Trees: Narra, Pili, Mango, Yakal, Molave, Malunggay
- Shrubs: Santan, Talinum, Ilang-ilang (Ylang-ylang)
- Groundcovers: Vetiver grass, Philippine sedge, native ferns
- Benefits: adapted to local climate, low irrigation need, wildlife value

## Philippine Practice Context

Philippine landscape architecture must respond to tropical conditions: high rainfall, salt spray near coasts, and typhoon exposure.
The National Greening Program encourages native species and reforestation. Barangay ordinances often mandate open space preservation and tree planting in new developments.
Urban heat island effects in Metro Manila drive demand for shade trees and green walls.
The integration of landscape with stormwater management (bioretention basins, permeable paving) is increasingly required in environmental compliance.
Indigenous plants reduce costs over the project lifecycle by minimizing irrigation and chemical inputs.
Community organizing around open spaces strengthens social cohesion in residential subdivisions, particularly when landscape is accessible and well-maintained.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Open Space Allocation and Compliance**
A 50,000 m² (5-hectare) subdivision is proposed with a density of 25 lots per hectare.
Using PD 1216 standards, calculate the minimum area required for parks and playgrounds (4.0% of 50,000 m² = 2,000 m²). Determine if the proposed site plan complies with the density-specific mandate.
**Pattern 2: Plant Selection for Site Conditions**
Given a site description (coastal exposure, seasonal flooding, acidic volcanic soil, steep slope), select appropriate native species that thrive under those conditions and explain their benefits for site resilience.
**Pattern 3: Hardscape-Softscape Balance**
A site plan shows 70% paving and 30% planting.
Assess whether this balance is appropriate for a residential neighborhood (where shade and social space are priorities) vs. a logistics facility (where durability and accessibility dominate).
Recommend adjustments.

**Pattern 4: Stormwater Management Integration**
Design a bioretention basin to handle a 50m × 20m catchment area sloping at 5%.
Estimate basin depth, infiltration rate, and planted species to achieve volume absorption and water quality improvement.
**Pattern 5: Outdoor Room Zoning**
A 10,000 m² park is planned.
Identify distinct functional zones (gathering, activity, buffer, circulation) and specify landscape treatments (paving, planting, furnishings) for each zone to support the intended uses.

<Tip>
  **Open Space Memory Aid:** PD 1216 = Parks/Playgrounds are density-based
  (3.5%-9%). NBC Rule VIII = Lot-level open space (TOSL). Native plants =
  tropical adapted, less irrigation, higher resilience. Hardscape + softscape =
  balanced design. Bioretention = stormwater + green space synergy.
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Plant selection criteria: Philippine climate (tropical wet/dry), microclimate (sun/shade/wind), soil conditions (pH/drainage), maintenance level, mature size (don't overplant), and root system (avoid foundation damage).
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-04-core-concept" type="image" caption="Landscape Zoning — Hardscape, Softscape, and Water Features" description="Landscape master plan showing zoning strategies: entry/arrival plaza (hardscape dominant), central lawn and gathering spaces (softscape/passive recreation), perimeter planting buffer (native species screens), water features (rain garden, reflecting pool), and path system connecting zones. Plant species selected for Philippine tropical conditions." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-005-01** (Landscape Design) for landscape fundamentals, **LEA-PLAN-005-02** (Native Species) for Philippine plant selection, and **LEA-DSGN-012-02** (Site Development) for landscape in site planning.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Using a blanket 30% rule for parks; PD 1216 requirement is density-dependent (3.5% to 9%)","Confusing subdivision-wide open space (PD 1216) with individual lot open space (NBC Rule VIII)","Allocating open space but leaving it undeveloped/unprogrammed (must be usable and accessible)","Overplanting tropical sites with non-native species that require excessive irrigation and pest management","Ignoring stormwater integration; treating landscape as purely aesthetic rather than functional","Calculating open space as percentage of buildable area instead of gross area","Failing to design accessible connections (BP 344) within and between open spaces","Underestimating tree root space; 
planting in constrained trenches causes failure and maintenance costs"]} />

rows.title: Architect's Guidelines (formerly 1979 UAP Doc 208-b
rows.content:
## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define urban design and planning as an architectural service.
- Describe the architect's role in site planning, subdivision design, and community planning.
- Explain the regulatory framework: HLURB, DPWH, LGU ordinances.
- Distinguish urban design from architectural building design.

The LEA tests your ability to identify the six methods of compensation, match each method to the service category where it applies, and compute fees using the MDPE formula and percentage-of-PCC method. Expect questions that present a project scenario and ask which compensation method is appropriate — or that require you to calculate the MDPE fee using the multiplier formula.

## Core Concept

The Architect's Guidelines (formerly 1979 UAP Doc 208-b, Methods of Compensation) establish **six methods of compensation** for architectural services. These methods are not contained in a single standalone SPP document — they are distributed across individual SPP documents (SPP 201 through SPP 209), with each document specifying the appropriate compensation method for its service category.

Understanding all six methods and knowing which SPP document calls for which method is a core LEA competency. The architect selects the compensation method based on the nature of the service, the project delivery method, and the ability to define scope in advance.

### The Six Methods of Compensation

**Method 1 — Percentage of Project Construction Cost (PCC)** calculates the architect's fee as a percentage of the estimated or actual construction cost. This is the primary method for **Regular Design Services under SPP 202**. The percentage is determined by the project's classification group (Groups 1–10 under the Architect's Guidelines). This method aligns architect compensation with project scope — as PCC increases, the fee increases proportionally (subject to the sliding scale for Groups 1–3).

**Method 2 — Multiple of Direct Personnel Expense (MDPE)** calculates the fee using the formula:

<Callout>Fee = ((manhour × rate) × multiplier) + reimbursable expenses</Callout>

The multiplier ranges from **1.5 to 2.5**, depending on office set-up costs, overhead, the architect's experience, and the complexity of the project. MDPE is the primary method for **Pre-Design Services under SPP 201**, **Group 10 (Technical Expertise)** projects, and services where scope cannot be precisely defined in advance. It is also used for **Comprehensive Design and Planning** under SPP 203.

**Method 3 — Professional Fee + Expenses** establishes a fixed professional fee with actual expenses billed separately. This method is used for **single-architect project series** — engagements where one architect handles a defined set of projects. The professional fee covers the architect's expertise; expenses (travel, reproduction, communications) are reimbursed at cost.

**Method 4 — Per Diem + Reimbursable Expenses** compensates the architect on a daily rate basis plus actual out-of-pocket expenses. This method suits short-duration consulting engagements, site visits, expert testimony, and advisory services where the engagement period is known but the total effort is uncertain.

**Method 5 — Lump Sum or Fixed Fee** establishes a single predetermined amount for a defined scope of services. This method is commonly used for **government projects** and situations requiring price certainty. It demands more extensive paperwork and scope definition upfront. The Architect's Guidelines note this method is "more paperwork and time-consuming" because the scope must be precisely defined to prevent disputes.

**Method 6 — Mixed Methods of Compensation** combines two or more of the above methods within a single engagement. This approach is appropriate when a project involves multiple service types requiring different compensation approaches — for example, percentage-of-PCC for design services combined with MDPE for pre-design consulting within the same commission.

### Which SPP Document Uses Which Method

Each SPP document specifies its recommended compensation method based on the nature of the service:

<WikiExamTable headers={["SPP Document", "Service", "Primary Compensation Method"]} rows={[["SPP 201", "Pre-Design Services", "MDPE"], ["SPP 202", "Regular Design Services", "% of PCC"], ["SPP 203", "Specialized Allied Services", "MDPE or % of PCC (varies by service)"], ["SPP 204-A", "Full-Time Supervision", "% of PCC or Lump Sum"], ["SPP 204-B", "Construction Management", "1.5–3% of PCC"], ["SPP 205", "Post-Construction Services", "4–6% of gross rentals or monthly salary"], ["SPP 206", "Comprehensive Services", "2–5% of PCC"], ["SPP 207 (Admin)", "Design-Build by Administration", "7% of PCC"], ["SPP 207 (GMC)", "Design-Build by Guaranteed Maximum Cost", "10% of PCC"]]} />

<Note>SPP 203 (Specialized Allied Services) uses different methods depending on the specific service: Architectural Interiors uses percentage of work cost, Acoustic Design Services depends on work complexity, Site Development Planning uses estimated civil work cost, and Comprehensive Design and Planning uses MDPE.</Note>

### Methods of Selection

The Architect's Guidelines also establish **three methods of selecting an architect**, which precede the compensation discussion:

| Method | Application |
| ------ | ----------- |
| Direct Selection | Used for residential projects |
| Comparative Selection | Used for institutions, corporations, or public agencies |
| Design Competition | Used for civic or monumental projects |

## Key Provisions

| Method | Formula/Basis | Best Used When |
| ------ | ------------- | -------------- |
| % of PCC | Fee = PCC × group percentage | Scope correlates with construction cost (SPP 202) |
| MDPE | Fee = ((manhour × rate) × multiplier) + expenses | Scope is uncertain or effort-based (SPP 201, Group 10) |
| Professional Fee + Expenses | Fixed fee + actual expenses | Single-architect project series |
| Per Diem + Reimbursable | Daily rate + actual expenses | Short consulting engagements |
| Lump Sum / Fixed Fee | Predetermined total amount | Government projects, defined scope |
| Mixed Methods | Combination of above | Multi-service commissions |

## Philippine Practice Context

In Philippine private practice, the percentage-of-PCC method dominates for building design projects because most commissions fall under SPP 202 Regular Design Services. MDPE is increasingly used for specialized consulting and pre-design work where scope is difficult to define at engagement. For government projects procured under RA 9184 (Government Procurement Reform Act), lump sum or fixed fee is standard because government procurement requires price certainty before contract award. Architects engaged in both design and construction management for the same project typically use mixed methods — percentage-of-PCC for design phases and a separate fee structure for CM services.

## How It's Tested

The LEA tests compensation methods in three patterns. First, the exam presents a service type and asks which compensation method applies — the student must match the method to the correct SPP document. Second, the exam provides manhours, hourly rates, and a multiplier, then asks the student to compute the MDPE fee using the formula. Third, the exam describes a multi-service engagement and asks the student to identify which combination of methods would apply under the mixed methods approach.

<Tip>Remember the MDPE formula as **"MRM + R"**: Manhours × Rate × Multiplier, plus Reimbursables. The multiplier (1.5–2.5) covers overhead and profit — it is NOT a separate line item.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Citing 'SPP 210' or 'SPP Document 210' as the source of compensation methods — no such document exists; compensation methods are distributed across individual SPP documents and the Architect's Guidelines", "Confusing the MDPE multiplier (1.5–2.5) with the fee percentage — the multiplier applies to personnel cost, not to PCC", "Assuming all architectural services use percentage-of-PCC — pre-design services (SPP 201) and technical expertise (Group 10) use MDPE, not percentage of PCC", "Forgetting that lump sum/fixed fee is the standard method for government projects, not percentage-of-PCC"]} />

---

## Related Articles

- [SPP Doc 202 Six-Phase Framework](lea-prac-svc-004)
- [Schematic Design Phase](lea-prac-svc-005)
- [Design Development Phase](lea-prac-svc-006)
- [Contract Documents Phase](lea-prac-svc-007)
- [Bidding and Construction Admin](lea-prac-svc-008)
- [Pre-Design Services](lea-prac-svc-001)
- [Specialized Services](lea-prac-svc-009)
- [Design-Build Delivery](lea-prac-svc-019)
- [Fee Compensation Methods](lea-prac-cmp-001)

rows.title: Human settlement
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Apply the human settlements framework treating housing within a holistic system of livelihood, services, infrastructure, and community institutions, evaluate settlement sustainability, and apply carrying capacity concepts to settlement planning.

Human settlements development treats housing within a holistic framework: housing is one component of a settlement system that includes livelihood, services, infrastructure, and community institutions. This integrated approach differs from viewing housing as an isolated supply problem. Key concepts are sustainability, social cohesion, basic services access, and balancing growth with resource carrying capacity.

## Core Concept

A human settlement is an organized spatial cluster of residential, commercial, and civic functions with sufficient density and diversity to sustain economic and social life. Housing is essential but insufficient; human settlements require integrated planning of land use, infrastructure, livelihood opportunities, and community services.

The integrated settlement development approach emerged from recognition that housing projects in isolation—especially when relocated to distant sites without services or economic opportunity—fail. Successful settlements balance:

**Infrastructure Provision:** Water supply, sanitation, electricity, solid waste management, and transportation connectivity. Access to reliable water is foundational; informal settlements in flood-prone or water-scarce areas face chronic crisis. Sanitation systems (both sewage treatment and stormwater management) determine health outcomes. Transportation connectivity determines whether residents can access urban job centers.

**Livelihood Integration:** Settlements must provide or connect to employment opportunities. Relocated communities far from economic centers often experience economic collapse as breadwinners face impossible commutes or cannot access informal income activities. Successful settlements include markets, service areas, and light commercial zones. In-situ upgrading (versus relocation) preserves existing livelihood networks—vendors remain near customers, artisans retain client bases.

**Social Service Accessibility:** Schools, health clinics, day care, and community facilities must be within walking distance or short transit time. The Philippines' focus on in-situ upgrading via the Community Mortgage Program (SHFC/CMP) is grounded in this principle: upgrading existing communities preserves access to established schools, clinics, and social networks.

**Governance and Community Organization:** Settlements require functioning community institutions—barangay organization, community associations, dispute resolution mechanisms. Top-down housing projects that ignore existing community structures often fail. Participatory planning and community involvement in design and implementation are essential success factors.

**Environmental Sustainability:** Carrying capacity—the settlement's capacity to absorb waste, provide water, and function without degrading surrounding ecosystems—is a critical constraint. Settlements on flood plains, slope-hazard zones, or water-scarce areas face inherent sustainability limits. Environmental impact assessment (EIA under **PD 1586**) is increasingly required for large settlements.

**Disaster Risk Reduction:** Post-Yolanda (2013) and post-COVID frameworks emphasize resilience. Settlements must account for typhoon, flood, and seismic hazards. Post-Yolanda no-build zones (40m from mean high tide) reshape coastal settlement patterns. Climate-aware settlement planning is now mandatory in CLUP requirements under **RA 10121** (DRRM Act).

Human settlements development, at its core, views housing as a vector for achieving integrated community well-being—economic, social, environmental, and institutional—rather than as a supply shortage to be solved through construction volume alone.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-003-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Human Settlements Framework — Housing Within a Holistic System" description="Radial ecosystem diagram showing housing at center within: livelihood/employment, basic services (water, power, sanitation), infrastructure (roads, drainage, transport), community institutions (schools, health centers, markets). Carrying capacity limits for settlement planning." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers=["Settlement Component", "What It Requires", "Philippine Mechanism"] rows=[["**Infrastructure**", "Water, sanitation, electricity, solid waste, transport", "CLUP utilities section; ECC requirement (PD 1586); local utilities master plan"], ["**Livelihood Opportunities**", "Markets, commercial zones, access to employment centers", "CLUP land use mix; zoning for commercial/industrial; transit connectivity"], ["**Social Services**", "Schools, clinics, day care, community centers", "CLUP facility siting; DPWH service radius standards"], ["**Community Governance**", "Barangay organization, community associations", "RA 7160 LGU structure; RA 10121 DRRM local organization"], ["**Environmental Sustainability**", "Carrying capacity; disaster risk limits", "ECC requirement; RA 10121 DRRM integration in CLUP"], ["**Disaster Resilience**", "Hazard mapping; no-build zones; building typologies", "Post-Yolanda framework; PHIVOLCS data; CLUP hazard zones"]] />

## Philippine Context

The Philippines faces simultaneous pressures: rapid urbanization (cities growing 3–4% annually), massive informal settlement expansion (estimated 2–3 million informal households in Metro Manila), and limited government housing production capacity. The policy response since the 1990s has shifted toward integrated settlement development:

**RA 7279 (UDHA, 1992)** established the principle that evicted families must have access to adequate resettlement sites—not just housing, but sites with services and livelihood access. This was a major step, though implementation remains inconsistent.

**SHFC's Community Mortgage Program** operationalized in-situ upgrading at scale, recognizing that keeping communities in place preserves livelihoods and social capital.

**RA 10121 (DRRM Act, 2010)** mandated disaster risk reduction mainstreaming into CLUPs, requiring settlements to account for climate and seismic hazards.

**Post-Yolanda National Zoning Framework (2014)** imposed coastal no-build zones, reshaping how new coastal settlements can be planned.

The shift is from "housing as construction" toward "housing as integrated community development"—a change reflected in DHSUD's 2018 National Housing Strategy and ongoing CLUP updates.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1 — Integration Concept:** "Which is NOT a component of human settlements development?" → Questions test whether students grasp that livelihood, services, governance, and environmental constraints are equal to housing supply.

**Pattern 2 — In-Situ vs. Relocation:** "Why is in-situ upgrading preferred over relocation when possible?" → Preserves livelihood networks, community institutions, social capital, and reduces economic disruption. Test is conceptual, not procedural.

**Pattern 3 — Sustainability Constraints:** "A proposed settlement in a flood-prone area faces what primary integrated planning challenge?" → Not just housing design, but infrastructure resilience, livelihood vulnerability, and carrying capacity. Test integrates environmental and social factors.

<Tip>Human settlements = integrated system: housing + infrastructure + livelihood + services + governance + sustainability. In-situ upgrading preserves existing community systems.</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** A human settlement is NOT just housing. It requires: land use, infrastructure, livelihood, social services, and community institutions. The LEA tests whether you recognize that settlements are holistic systems, not just shelter.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-003-04** (Housing Production) for delivery methods, **LEA-PLAN-003-06** (Informal Settlements) for settlement upgrading, and **LEA-PLAN-005-04** (DRRM) for resilient settlement planning.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating human settlements development as synonymous with housing production (they are different: one is integrated; one is just construction)","Assuming relocation is always safer than in-situ upgrading (relocation can be more harmful to livelihoods and community cohesion)","Forgetting that livelihood access is a core settlement component (not peripheral; central to survival)","Neglecting disaster risk in settlement planning (climate/seismic hazards now mandatory CLUP components)","Believing CMP is just another housing finance program (it is fundamentally a settlement preservation and community development approach)"]} />

rows.title: Islamic architecture
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

<Callout>The LEA tests your ability to identify and explain the foundational architectural vocabulary of Islamic design. You must recognize the defining structural and decorative elements that appear across regional variations.</Callout>

## Learning Goal

Identify the five pillars of Islamic architectural vocabulary (Mosque, Minaret, Mihrab, Muqarnas, Arabesques/Calligraphy) by their function, form, and regional variation, and distinguish Islamic structural elements from decorative features.

## Core Concept


<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-004-01-courtyard-typology" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="Comparative diagram of four Islamic courtyard types: (1) Sahn — open prayer courtyard with central fountain for ablution, surrounded by arcaded riwaq (colonnaded gallery), typical of hypostyle mosques; (2) Four-Iwan Court — cruciform courtyard with vaulted recesses on each axis, characteristic of Persian madrasas and mosques; (3) Andalusian Patio — intimate courtyard with water channel (acequia), reflecting pools, and surrounding rooms, exemplified by the Alhambra's Court of the Myrtles; (4) Charbagh — four-part paradise garden divided by water channels, Mughal funerary and palace gardens. Each type annotated with climatic function (cooling, light, ventilation) and symbolic meaning." caption="Islamic Courtyard Typologies — Sahn, Riwaq, Iwan, and Charbagh" suggestedAsset="Architectural reference image or diagram" placementIntent="Visual reference for architectural period/typology" />

Islamic architecture developed a distinct visual and functional vocabulary shaped by religious practice, climate adaptation, and geometric philosophy. Unlike Gothic verticals or classical columns, Islamic design prioritizes the interior court (courtyard), the prayer hall, and intricate surface decoration. The **mosque** forms the core building type, but Islamic architectural principles extend to palaces, madrasas, and domestic spaces.


<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-004-01-core-concept" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="View of the Dome of the Rock (Jerusalem, completed 691 CE, Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik), showing the golden dome on an octagonal base, Byzantine-influenced mosaics, and the earliest surviving Islamic monument." caption="Dome of the Rock — Jerusalem (691 CE)" suggestedAsset="Architectural reference image or diagram" placementIntent="Visual reference for architectural period/typology" />


The five pillars of Islamic architectural vocabulary anchor the tradition:

**The Mosque** is the foundational structure—not a temple but a space for community prayer. It houses no idols or altar; the plan follows function: a courtyard (sahn) for ablution and overflow, covered prayer hall (musallah), and a wall (qibla) indicating prayer direction toward Mecca. The prayer hall emphasizes horizontality and openness rather than vertical hierarchy.

**The Minaret** serves as both functional (the call to prayer broadcast point) and symbolic marker. These towers rise above the urban fabric, typically circular, square, or polygonal in section. Their height and visibility make them the defining silhouette of Islamic cities.

**The Mihrab** is the niche in the qibla wall pointing toward Mecca. Architecturally modest in some examples, ornate in others, it focuses prayer direction and receives special decorative treatment—often framed by arches, calligraphy, or tilework.

**Muqarnas** (honeycomb vaulting) represents the apex of Islamic spatial complexity. These corbelled, faceted vault systems create depth through repetitive geometric subdivision. The muqarnas dissolves hard surfaces into infinite fragmented planes, generating dazzling visual and acoustic effects. Construction requires intricate wood or stone joinery; the forms never repeat exactly, creating mathematical sophistication hidden in decoration.

**Arabesques and Calligraphy** replace figurative imagery. Arabesque patterns—interlocking geometric and vegetal motifs—tile across every surface: walls, ceilings, floors, textiles. Calligraphy (Quranic verses in stylized script) serves decorative and spiritual purposes simultaneously. These elements avoid idolatry while maintaining visual richness.

<Tip>

**Five pillars of Islamic vocabulary—memorize acronym M-M-M-A-C:**

1. **Mosque** = prayer hall + courtyard + qibla wall
2. **Minaret** = tower for call to prayer
3. **Mihrab** = niche indicating prayer direction
4. **Muqarnas** = 3D honeycomb ceiling vaults
5. **Arabesques & Calligraphy** = geometric + Quranic decoration

All appear in major Islamic buildings. Muqarnas and iwans develop regionally over time.</Tip>

These five elements work together: the mosque's courtyard and prayer hall establish the plan; the minaret marks the building externally; the mihrab orients prayer; muqarnas and arabesques transform surfaces into mathematical meditation.

Material choices vary by region: stone in the Levant, brick in Mesopotamia and Persia, tile and stucco everywhere. Climate drives design—massive walls resist heat, courtyards create microclimates, narrow streets in medinas shade urban space. Columns (when used) typically come from reused Roman or Byzantine structures, a practical economy.

<Note>Muqarnas is a three-dimensional corbelled vault system, NOT flat decoration. Each facet creates shadow and catches light differently, producing constantly shifting visual depth—it's advanced geometric engineering. The LEA tests whether you understand this distinction: muqarnas is mathematical, structural sophistication expressed as ornament, not mere surface pattern.</Note>


<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-004-01-core-concept" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="Comparative plan diagram of the three major mosque typologies: the hypostyle hall mosque (e.g., Great Mosque of Cordoba), the four-iwan mosque (e.g., Friday Mosque of Isfahan), and the central-domed Ottoman mosque (e.g., Selimiye Mosque)." caption="Islamic Mosque Types — Hypostyle, Iwan, Central Dome" suggestedAsset="Architectural reference image or diagram" placementIntent="Visual reference for architectural period/typology" />


## Key Facts and Testable Items

<WikiExamTable headers={["Element", "Function", "Common Characteristics", "Regional Notes"]} rows={[["**Mosque (Masjid)**", "Prayer and community gathering", "Courtyard, prayer hall, ablution facilities, qibla wall", "Becomes larger in major cities; multiple minarets added over time"], ["**Minaret**", "Call to prayer; urban marker", "Tall tower, circular/square/polygonal section, balcony(ies) for muezzin", "Umayyad: towers integral to qibla wall; Ottoman: more slender, multiple per mosque"], ["**Mihrab**", "Prayer direction indicator", "Niche in qibla wall, arched frame, ornate decoration", "Often most elaborate interior feature; size increases with mosque importance"], ["**Muqarnas**", "Spatial/visual ceiling treatment", "Corbelled, faceted vault; repeated geometric subdivision", "Persian and Central Asian mastery; limited in early Umayyad; peak in Ottoman"], ["**Arabesque/Calligraphy**", "Decoration; spiritual expression", "Interlocking vegetal/geometric patterns; Quranic script; non-figurative", "Covers every surface area; no human or animal imagery"], ["**Courtyard (Sahn)**", "Ablution, prayer overflow, climate", "Open to sky, central fountain, arcaded edges", "Essential for thermal comfort and ritual purity"], ["**Iwan (Vaulted Portal)**", "Monumental entrance; spatial drama", "Four-centered arch, deep recessed vault, often paired on opposite sides", "Mesopotamian origin; adopted in Abbasid and later; peak in Persian design"]]} />

## How It's Tested on the LEA

<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Identification by Function and Description**
"In Islamic architectural tradition, which element serves as the focal point for prayer direction and typically occupies the qibla wall?" (Answer: **Mihrab**) or "Describe the purpose of the **minaret** in Islamic mosques and urban contexts."
</ExamTip>
<ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Structural and Decorative Distinction**
"Contrast **muqarnas** (honeycomb vaulting) with traditional dome or barrel vault. Why did Islamic architects favor this form?" (Tests understanding of aesthetic, structural, and mathematical sophistication.) Or: "What distinguishes **arabesques** from figurative European decoration, and what religious principle drives this choice?"
</ExamTip>
<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Regional Application**
"Which of these five elements appear across all Islamic regions, and which show significant regional variation?" (Answer: **Mihrab**, **mosque**, **minaret**, and **courtyard** are universal; **muqarnas** develops later and becomes more complex in Persian and Ottoman traditions; **iwan** is concentrated in Central Asian and Persian regions.)</ExamTip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing the Minaret with Architectural Structure" correction="Students sometimes treat the minaret as merely decorative. In fact, the minaret is functionally essential—it amplifies the call to prayer—and symbolically marks Islamic presence in the urban skyline." context="Umayyad minarets were integral to the qibla wall (not separate structures); this design evolved in later periods." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Equating Muqarnas with Simple Ceiling Decoration" correction="Muqarnas is not a flat or stamped pattern. It is a three-dimensional corbelled vault system requiring complex geometry and joinery. Each facet casts shadow and receives light differently, creating constantly shifting visual depth." context="This is advanced mathematical decoration, not ornament." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Misidentifying the Mihrab as a Doorway or Ablution Feature. The mihrab is a niche (not a doorway) set into the qibla wall specifically to indicate prayer direction. Ablution takes place in the courtyard or a separate fountain room, never in the mihrab.", "Assuming All Islamic Mosques Follow an Identical Plan. Early mosques (7th century) were often simple rectangular prayer halls with a courtyard. Hypostyle mosques (Umayyad period) use columns for structural support.
