Later mosques introduce central domes, multiple minarets, and iwans. The \"core\" vocabulary remains constant, but regional and temporal variation is significant."]} />

## Key Terms

**Mosque (Masjid)** — A building for Islamic prayer and community gathering; contains a courtyard, prayer hall, and qibla wall oriented toward Mecca.

**Minaret** — A tall tower from which the muezzin calls the faithful to prayer; serves as urban landmark and symbol.

**Mihrab** — The niche in the qibla wall indicating prayer direction toward Mecca; typically the most elaborately decorated interior feature.

**Muqarnas** — Three-dimensional corbelled or pendentive vaulting with repeated geometric subdivision; creates prismatic, honeycomb-like effect on ceilings and vaults.

**Arabesque** — Non-figurative decoration using interlocking geometric and stylized vegetal motifs; appears on walls, ceilings, and textiles throughout Islamic architecture.

**Qibla Wall** — The wall of the mosque oriented toward Mecca; contains the mihrab and serves as the focus for prayer.

**Sahn** — The open courtyard of a mosque, used for ablution, prayer overflow, and cooling.

**Iwan** — A vaulted recessed portal or gateway, typically framed by a four-centered arch; common in Persian and Central Asian Islamic architecture.

<Warn>Do not confuse the mihrab with a doorway or ablution feature. The mihrab is exclusively a prayer-direction niche set into the qibla wall—it is not functional for movement or ablution (which occurs in the courtyard fountain). This distinction is directly tested on the LEA.</Warn>

**Calligraphy** — Stylized Quranic script used as both decoration and spiritual expression on walls, domes, and prayer rugs; replaces figurative imagery.

**Hypostyle Mosque** — A mosque plan in which the prayer hall uses columns to support the roof; common in early Islamic and Umayyad periods.

<ArticleMedia id="media-hist-004-01-core-concept-timeline" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder" alt="Timeline of Islamic architectural dynasties (7th–19th centuries) tracing the evolution from Umayyad hypostyle mosques through Abbasid brick construction, Andalusian horseshoe arches, Ottoman domes, Mughal mausoleums, and Safavid tilework, with key regional characteristics." caption="Islamic Architecture — Dynastic Timeline and Regional Styles" suggestedAsset="Timeline diagram" placementIntent="Timeline diagram for architectural period" />

## Related Articles

See also within Islamic Architecture: **lea-hist-004-02-core-concept**, **lea-hist-004-05-core-concept**, **lea-hist-004-06-core-concept**, **lea-hist-004-07-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** overview-history-of-architecture for the full curriculum structure and study strategy for History of Architecture.

rows.title: Sustainable architecture
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
<Callout>
Sustainable architecture has matured from ethical preference to systematic methodology encoded in certification systems (LEED, BREEAM, BERDE) and measurable performance standards. The LEA tests your understanding of the theoretical distinction between **genuine sustainability** (reducing total environmental impact across a building's lifecycle) and **greenwashing** (cosmetic environmental claims without systematic change). You must master performance metrics, embodied carbon analysis, and passive design strategies as core architectural knowledge.
</Callout>

## Learning Goal

- Define the methodological revolutions in contemporary architecture: parametric design (algorithmic form-generation), computational biomimicry (learning from biology), and AI-assisted design.
- Distinguish parametricism from previous movements by its use of algorithmic optimization and data-responsive systems.
- Explain how digital design tools extend architects' capacity to explore complex problems beyond conventional methods.

## Core Concept

<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-theo-007-09-sustainable-building" type="image" caption="Sustainable Architecture — The Building as a System Embedded in Metabolic Flows" alt="Concept diagram showing a building at center with interconnected metabolic flows: Energy (solar gain, PV generation, heat recovery), Water (rainwater harvesting, greywater treatment, stormwater management), Materials (embodied carbon, lifecycle assessment, recycled content), and Waste (composting, recycling streams, circular economy). Arrows show passive strategies (orientation, thermal mass, natural ventilation) reducing mechanical load. Callout box: 'Passive → Active → Passive Again (reconciliation)'." suggestedAsset="Diagram of building as metabolic system with energy, water, materials, waste flows" status="placeholder" />

Sustainable architecture represents a fundamental philosophical reorientation: the building is no longer isolated from its environmental context but is understood as a **system embedded in metabolic flows** (water, energy, materials, waste). Traditional architecture treated environmental factors as constraints (climate, site, materials available). Sustainable architecture treats environmental performance as a primary design generator equivalent to program, structure, and aesthetics.

<Tip>
**Three-phase evolution of sustainable thinking**: Passive (let climate do the work), then Active (mechanical systems add intelligence), now Passive-Active synthesis (maximize passive, minimize mechanical load, make mechanics ultra-efficient). The pattern: "Simple is best, complexity should serve genuine need." Design first for climate responsiveness, add systems only where passive strategies cannot achieve comfort.
</Tip>

**From Passive to Active to Passive Again: The Epistemological Shift**

Early sustainable architecture (1970s–1990s) emphasized **passive design strategies**: building orientation, natural ventilation, thermal mass, daylighting, and site-integrated water management. These strategies require no mechanical systems and operate through thermodynamic principles. A south-facing glazed wall in the Northern Hemisphere captures winter solar gains; thermal mass (concrete, stone, water) absorbs heat and releases it at night, moderating temperature swings. Cross-ventilation through properly positioned openings provides cooling without air conditioning.

Examples: Passive House standard (German standard established 1988, popularized by physicist Wolfgang Feist) specifies rigorous envelope performance—extreme insulation, minimal air leakage, triple-glazed windows—allowing comfortable temperatures with minimal or no mechanical heating/cooling. The first Passivhaus building in Darmstadt demonstrated that cold-climate housing required no conventional heating system. This validated what climate-responsive vernacular architecture always knew: the envelope itself is the primary environmental control strategy.

The intermediate period (1990s–2010s) saw the rise of **active systems and smart mechanical integration**: heat recovery ventilation (HRV), radiant heating/cooling, thermal energy storage, sophisticated controls. These systems are still energy-efficient (superior to conventional HVAC) but introduce mechanical complexity and operational dependency. The theoretical risk: occupants become passive consumers of calculated comfort, and system failures cascade catastrophically.

Contemporary sustainable architecture increasingly reconciles passive and active: **maximize passive performance, minimize mechanical load, make mechanical systems highly efficient and resilient**. The Passive House standard now includes mechanically assisted cooling for warming climates. High-performance buildings often use 80% less energy than baseline codes, with passive strategies providing 70% of that reduction and mechanical efficiency providing the remaining 10%.

**Lifecycle Carbon and Embodied Impact**

Operational energy has dominated sustainability discourse for two decades—how much energy does the building consume during occupancy? This is measurable, standardizable, and incentivized by utility economics. However, **embodied carbon** (emissions from material extraction, manufacturing, transportation, and assembly) has been systematically undervalued.

A conventional reinforced concrete structure locks in significant carbon at construction: cement production generates ~8% of global CO2 emissions (the chemical calcination of limestone, plus fuel combustion). A building reducing operational carbon by 50% through mechanical efficiency but constructed with carbon-intensive materials may have higher total lifecycle carbon than a simpler, less-optimized building in low-carbon materials.

Sustainable architecture must now integrate **lifecycle assessment (LCA)**: quantifying embodied carbon plus operational carbon across a 50–100-year building life. The metric is often **kg CO2-eq per m² per year** (carbon intensity per unit area per year of operation).

Strategies to reduce embodied carbon:

1. **Material Substitution**: Timber (renewable if sustainably harvested) replaces concrete and steel; rammed earth, straw clay, and earth plasters replace cement-based finishes; recycled content materials reduce virgin extraction.

2. **Structural Efficiency**: Optimized structural systems (parametric form-finding, load-responsive geometry) reduce material quantity without sacrificing safety.

3. **Longevity and Adaptability**: Buildings lasting 100+ years amortize embodied impact; adaptable interiors postpone major renovations; modular systems enable component replacement rather than demolition.

4. **Adaptive Reuse**: Preserving existing buildings is nearly always lower-carbon than demolition and reconstruction, even when mechanical upgrades are required.

Contemporary theoretical debate: Should embodied carbon be weighted equally to operational carbon in sustainability assessment? Operational carbon is perpetual—a 100-year building accrues it every year. Embodied carbon is front-loaded but finite. If a low-embodied-carbon timber building requires 30% more operational energy than a concrete building, when does operational excess offset embodied advantage? The answer depends on climate, grid energy sources, and discount rates—there is no universal answer. The LEA may test whether you can articulate this complexity rather than default to certainty.

<Note>
Embodied vs. operational is not a binary choice. Lifecycle assessment (LCA) must account for both, but the weighting depends on context. Cold climates where heating dominates favor high-insulation construction (higher embodied carbon) that dramatically reduces operational carbon. Hot climates might favor lower-embodied materials if passive cooling is effective. One-size-fits-all sustainability scoring misses this context-dependency.
</Note>

**Performance Certification Systems and Their Theoretical Limits**

**LEED** (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design, USA/global, established 1998) awards points across categories: site selection (proximity to transit, reductions in heat island), water efficiency, energy performance, materials (recycled content, local sourcing), indoor air quality, and innovation. LEED evolved from checklist-based (initial versions) to performance-based (LEED v4 requires measured data). Theoretical strength: standardizes environmental criteria across geographies. Weakness: point systems can incentivize "easy" credits (recycled content labeling) over systemic performance (structural efficiency); can subsidize greenification of environmentally problematic building types (efficient parking garage is still a parking garage).

**BREEAM** (Building Research Establishment Environmental Assessment Method, UK, established 1990) similarly rates buildings across environmental performance. BREEAM developed first and influenced LEED; regional variants (BREEAM Middle East, BREEAM Southeast Asia) adjust weighting for local climate and practices.

**BERDE** (Building for Ecologically Responsive Design Excellence, Philippines, established 2010) adapts LEED/BREEAM frameworks for Philippine context: weighs typhoon resilience, tropical solar gain, water management in monsoon climates, and integration with local vernacular principles. BERDE recognizes that Northern Hemisphere-optimized standards (large windows for daylighting, open floor plates) can be thermally dysfunctional in Manila's equatorial climate.

**Net-Zero Energy and Beyond**

Net-zero energy buildings produce as much renewable energy (typically solar photovoltaic) as they consume annually, resulting in zero net purchase from the grid. This requires: (1) ultra-high efficiency (reducing load to minimum), (2) on-site or nearby renewable generation.

Theoretical risk: A building producing net-zero energy through rooftop solar panels while consuming 100,000 kWh annually is "zero-energy" on paper but embeds far higher material quantity and manufacturing impact than a building consuming 40,000 kWh and importing grid-sourced electricity (if grid includes renewables).

Emerging standards propose **net-zero carbon** (accounting for grid carbon intensity) and **net-zero materials** or **circularity** (materials at end of life are recovered and remanufactured rather than landfilled). These are more complex than net-zero energy but more meaningful.

**Greenwashing and the Problem of Certification Theater**

Greenwashing occurs when buildings or developers claim sustainability through superficial measures while ignoring systemic environmental impact. Examples:

- A shopping mall with extensive rooftop gardens and rain collection (visible, photographed) but consuming 50,000 kWh annually, poorly insulated, reliant on extensive mechanical cooling, in a sprawling suburban location (high transportation carbon).
- Facade cladding with high recycled content marketed as sustainable while the building envelope remains thermally inefficient.
- "Green" development in sensitive ecosystems marketed as ecological because of site landscaping, while development itself fragments habitat.

Theoretical problem: Certification systems, if not rigorously applied, enable greenwashing. A LEED-certified building earning 50 of 100 available points might boast "LEED certification" without acknowledging that 50% of possible environmental improvements were not pursued. Sustainable architecture must resist the reduction of environmental complexity to marketing language.

<Warn>
Greenwashing masquerades as sustainability. A LEED-certified building earning minimum points can claim "LEED certified" status despite pursuing only 25% of available improvements. Similarly, visible green features (rooftop gardens, rainwater collection) photograph well but may mask poor envelope performance or excessive mechanical systems. Always examine full lifecycle data, not marketing claims. Distrust buildings where the most visible features are the most easily publicized rather than the most impactful.
</Warn>

**Passive Design in Philippine Context**

The Philippine climate—tropical, monsoon-affected, with extreme solar radiation and typhoon risks—provides specific passive design opportunities often overlooked by imported standards:

1. **Deep Overhangs and Shading**: Solar radiation in Manila is 5–6 kWh/m²/day; preventing direct solar gain through windows is thermally superior to managing it. Traditional Filipino architecture (bahay kubo) features deep eaves, louvered window screens, and elevated designs allowing air circulation beneath.

2. **Natural Ventilation Over Mechanical**: The Philippines has consistent trade winds; cross-ventilation through operable windows is reliable. This enables warm-humid climate comfort without air conditioning for much of the year, reducing embodied carbon of mechanical systems.

3. **Water Integration**: Monsoon rains are abundant (Manila receives 1,600+ mm annually); groundwater is accessible. Rainwater harvesting, grey-water reclamation, and bioswleas can manage stormwater locally, reducing flooding risk and municipal water dependency.

4. **Vernacular Integration**: Indigenous architectural typologies (bahay kubo framing, bahay na bato masonry) embodied climate responses developed over centuries. Sustainable architecture should learn these principles rather than imposing standardized international solutions.

## Key Facts and Testable Items

<WikiExamTable headers={["Standard", "Origin", "Key Metrics", "Relevant for Philippine Context"]} rows={[['["LEED", "USA, 1998", "Points-based; site, water, energy, materials, IEQ", "Global but Northern Hemisphere bias"]', '["BREEAM", "UK, 1990", "Performance-based; energy, water, waste, health", "Regional variants adapt to climate"]', '["BERDE", "Philippines, 2010", "Tropics-optimized; typhoon resilience, monsoon water, solar control, vernacular integration", "Direct Philippine applicability"]', '["Passive House", "Germany, 1988", "Envelope R-values, air leakage, heating/cooling demand (<15 kWh/m²/year)", "Works in cold climates; heating-focused standard"]', '["Net-Zero Energy", "Various, 2000s+", "Annual energy production = consumption", "Can mask high embodied carbon if PV-heavy"]', '["Carbon Trust/embodied", "UK, 2010s", "kg CO2-eq per m² across lifecycle", "Increasingly required; complements operational metrics"]']]} />
## How It's Tested on the LEA

<ExamTip>1. **Lifecycle Vs. Operational**: "A timber-framed building requires 10% more operational energy than a concrete building but has 40% lower embodied carbon. Over a 50-year lifecycle, which is more sustainable?" (Answer: Requires LCA calculation; depends on grid carbon intensity and discount rate; both are viable if properly optimized)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>2. **Certification Literacy**: "A building achieves LEED Platinum certification. What does this tell you about actual environmental performance?" (Answer: It meets high standards across categories; but point-system may enable credit-stacking without systemic optimization; must review actual performance data)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>3. **Greenwashing Recognition**: "A development advertises 'green roofs and rainwater harvesting' prominently but provides minimal information on envelope insulation or operational energy. What is your critical assessment?" (Answer: Visible green features may mask poor thermal performance; greenwashing likely; require full LCA and actual performance projections)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>4. **Passive Design Application**: "Design a tropical office building in Manila. Which passive strategies are most critical?" (Answer: Solar shading (overhangs, louvers), natural ventilation (cross-flow, operable windows), elevated design for airflow, rainwater harvesting, minimal air-conditioning load)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>5. **Philippine Standard Competency**: "How does BERDE differ from LEED in tropical application?" (Answer: BERDE weights tropical climate factors—solar control, monsoon water management, typhoon resilience; incorporates vernacular principles; avoids Northern Hemisphere bias)</ExamTip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing Energy Efficiency with Sustainability" correction="An energy-efficient air-conditioned building in an unsustainable suburban location, constructed with high embodied carbon, is not sustainable." context="Sustainability requires systems-level integration of location, envelope, mechanical, materials, and operational phases." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Assuming Certifications Guarantee Performance" correction="LEED/BREEAM/BERDE certifications are design-stage projections. Many certified buildings underperform operationally due to occupant behavior, commissioning failures, or maintenance issues." context="Certification is necessary but insufficient." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Prioritizing Operational Over Embodied in High-Carbon Materials. Building a super-efficient office tower in high-carbon concrete can lock in more total lifecycle carbon than a less-optimized timber building. Modern sustainability cannot ignore embodied carbon.", "Undervaluing Passive Strategies as \"Low-Tech\". Passive design is intellectually demanding—it requires climate analysis, orientation optimization, envelope physics, and occupant education. It is not primitive; it is sophisticated applied physics.", "Applying Standards Without Local Context. Importing LEED criteria wholeslea into Philippine context can incentivize large windows (standard daylighting credit) that increase solar gain in tropical climates. BERDE's localization reflects genuine need, not regional protectionism.", "Treating Renewable Energy as Sustainability. On-site solar is excellent; it should not substitute for efficiency. A building consuming 100 kWh/day that produces this via PV has higher embodied impact than a building consuming 40 kWh/day from the grid."]} />

## Key Terms

**Embodied Carbon** — CO2 emissions locked in materials and construction processes (extraction, manufacturing, transportation, assembly), released upfront rather than over time.

**Lifecycle Assessment (LCA)** — Quantitative analysis of environmental impact across a building's full lifespan—from material sourcing through demolition.

**Passive Design** — Environmental control through building form, orientation, envelope, and natural systems (ventilation, thermal mass, solar gain/shading) without mechanical conditioning.

**Thermal Mass** — Material property (concrete, masonry, water) that absorbs heat at high temperatures and releases it at low temperatures, moderating swings.

**Cross-Ventilation** — Natural airflow through a space driven by pressure differences across openings; enables cooling without mechanical systems in appropriate climates.

**Heat Recovery Ventilation (HRV)** — Mechanical system that extracts heat or cooling from exhaust air and transfers it to incoming fresh air, reducing conditioning load.

**Envelope Performance** — Combined insulation (R-value), air-tightness (ACH—air changes per hour), and window performance (U-value, solar heat gain coefficient) that determine heating/cooling demand.

**Net-Zero Energy** — Building producing as much renewable energy annually as it consumes from the grid (zero net energy purchase).

**Greenwashing** — Marketing claims of environmental benefit that are superficial, unverified, or contradicted by actual performance; certification theater.

**BERDE** — Philippine sustainability standard adapted for tropical climate, monsoon hydrology, typhoon resilience, and vernacular integration (distinct from LEED's Northern Hemisphere bias).

**Rainwater Harvesting** — Collection and storage of precipitation for non-potable uses (irrigation, toilet flushing, cleaning), reducing municipal water demand and flooding risk.

**Typhoon Resilience** — Building design for extreme wind and water loads; relevant to Philippine context, often overlooked in imported international standards.

## Related Articles

See also within Contemporary Movements & Discourse: **lea-theo-007-01-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-02-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-10-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-11-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** overview-theory-of-architecture for the full curriculum structure and study strategy for Theory of Architecture.

rows.title: Stair Design
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Verify design compliance with PD 1096, RA 9514, BP 344, and applicable codes at each design phase, identify code violations in plans and specifications, prepare code compliance checklists, and apply for variances where necessary.

Vertical circulation — stairs and elevators — is designed using precise dimensional and egress rules. 
---

## Core Concept

**Stair Design** is governed by several core factors:

1. **Riser and Tread Proportions (PD 1096 / 2004 IRR)**  
   - **Maximum riser height**: 200 mm  
   - **Minimum tread depth (run)**: 280 mm (measured nosing to nosing)  
   - These are legal limits; actual design often uses more conservative dimensions for comfort.

2. **Blondel’s Formula** (ergonomic guideline, not a code mandate)  
   - \( R + T \approx 430\text{–}450 \text{ mm} \)  
   - This range is widely accepted as comfortable proportioning for stairs.  
   - **PD 1096** enforces only the maximum riser and minimum tread; Blondel is a design aid, not a legal requirement.

3. **Number of Risers from Floor Height**  
   - \( \text{Number of risers} = \dfrac{\text{Floor height}}{\text{Riser height}} \) (always round **up** to the next whole integer).  
   - Example: Floor height 3.0 m  
     - \( 3{,}000 \text{ mm} \div 180 \text{ mm} = 16.67 \rightarrow 17 \text{ risers} \).

4. **Stair Width (RA 9514 / Fire Code IRR)**  
   - Minimum clear width is governed by occupant load and use.  
   - RA 9514 IRR gives typical minimum widths such as:  
     - For new stairs serving a total cumulative occupant load **less than 2,000 persons**: **1,120 mm** minimum width.  
     - For **2,000 persons or more**: **1,420 mm** minimum width.  
   - For smaller occupancies, the minimum stair width may be lower but must still satisfy both PD 1096 and RA 9514.

5. **Stair Flight Limits and Landings**  
   - Landings are required at the top and bottom of every flight and at required intermediate levels.  
   - RA 9514 sets a **maximum height between landings** of 3.60 m and a minimum headroom of 2.0 m.  
   - Landing depth must be at least equal to the stair width for safe movement.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-007-10-core-concept" type="image" caption="Code Compliance Checklist — Design Phase Verification Flowchart" description="Decision tree/flowchart for code compliance verification at each design phase: schematic (occupancy, setbacks, height limits), design development (egress, fire-rated separations, accessibility), and contract documents (detailed compliance per PD 1096, RA 9514, BP 344)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

---

### Worked Example: Stair Calculation for 3.0 m Floor-to-Floor

**Given:**

- Floor-to-floor height: 3.0 m = 3,000 mm  
- Occupant load served by stair: 120 persons  
- Proposed riser: 180 mm

**Step 1: Calculate number of risers**

\[
\text{Risers} = \dfrac{3{,}000 \text{ mm}}{180 \text{ mm}} = 16.67 \rightarrow 17 \text{ risers}
\]

\[
\text{Actual riser height} = \dfrac{3{,}000}{17} \approx 176.5 \text{ mm} \quad (\leq 200 \text{ mm} \; \checkmark)
\]

**Step 2: Verify ergonomic proportion (Blondel)**

Assume tread \( T = 260 \text{ mm} \):

\[
R + T = 176.5 + 260 = 436.5 \text{ mm} \quad (\text{within 430–450 mm guideline} \; \checkmark)
\]

For strict code compliance, adjust the final solution so that \( T \geq 280 \text{ mm} \) while still keeping \( R + T \) within a comfortable range.

**Step 3: Stair width (occupant-load based)**

Using RA 9514 IRR, an occupant load of 120 persons is well below 2,000 persons, so the typical **minimum stair width** of **1,120 mm** applies. For design quality, you may increase the width (e.g., 1,200–1,400 mm), but you cannot go below the applicable minimum for the primary egress stair serving this load.

**Step 4: Flights and landings**

- With 17 risers, a common arrangement is a dogleg stair (for example, 9 risers + landing + 8 risers).  
- Ensure the **vertical height between landings** does not exceed 3.60 m and that the **landing length** is at least equal to the chosen stair width.

---

## Elevator Design (Accessibility Context)

Under the **2024 Revised IRR of BP 344** and related accessibility guidance, elevators that serve as accessible vertical circulation must satisfy specific minimum internal dimensions and door clearances.

1. **Accessible Elevator Car**  
   - Minimum clear **depth**: 1,400 mm  
   - Minimum clear **width**: in the range of 1,200–1,500 mm depending on the configuration; a commonly adopted accessible layout is **1,400 mm (depth) × 1,500 mm (width)**.  
   - Clear door opening: **at least 900 mm**.  
   - Control panel height: generally **900–1,200 mm** above the finished floor.

2. **Service and Fireman’s Elevator Considerations**  
   - For high-rise and critical-use buildings, separate service or fireman’s elevators are often required by fire and building regulations or by project brief.  
   - The hoistway must provide adequate clearances around the car to accommodate guide rails, safety gear, and tolerances; final dimensions are set by the elevator manufacturer and applicable standards rather than a single fixed code number.

---

## Key Provisions

| Element                    | Specification                               | Notes                                               |
|:-------------------------- |:------------------------------------------- |:--------------------------------------------------- |
| **Max Riser**              | 200 mm                                      | PD 1096 / IRR limit for straight stairs            |
| **Min Tread (Run)**        | 280 mm                                      | Measured nosing to nosing                          |
| **Blondel Check**          | \( R + T \approx 430\text{–}450 \text{ mm} \) | Ergonomic guideline, not a legal requirement       |
| **Stair Width**            | 1,120 mm (for many new stairs with OL < 2,000) | RA 9514 IRR egress minimum; verify per occupancy  |
| **Headroom**               | 2.00 m minimum                              | Clear vertical height above nosings                |
| **Height Between Landings**| 3.60 m maximum                              | RA 9514 IRR requirement                            |
| **Landing Length**         | ≥ stair width                               | For safe transition; mirrored in both codes        |
| **Handrail Height**        | 860–965 mm                                  | Above stair nosing (from PD 1096 / BP 344 practice)|
| **Elevator Car**           | ~1,400 mm depth × 1,200–1,500 mm width      | BP 344 accessibility standard range                |
| **Elevator Door**          | 900 mm clear opening                        | Minimum accessible entry width                     |

---

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, stair design is dictated primarily by the **National Building Code (PD 1096 and its IRR)** for geometry and by **RA 9514 (Fire Code)** for egress width, landings, and headroom. **Blondel’s formula** is widely used in review materials as a comfort check, but LEA questions will prioritize compliance with the **maximum riser**, **minimum tread**, **minimum width**, and **headroom** requirements set by PD 1096 and RA 9514. Accessibility rules from **BP 344 and its 2024 IRR** govern elevator dimensions, handrail details, and usability for persons with disability. For the LEA, always base your numerical answers on the codes, using Blondel and similar rules to justify good ergonomic practice.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-007-10-core-concept" type="image" caption="Code Compliance Workflow — Design Phase Regulatory Checklist" description="Flowchart showing code compliance verification at each design phase: Pre-Design (zoning, site code), Schematic (occupancy, egress concept), Design Development (fire separation, accessibility), Construction Documents (permit-ready checklist). Key PD 1096, RA 9514, and BP 344 checkpoints at each gate." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-008-01** (Fire Egress) for occupant load calculations, **LEA-DSGN-008-02** (Fire Separation) for fire-rated assemblies, and **LEA-PLAN-004-07** (Zoning Analysis) for zoning ordinance compliance.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
 mistakes={[
 'ERR-DSGN-022: Treating a “preferred” riser (e.g., 175–180 mm) as the legal maximum instead of the PD 1096 limit of 200 mm',
 'Failing to round UP the number of risers, which can push actual riser height above the 200 mm maximum',
 'Ignoring RA 9514 stair-width requirements and using a generic 1,000 mm minimum for all occupancies',
 'ERR-DSGN-033: Using outdated or undersized elevator car dimensions instead of current BP 344 accessibility standards',
 "Treating Blondel's formula as a strict legal requirement rather than an ergonomic check layered on top of code limits"
 ]}
/>

rows.title: MEP space allocation
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Coordinate structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection systems within the architectural design, identify spatial requirements for each system, resolve system conflicts, and prepare integrated ceiling plans.

Mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) systems require dedicated space within a building envelope. For the LEA, you must understand how much of your total floor area is consumed by MEP and related support areas — and how to budget for them during architectural planning so usable space is not compromised.

## Core Concept

MEP space allocation begins with understanding the **net-to-gross ratio** (NGR), which quantifies the proportion of built space used for structure, MEP, and circulation versus actual usable area.

**NGR = Usable Floor Area ÷ Total Built Area**

Or inverted:

**Structure + MEP + Circulation (as % of GFA) = 100% − NGR**

Typical NGR ranges by building type (planning norms, not code):

- **Hospital**: 0.55–0.65 (about 35–45% consumed by structure, MEP, shafts, and circulation)
- **Office (standard / A-Class)**: 0.70–0.80 (about 20–30% consumed)
- **Residential**: 0.75–0.85 (about 15–25% consumed)
- **Retail**: 0.80–0.90 (about 10–20% consumed)

### Why High MEP Demand?

1. **Vertical systems**: Mechanical rooms, electrical rooms, and plumbing cores occupy a noticeable percentage of the footprint and repeat vertically.
2. **Horizontal runs**: HVAC ducts, electrical conduits, and water lines under floors and above ceilings occupy depth within the floor-to-floor height and compete with structure.
3. **Shafts**: Elevator, stair, and utility cores run continuously, reducing assignable floor area per level while satisfying egress and services.
4. **Redundancy**: Hospitals and critical facilities require emergency power, backup water, and redundant HVAC systems, multiplying MEP space demand.

### Standard MEP-Related Allocations (Order-of-Magnitude Planning)

**Mechanical Room Size (central equipment)**  
- Small office (about 10 storeys, ~5,000 sqm total typical floors): on the order of 150–200 sqm for central mechanical plant.  
- Mid-size office (about 20 storeys, ~4,000 sqm total typical floors): on the order of 250–350 sqm, often split between a central plant and fan rooms.  
- Hospital per 100 beds: several hundred square meters (e.g., 400–500 sqm) distributed across multiple mechanical and support rooms.

**Electrical Room Size**  
- Office / residential: roughly 50–80 sqm per floor or per zone, depending on distribution strategy and equipment.  
- Hospital: larger electrical rooms (on the order of 100 sqm and up) due to redundancy, emergency power, and specialized systems.

**Plumbing Core**  
- Vertical stacks and risers typically occupy a modest but continuous percentage of the plan, often bundled with toilets and wet areas.  
- Sanitary, storm, and water supply risers require coordinated shafts; exact diameters are determined by engineers from load calculations rather than fixed exam numbers.

**Vertical Circulation and Cores**  
- Elevator and stair cores are part of the gross area, not usable area, and typically contribute a significant share of the “non-assignable” component.  
- Total core and circulation area commonly falls within the non-usable fraction reflected in the NGR ranges above.

### Floor-to-Floor Impact on MEP

A floor-to-floor height of about 3.0 m (common in many RC buildings) must accommodate:

- Structural slab and beams.  
- MEP runs (HVAC ducts, fire protection, electrical, plumbing).  
- Suspended ceiling and finishes where provided.

If MEP depth is underestimated, clear finished ceiling height is reduced, creating comfort and proportion issues and potentially breaching minimum ceiling height standards (e.g., PD 1096 requires at least 2.40 m for upper-storey habitable rooms, with 2.70 m minimum at the first storey). Proper early allocation of vertical depth protects both compliance and design quality.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-007-09-core-concept" type="image" caption="Building Systems Coordination — Integrated Ceiling Plan Diagram" description="Composite reflected ceiling plan showing coordination of: structural grid, mechanical ductwork, electrical lighting layout, plumbing, fire sprinkler heads, and fire alarm devices. Conflict resolution zones highlighted with annotation." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

| Building Type          | NGR (approx.) | Non-Usable % of GFA* | Typical Issues                                      |
|------------------------|---------------|----------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| **Hospital**           | 0.55–0.65     | ~35–45%              | Redundant systems, sterile and support zones       |
| **Office (A-Class)**   | 0.70–0.80     | ~20–30%              | Dense cabling, HVAC zoning, large cores            |
| **Residential**        | 0.75–0.85     | ~15–25%              | Vertical stacks, small cores distributed by stacks |
| **Retail**             | 0.80–0.90     | ~10–20%              | Simple services, large open spaces                 |
| **Hotel**              | 0.70–0.78     | ~22–30%              | Services to rooms, laundry, back-of-house support  |

\*Non-usable includes structure, MEP, circulation, and non-assignable support areas.

**Shaft and Plant Zoning by Building Height (Planning Patterns)**

- **1–5 storeys**: A single main mechanical/electrical core with distributed plumbing in walls may be adequate.  
- **6–15 storeys**: A central mechanical core, electrical distribution per floor or per zone, and duplicated plumbing stacks for efficiency and redundancy.  
- **16+ storeys**: Zoned mechanical floors (mechanical “interstitial” levels or sky lobbies) every several floors, redundant electrical feeds, and multiple pressure zones for plumbing.

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, MEP space has historically been under-allocated in many projects, resulting in congested ceiling spaces, difficult retrofits, and service visibility in supposedly finished areas. Contemporary practice allocates more realistic percentages for cores, risers, and plant rooms, especially in hospitals and high-rise offices, where 20–30% (or more for hospitals) of GFA may be used by non-assignable space. High-rise residential towers commonly require carefully planned mechanical floors and service zones to handle water pressure, vertical distribution, and fire protection. Poor acoustic separation of plumbing risers and inadequate shaft sizing remain frequent pain points, and LEA questions often test your ability to foresee these issues from the planning stage.

## How It's Tested

1. **NGR and Area Breakdown**  
   Given a total GFA and a target NGR for a specific building type, you compute usable floor area versus space consumed by structure, MEP, and circulation.

2. **Floor-to-Floor and Ceiling Height Trade-Offs**  
   You analyze how increased MEP depth affects clear ceiling height and whether the resulting height still complies with PD 1096 minimums and meets comfort and market expectations (e.g., office ceilings versus residential).

3. **Core and Shaft Planning**  
   You design or evaluate the size and location of mechanical, electrical, and plumbing cores for a mid- or high-rise building, justifying whether they are adequate for the stated occupancy, storey count, and redundancy requirements.

<Tip>
**“MEP is invisible but not free.”** If you design to an aggressive net-to-gross ratio without reserving enough space for plant, risers, and cores, the “missing” area will reappear later as exposed services, cramped ceilings, and costly revisions. Budget MEP and core space explicitly from day one.
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Ceiling plenum depth (typically 600-900mm) accommodates ductwork, piping, and conduit. Coordinate structural depth (+500-800mm) with MEP zone for total floor-to-floor height calculation.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-007-09-core-concept" type="image" caption="Integrated Ceiling Plan — MEP, Structural, and Lighting Coordination" description="Reflected ceiling plan showing coordination of: structural beams and soffits, HVAC duct routing (with diffusers), lighting fixtures (recessed, pendant, emergency), sprinkler head coverage, and ceiling grid. Conflict zones where structural, MEP, and architectural elements intersect are highlighted." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-007-06** (Building Integration) for system coordination process, **LEA-DSGN-008-03** (Sprinkler Systems) for fire protection integration, and **LEA-DSGN-009-03** (IAQ) for mechanical ventilation coordination.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
  mistakes={[
    'Designing to a high NGR target without checking whether core, MEP, and structure can realistically fit within the remaining percentage',
    'Allocating a single small electrical or mechanical room for a high-rise building that requires zoned or per-floor distribution',
    'Underestimating riser and shaft sizes, resulting in last-minute encroachment into rentable or sleaable areas',
    'Placing all major mechanical equipment only on the roof in tall buildings, leading to excessive duct and pipe runs and energy penalties',
    'Ignoring plumbing and mechanical noise transmission when locating risers adjacent to bedrooms or quiet spaces'
  ]}
/>

rows.title: Paint systems
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Classify paint and coating systems (latex, oil-based, epoxy, polyurethane, stain, varnish, enamel, textured) by binder type, durability, sheen level, cleanability, and appropriate substrate for interior and exterior architectural applications.
## Core Concept

Paint systems consist of binder (resin), solvent, pigment, and additives. The binder determines performance: latex (acrylic or vinyl acrylic) uses water as solvent and offers low odor and easy cleanup; oil-based enamel uses mineral spirits and offers superior durability on metal; epoxy uses two-part curing for maximum adhesion and chemical resistance; polyurethane offers flexibility and UV resistance; lacquer provides rapid drying and high gloss but requires ventilation; stain penetrates wood fibers without forming a film.

Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) are regulated in many jurisdictions. Interior latex paints typically contain <300 g/L VOC (low-VOC), a regulatory threshold in many regions. Oil-based enamels range from 300-650 g/L VOC and are restricted in some areas. The Philippines does not yet enforce strict VOC limits uniformly; however, architects and builders increasingly specify low-VOC products for health and indoor air quality (IAQ) benefits. Boysen, Davies, and Island Paints market low-VOC latex and acrylic-enamel hybrid products that balance durability and environmental responsibility.

Dry film thickness (DFT) is critical. Spreading rate (coverage rate) is typically 8-12 m²/L for interior latex, allowing calculation of coats needed. A 2000 m² project at 10 m²/L needs 200L per coat; 2 coats = 400L of paint. Specifying DFT (75-150µm for topcoats) ensures adequate protection; underspray creates color variation and reduced durability.

Surface preparation determines success. Wood stains require sanding to open grain; enamel requires primer on metal; epoxy demands concrete scarification (removal of surface laitance) for mechanical bond. Primer types vary: latex primer on drywall, epoxy primer on metal in wet environments, and shellac-based primer to block stains and odors.

Specialty finishes include anti-slip coatings for ramps (adding aggregate to paint), anti-bacterial finishes (copper-based additives), and intumescent paint (expands when heated to provide fire protection). These are specified for functional performance beyond aesthetic requirements.


<ArticleMedia id="media-paint-coating-comparison" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison chart of paint and coating systems: latex, oil-based, epoxy, polyurethane, stain, varnish, enamel, and textured with binder type, durability, sheen, and substrate compatibility"
  caption="Future chart: paint and coating systems comparison — binder type, sheen, durability, and substrate"
  suggestedAsset="Material selection chart with finish sample illustrations"
  placementIntent="Provides reference for coating selection by application and substrate" />

## Key Provisions

| Property | Specification | Standard | LEA Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VOC Limit (Interior Latex) | <300 g/L | ASTM D3960, EPA guidelines | Low-VOC compliance; indoor air quality |
| VOC Limit (Oil Enamel) | 300-650 g/L | ASTM D3960 | Higher VOC; restricted in some regions |
| Spreading Rate (Latex) | 8-12 m²/L | Manufacturer specs | Covers ~8-12 m² per liter per coat |
| Dry Film Thickness (DFT) | 75-150µm (topcoat) | ASTM D3359 | Ensures adequate protection and color |
| Recoat Time (Latex, 23°C, <50% RH) | 2-4 hours | Manufacturer specs | Determines application schedule |
| Recoat Time (Oil Enamel) | 16-24 hours | Manufacturer specs | Requires longer schedule than latex |
| Adhesion (Cross-Hatch) | Rating ≥3 on ASTM D3359 | ASTM D3359 | Substrate bond strength |
| Primer Type (Drywall) | Latex, universal primer | ASTM D3276 | Seals substrate, promotes topcoat adhesion |
| Primer Type (Metal) | Epoxy or polyurethane | ASTM D3276 | Corrosion resistance; marine environments |
| Substrate Preparation (Wood) | Sand to 120-150 grit; remove dust | ASTM D3276 | Opens grain; removes contaminants |
| Intumescent Paint DFT | 2-3mm per coating specification | Fire-rating assembly | Expands to protect steel during fire |
| Anti-Slip Coating (Ramps) | DFT 150-250µm with aggregate | Accessibility standards | High friction; prevent slipping in wet |
| Shelf Life (Once Opened) | Use within 1-2 years | Manufacturer specs | Paint oxidation reduces performance |

## Philippine Construction Context

Boysen, as Pacific Paint (Boysen), dominates the Philippine market with brands including Permacoat (acrylic latex), Acrytex (enamel/acrylic hybrid), and KNOxOUT (titanium dioxide NOx-reducing paint). Davies Paints competes in the premium segment with wide color selection. Island Paints offers cost-competitive options. All three brands are now formulating low-VOC products in response to market demand and to align with future regulatory tightening.

Tropical humidity and salty coastal air drive premium product selection. Oil-based enamel offers superior durability on metal railings and exterior trim in high-corrosion environments, but high VOC and longer recoat times challenge project schedules. Latex alternatives with rust-inhibiting primers (e.g., Boysen's metal primers) are increasingly used in residential projects to reduce schedule impact.

Intumescent paint is typically specified for structural steel fire protection in high-rise buildings (>15m height per PD 1096) where required by fire resistance ratings in RA 9514 2019 IRR Table 602. Specification must include DFT requirement (typically 2-3mm per fire-rating hour) and testing per ASTM E119. Many contractors and architects are unaware of the distinction between aesthetic paint fire rating and structural steel protection, leading to under-specification.

Anti-slip coatings gain importance as BP 344 accessibility enforcement increases. Exterior ramps and interior accessible routes benefit from anti-slip paint (150-250µm DFT with silica or polymer aggregate). Cost premium is 20-30% over standard paint; specifying where required is cost-effective risk management.


<ArticleMedia id="media-paint-system-layers" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Cross-section showing paint system layers: primer, intermediate coat, and finish coat on wood, metal, masonry, and gypsum substrates"
  caption="Future diagram: paint system layers by substrate — wood, metal, masonry, and gypsum"
  suggestedAsset="Cross-section detail of coating build-up on each substrate type"
  placementIntent="Visualizes proper paint system specification for different substrates" />
## How It's Tested

**Question Type 1 (VOC Compliance):** A project in an occupied high-rise specifies interior paint. What VOC limit ensures air-quality compliance and occupant safety? Answer: <300 g/L per EPA/ASTM guidelines. Oil-based enamel (300-650 g/L) would create indoor air quality issues.

**Question Type 2 (Coverage Rate):** A 5000 m² interior wall area requires 2 coats. Specify paint coverage at 10 m²/L. How many liters are needed? Answer: (5000 m² × 2 coats) / 10 m²/L = 1000L. Cost estimate and timeline depend on this accuracy.

**Question Type 3 (Primer Selection):** A steel column in a parking structure near the ocean requires paint. Should you specify latex primer, oil-based primer, or epoxy primer? Answer: Epoxy primer in high-corrosion coastal environment. Oil-based or latex are insufficient for salt-spray resistance.

**Question Type 4 (Fire Protection):** Structural steel beams in a 15-story office building must achieve 2-hour fire rating. Should you specify standard latex paint or intumescent paint? Answer: Intumescent paint with specified DFT (2-3mm, verified per ASTM E119). Standard paint has no structural fire rating.

<Tip>Memory aid: VOC <300 g/L for interior latex (low-VOC). Oil enamel has higher VOC but better durability on metal. Primer is 90% of paint success—don't skip it. Intumescent paint is required for structural steel fire protection, not aesthetic protection. Coverage rate drives project cost and timeline.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Specifying high-VOC oil-based enamel for interior occupied buildings, creating indoor air quality issues" correction="Use latex (acrylic) or low-VOC enamel (<300 g/L) for interior spaces. Oil enamel (300-650 g/L) is reserved for metal in corrosive exterior environments or industrial spaces." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Omitting primer on drywall or metal, assuming topcoat alone provides adhesion" correction="Primer is 90% of adhesion. Latex primer on drywall seals substrate and promotes topcoat bond. Epoxy or rust-inhibiting primer on metal is non-negotiable in corrosive zones." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Under-specifying intumescent paint on structural steel, assuming aesthetic fire-rated paint provides structural protection" correction="Aesthetic paint fire rating (surface-only) is different from structural fire rating. Structural steel requires intumescent paint per ASTM E119, with DFT verified by testing. Two different specifications." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Calculating paint volume without accounting for spreading rate, under-budgeting materials" correction="Coverage rate (8-12 m²/L) determines volume needed. A 5000 m² wall at 10 m²/L needs 500L per coat. Multiply by number of coats. Budget contingency for waste (5-10%)." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Specifying standard latex for wood without stain-blocking primer, allowing tannins to bleed through", "Failing to account for recoat time in project schedule (16-24 hours for oil enamel vs. 2-4 hours for latex)", "Over-specifying premium paint for low-visibility or protected areas (cost optimization opportunity)", "Mixing incompatible systems (oil topcoat over latex primer, or vice versa) without sanding and re-priming", "Applying anti-slip coating to interior floors without specifying ramp-specific product and DFT"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Interior Finishes: **lea-matl-007-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-02-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-05-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Site grading
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Read contour maps and calculate slopes (%, degrees, ratios), determine cut and fill volumes, design positive drainage grading (2% minimum for paved surfaces), apply drainage to direct water away from buildings, and verify erosion control measures.

Grading and drainage are the physical foundations of site development. Understanding contour reading, slope calculation, and drainage principles ensures that water moves safely away from buildings, preventing flooding, foundation damage, and landscape erosion. This is among the most calculation-heavy topics in LEA-DSGN.

## Core Concept

Site grading is the systematic re-shaping of land elevations to achieve positive drainage, safe slopes, and buildable platforms. Drainage directs water away from structures and toward natural discharge points. The slope gradient—expressed as a percentage—is the primary tool for controlling water movement and determining site safety.

**Slope Gradient Calculation:**

Slope % = (Rise ÷ Run) × 100

Where Rise is the vertical elevation change and Run is the horizontal distance.

**Worked Example:**
A contour map shows elevation lines 5 meters apart (horizontally) with a 2-meter elevation change between them. Calculate the slope gradient:

Slope % = (2m ÷ 5m) × 100 = 40%

This represents a steep slope. Contours that are closely spaced indicate steep terrain; widely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes.

**Slope Gradient Classification:**

| Gradient Range | Classification | Characteristics | Design Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–3% | Flat | Poor natural drainage; water ponds | Grading/swleas required |
| 3–8% | Gentle | Ideal for development | Minimal grading; good drainage |
| 8–15% | Moderate | Manageable slopes | Standard grading; retaining walls possible |
| 15–25% | Steep | Significant elevation change | Retaining walls likely; geotechnical review |
| >25% | Very Steep | Unsuitable without major engineering | Slope stabilization; terracing; difficult development |

**Contour Spacing and Slope Relationship:**

On a contour map with a consistent contour interval (e.g., 1m or 5m elevation steps):
- Closely spaced contours = steep terrain (slope % is high)
- Widely spaced contours = gentle terrain (slope % is low)

**Positive Drainage Principle:**

All surface water must drain away from buildings. The recommended The recommended minimum slope for effective surface drainage is **2% (1:50 ratio)** (PD 1096 Rule XIII). (NSCP Section 302 or standard engineering practice). This ensures water flows reliably and does not accumulate near foundations, reducing risk of seepage, hydrostatic pressure, and structural damage.

**Cut-and-Fill Concepts:**

- **Cut:** Removing soil from high areas to lower the elevation or create a building platform
- **Fill:** Placing soil in low areas to raise elevation or create finished grades
- **Cut-and-fill balance:** Ideally, the volume of material cut equals the volume filled on site, minimizing off-site disposal and import costs

A site with 2m average cut and 3m average fill requires importing soil (or exporting excess cut material).

**Ramp and Pedestrian Slope Standards:**

- Accessible pedestrian ramps (BP 344 2024 IRR): 1:20 gradient = 5.0% maximum
- Vehicular ramps to parking: 1:10 gradient = 10% maximum (PD 1096)
- Short vehicular ramps (<1.5m rise): 1:8 gradient = 12.5% (maximum)
- Driveway from street: 1:10 gradient = 10% (comfortable maximum)
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Contour Map Reading — Slope Calculation and Cut-Fill Grading" description="Contour map diagram showing slope calculation methods (% gradient = rise/run × 100, degrees, ratio), cut and fill volume determination, building pad grading design, positive drainage (2% minimum for paved surfaces), and erosion control swales." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

**Slope Calculation Formula:**
Slope % = (Elevation Change ÷ Horizontal Distance) × 100

**Surface Drainage Minimum:** 2% slope away from building perimeters (1:50 ratio)

**Contour Interval and Area:** On a 1:100 scale plan with 1m contour intervals, each contour line represents a 1m vertical change. The spacing between contours (measured on the plan) indicates slope steepness.

**Grading Accuracy Standards:**
- Finished grades within ±0.1m of design elevation (site engineering standard)
- Storm drainage slopes minimum 0.5% (1:200) if surface drainage infeasible
- Subsurface drainage (French drains, perforated pipes) required in zones where surface slope <2%

**Pedestrian and Vehicular Ramp Standards:**

| Type | Gradient Ratio | Slope % | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accessible Pedestrian | 1:20 | 5.0% | BP 344 2024 IRR |
| Vehicular to Parking | 1:6 | 16.7% | Standard Practice |
| Short Vehicular (<1.5m) | 1:4.5 | 22% | Maximum Allowable |
| Driveway from Street | 1:10 | 10% | Typical Maximum |
|Wheelchair Ramp | 1:12 | 8.33% | BP 344 2024 IRR BP 344 2024 IRR |

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, where monsoon rains deliver intense precipitation and many sites have challenging topography, grading and drainage design are critical. Tropical storms can produce 100+ mm rainfall in hours, overwhelming poorly designed drainage systems. Low-lying areas near Manila Bay and major rivers face seasonal flooding; thus, finished floor elevations must be set well above projected flood levels. Site grading often requires coordination with DPWH flood control initiatives and local watershed management. Hard-to-develop sites (steep hillsides, swampy areas) demand specialized engineering and sometimes cannot be developed economically. The combination of volcanic and sedimentary geology creates variable soil bearing capacity, making geotechnical investigation essential before grading design.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Slope Percentage Calculation**
Given contour spacing and elevation change, calculate slope %. LEA presents a contour map segment with numeric elevation labels and asks you to determine if a slope meets a design threshold (e.g., "Is this slope steeper than 15%?").

**Pattern 2: Drainage Direction and Grading Logic**
A site plan shows a building and contours. Identify the direction surface water will flow and whether additional grading (swleas, ramps, terracing) is needed to achieve 2% minimum drainage slope away from the building.

**Pattern 3: Ramp Design and Gradient Compliance**
Calculate the required length of a ramp given rise and maximum allowable gradient (e.g., "A wheelchair ramp must clear a 1.2m height limit; what minimum horizontal length is required at 1:20 slope?"). Answer: 1.2m × 20 = 24.0m.

**Pattern 4: Cut-and-Fill Volume Estimation**
Estimate whether a site grading plan will require soil import/export by comparing average cut depth to average fill depth across the site.

**Pattern 5: Contour Reading Under Pressure**
Multiple contour maps are presented; identify which represents the steepest terrain, or calculate slopes from maps with varying scales and contour intervals.

<Tip>**Slope % Memory Aid:** Slope % = Rise ÷ Run × 100. For quick estimates: 1:10 slope ≈ 10%, 1:5 ≈ 20%, 1:3 ≈ 33%. Pedestrian ramp is 1:20 (≈5%, BP 344 2024 IRR), vehicle ramp is 1:6 (≈17%). Contours close together = steep; far apart = gentle.</Tip>

**Exam Tip — ERR-DSGN-014:** Minimum slope for paved surfaces = 2% (20mm/m). Minimum for unpaved/graded areas = 1.5%. Maximum slope for parking areas = 5%. Slope formula: % = rise/run × 100.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Grading and Drainage — Contour Modification and Runoff Management" description="Site section and plan showing: original vs. finished grade contours, cut and fill areas (annotated with volume quantities), 2% minimum paved surface slope, swale and detention basin locations, stormwater flow paths, and building pad elevation above flood level. Slope calculation formula (rise÷run×100) shown." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-012-02** (Site Development) for grading within site planning, **LEA-PLAN-005-05** (Site Grading) for comprehensive grading analysis, and **LEA-PLAN-005-06** (Drainage) for stormwater management integration.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Calculating slope as Run ÷ Rise instead of Rise ÷ Run (inverted formula)","Using 1:20 for pedestrian ramps instead of 1:12 (BP 344 2024 IRR)","Applying 1:8 for vehicular ramps instead of correct 1:6 (ERR-DSGN-026)","Misreading contour maps: assuming closely spaced contours indicate gentle slopes (opposite is true)","Forgetting the 2% minimum surface drainage slope requirement; assuming flat grades are acceptable","Confusing contour interval (on legend) with spacing (on map); not scaling correctly for slope calculation","Calculating cut-and-fill volumes without accounting for soil consolidation/settlement factors","Assuming positive drainage is optional; inadequate slope causes foundation damage"]} />

rows.title: Site analysis
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Conduct site analysis evaluating topography, climate, access, utilities, views, noise, and vegetation, produce site analysis diagrams documenting existing conditions, and apply findings to building orientation and site planning decisions.

Site analysis is the systematic study of existing site conditions—topography, climate, access, utilities, views, noise, and vegetation—that informs design decisions. The LEA expects you to conduct and interpret site analysis and apply its findings to site planning and building orientation decisions.

## Core Concept

A **site analysis** evaluates the built and natural environment of a property to identify opportunities and constraints for development. Unlike site plans, which show proposed building placement, a site analysis communicates the _existing conditions_ that must be understood before design begins.

**Key site analysis elements:**

1. **Topography and slope classification:**
   - Topography is represented on site plans and sections using contour lines (lines of equal elevation). Contour lines that are close together indicate steep slopes; widely spaced lines indicate gentle slopes.
   - **Slope classification:**
     - 0–3%: Flat (minimal drainage challenges)
     - 3–8%: Gentle (suitable for most building placement)
     - 8–15%: Moderate (requires split-level or stepped design; good for passive drainage)
     - 15–25%: Steep (requires significant site work; often unsuitable for building without terracing)
     - >25%: Very steep (natural slopes; building placement difficult without substantial engineering)
   - Slope percentage is calculated as: Slope (%) = (Vertical rise ÷ Horizontal run) × 100

2. **Climate and solar orientation:**
   - In the Philippines (approximately 14.5°N latitude), the sun's path varies seasonally. Equinox sun angles differ from winter and summer extremes.
   - **Building orientation best practice:** Long axis E-W (east-west). This minimizes the building's exposure to the intense morning (east) and afternoon (west) sun while maximizing north and south exposures, which are lower angle sun in tropical latitudes. This is critical for energy efficiency and thermal comfort.
   - **Sun path analysis:** Shows the sun's position at different times and seasons. In the Philippines, the sun is nearly overhead year-round (high altitude angle), making shading critical for reducing heat gain.

3. **Prevailing wind and ventilation:**
   - In the Philippines, prevailing winds are from the northeast (December–February, cooler) and southwest (June–September, monsoon rainfall). Building orientation and window placement should capitalize on northeast breezes for natural ventilation.

4. **Access and circulation:**
   - Identify street frontage, entry points, emergency access, pedestrian movement, and vehicular circulation. Analyze traffic patterns, sight lines, and safety. For buildings >4 stories, multiple stairs and elevators are required (NBC accessibility).

5. **Views and vistas:**
   - Identify desirable views (water, landscape, monuments) and obstructed or undesirable views. Orientation of glazing and balconies can frame views while blocking visual clutter.

6. **Noise and vibration sources:**
   - Identify sources: traffic (roads, highways), industrial facilities, commercial activities (markets, construction). Locate quiet zones and high-noise zones. Design accordingly: place noise-sensitive spaces (bedrooms, offices) away from noise sources.

7. **Utilities and infrastructure:**
   - Mark existing water supply, sewer connections, electrical service, gas, and communications. Identify utility easements and access points. Verify with local authorities before finalizing utility strategy.

8. **Vegetation and ecological features:**
   - Identify existing trees, vegetation, and ecological value. Large trees provide shade and stormwater management. Native vegetation reduces maintenance and irrigation. In the Philippines, banyan, calamansi, and narra trees are common and valuable.

**Building orientation in the Philippines:**
Per ERR-DSGN-035, the correct building orientation for tropical regions is **long axis E-W (east-west)**. This minimizes east-west sun exposure and maximizes north-south facades (which receive lower-angle, less intense sun). Incorrect orientation (long axis N-S) is a common exam error.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-01-core-concept" type="image" caption="Site Analysis Diagram — Sun Path, Wind Rose, and Topography" description="Composite site analysis diagram showing: sun path chart with seasonal arcs, wind rose diagram (prevailing wind direction and speed), topographic contour lines, existing vegetation, views/vistas, noise sources, and access points. Philippine tropical climate context." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-01-core-concept" type="image" caption="Site Analysis Factors — Climate, Access, Utilities, and Context Mapping" description="Multi-layer site analysis mapping: base map with property boundaries, climate overlay (solar radiation, rainfall, wind), access/circulation overlay, utility infrastructure overlay, and environmental constraints (easements, flood zones, geological hazards)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

| Analysis Element | Method | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| **Slope classification** | Contour spacing; slope % = (rise÷run)×100 | 0–3% flat; 3–8% gentle; 8–15% moderate; 15–25% steep; >25% very steep |
| **Solar orientation** | Sun path diagram at project latitude | Tropical (14.5°N): long axis E-W optimal; minimize E-W sun exposure |
| **Prevailing winds** | Wind rose diagram | NE winds (cool); SW monsoon (rain). Orient for cross-ventilation. |
| **Daylighting** | Distance from window = 2.5 × ceiling height | Effective natural light penetration for interior spaces |
| **Contour line reading** | Lines of equal elevation; spacing indicates slope steepness | Close lines = steep; far lines = gentle; use for 3D site visualization |
| **View analysis** | Diagram sight lines from building to landmarks | Identify frames, vistas, visual corridors; place viewing areas accordingly |
| **Noise zones** | Distance from source; wall construction | High noise near roads; quiet zones farther away. Design buffer spaces. |

## Philippine Practice Context

Site analysis in the Philippines must account for tropical climate factors: intense solar radiation year-round, high humidity, seasonal rainfall (May–November monsoon), and coastal considerations (salt spray, storm surge). Building orientation to capitalize on northeast breezes and minimize heat gain is essential for energy efficiency and comfort without mechanical cooling. Sloping sites are common in upland and hilly regions (Luzon, Visayas); site analysis must evaluate terracing, cut-and-fill, and drainage. Vegetation analysis is important because large trees (mango, calamansi, coconut) provide natural shade and cooling, reducing construction and operating costs. Noise analysis is critical in dense urban areas (Metro Manila, Cebu, Davao) where traffic and commercial activity create significant sound levels.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Slope classification and interpretation**
A site plan shows contour lines at 2 m intervals. Over a 50 m horizontal distance, the contour lines drop 8 m (elevation change). The candidate must calculate the slope percentage (8 ÷ 50 = 16%) and classify it as "moderate" (8–15% range, actually 16%, so boundary case or slightly steep). This tests quantitative and qualitative interpretation.

**Pattern 2: Building orientation decision**
A candidate is given a site with primary street frontage on the east side and asked to position a building. Correct reasoning: orient the long axis E-W so the street-facing side is north or south (lower sun angle), not east (direct morning sun). Incorrect orientation (long axis N-S) is a common error.

**Pattern 3: Site constraint analysis**
A site analysis shows high noise on the western boundary (major road), view opportunities to the north, and gentle slope (5% gradient). The candidate must infer: place noise-sensitive spaces (bedrooms, offices) on eastern side; orient living areas and views toward north; use the gentle slope for terracing or multi-level design. This integrates multiple site analysis findings.

<Tip>
**Memory aid:** "E-W Orientation Rule" — In tropical Philippines, orient buildings with long axis E-W (east-west). This minimizes harsh E and W sun, maximizes gentle N-S sun. Place primary views and living spaces on N or S facades. This is ERR-DSGN-035 territory—incorrect orientation is a common exam error.
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Site analysis must document: N arrow, prevailing wind direction, sun path, adjacent uses, access points, utility locations, easements, flood hazards, noise sources, and significant vegetation. Omissions = design errors.

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-012-02** (Site Development) for applying site analysis findings, **LEA-PLAN-004-01** (Physical Site Considerations) for comprehensive site analysis methodology, and **LEA-DSGN-009-01** (Passive Design) for climate-responsive orientation.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["ERR-DSGN-035: Orienting buildings with long axis N-S instead of E-W in tropical Philippines; always prioritize E-W orientation for energy efficiency.","Misinterpreting contour lines as individual building levels rather than topographic data; contours show existing grades and slopes, not proposed floor levels.","Calculating slope percentage incorrectly (using vertical only, or forgetting to convert percentage); always use slope % = (rise÷run)×100.","Placing noise-sensitive spaces (bedrooms, offices) near noise sources (streets, highways) without considering acoustic design or buffers.","Ignoring utility locations and easements; utilities require clear access and cannot be built over.","Failing to account for seasonal wind changes (NE in winter, SW in monsoon) in ventilation and facade design.","Underestimating tree preservation value; existing large trees provide shade, stormwater absorption, and cost savings.","Not analyzing view opportunities and sight lines; overlooking chances to frame desirable views or block undesirable ones.","Assuming all sloping sites are unsuitable for building; slopes 0–15% are buildable and often provide design opportunities.","Omitting flood risk analysis in low-lying or coastal areas; critical for site safety and code compliance."]} />

rows.title: Concrete Materials and Mix Design
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Identify the components of concrete: cement, aggregates, water, and admixtures
- Explain how the water-cement ratio (w/c) controls strength and durability
- Define slump and its relationship to workability
- State standard concrete unit weight (2,400 kg/m³) and common compressive strengths
- Describe proper curing procedures and their importance

Concrete is a composite material made from cement, aggregates (fine and coarse), water, and optional admixtures. Understanding these components and their proportions—especially the water-cement ratio—determines concrete workability, strength, durability, and long-term performance in reinforced concrete structures.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-006-01-core-concept" type="image" caption="Concrete Mix Composition — Cement, Aggregates, Water, Admixtures" description="Cross-section diagram of concrete showing: (1) Fine aggregate (sand) filling voids between coarse aggregate; (2) Coarse aggregate (gravel/crushed stone) as primary bulk; (3) Cement paste binding aggregates; (4) Water-filled capillary pores; (5) Air voids. Proportioning pie chart for typical mix (cement 10-15%, water 15-20%, aggregates 60-75%). Water-cement ratio effect on strength shown as comparison chart." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

Concrete is created by mixing Portland cement with fine aggregate (sand), coarse aggregate (gravel or crushed stone), water, and sometimes chemical or mineral admixtures. The cement chemically reacts with water in a process called hydration, binding the aggregates into a solid mass.

**Portland Cement** is the primary binder. When mixed with water, it undergoes hydration reactions that develop strength over time. The strength gain is most rapid in the first 28 days (the standard curing period) but continues for years.

**Aggregates** comprise 70–80% of concrete volume. Fine aggregate (sand) fills spaces and improves workability; coarse aggregate (gravel, typically 10–40 mm) provides bulk and stiffness. Well-graded aggregates—with proper particle size distribution—minimize voids and produce stronger, denser concrete.

**Water-Cement Ratio (w/c)** is the mass ratio of water to cement. It is the single most critical factor controlling concrete strength and durability. A lower w/c ratio (typically 0.40–0.55 for structural concrete) produces stronger, denser, less permeable concrete but reduces workability. A higher w/c ratio improves workability but reduces strength and increases long-term creep and shrinkage.

**Slump** measures concrete workability—the distance a concrete cone subsides vertically after the cone is lifted. Higher slump (e.g., 100–150 mm) indicates more flow and easier placement; lower slump (e.g., 25–50 mm) indicates stiffer, denser concrete. Slump varies by application: thin slabs and heavily reinforced sections need higher slump; massive sections may use lower slump.

**Curing** is the process of maintaining moisture and temperature after placement to allow hydration to continue. Proper curing—typically 7 days moist or covered, or 28 days in air—is essential for reaching design strength and durability. Early thermal stresses and drying shrinkage during poor curing reduce long-term performance.

**Admixtures** are optional additives that modify concrete properties. Water reducers lower the water needed for a given slump, allowing lower w/c without loss of workability. Air entrainers create tiny air bubbles (3–7% by volume) to improve freeze-thaw durability. Retarders slow hydration for longer working time in hot weather. Pozzolans (fly ash, silica fume) react with cement hydration products, improving long-term strength, reducing permeability, and reducing heat of hydration.

**Concrete Unit Weight** for normal-weight concrete is approximately 2,400 kg/m³. Lightweight concrete weighs 1,600–1,840 kg/m³ and uses expanded clay or slate aggregates; heavyweight concrete (2,800–3,200 kg/m³) uses iron ore or barites for radiation shielding.

**Concrete Properties at 28 Days:**
- Compressive strength: _f'_c (cylinder strength) is the standard design parameter. Common values: residential 21 MPa, commercial 24–28 MPa, high-rise columns 35–41 MPa.
- Modulus of elasticity: _E_c = 4,700√_f'_c MPa (normal-weight concrete).
- Flexural strength (modulus of rupture): _f_r = 0.62λ√_f'_c MPa (λ = 1.0 for normal weight).
- Strain at crushing: ε_u = 0.003 (3 parts per thousand). This is the assumed ultimate compressive strain for reinforced concrete design.

Creep—the long-term increase in strain under sustained load—is a time-dependent property controlled by w/c, curing, and humidity. Higher w/c and poor curing increase creep; low humidity reduces creep compared to continuous wet conditions.

## Key Provisions

| Component | Definition | Typical Range/Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Cement Content** | Mass of Portland cement per m³ | 280–420 kg/m³ |
| **Water-Cement Ratio** | Mass of water ÷ mass of cement | 0.40–0.65 |
| **Fine Aggregate** | Sand, particles < 5 mm | 35–45% of total aggregate |
| **Coarse Aggregate** | Gravel/stone, 10–40 mm | 55–65% of total aggregate |
| **Slump (Workability)** | Vertical subsidence of standard cone | 25–150 mm (varies by use) |
| **Standard Strength Test** | 150 mm diameter × 300 mm tall cylinder | Tested at 28 days |
| **Unit Weight (Normal)** | Density of hardened concrete | ~2,400 kg/m³ |
| **Lightweight Concrete** | Unit weight ≤ 1,840 kg/m³ | Density ≤ 1,840 kg/m³ |
| **Common _f'_c Values** | Residential / Commercial / High-rise | 21 / 24–28 / 35–41 MPa |

**Compressive Strength Relationship:**
- _E_c = 4,700√_f'_c MPa
- _f_r = 0.62√_f'_c MPa (normal weight, λ = 1.0)
- Ultimate strain: ε_u = 0.003

**Water-Cement Ratio Effect on Durability (Philippine Practice):**
For exposure to seawater or aggressive environments (common in coastal regions), w/c ≤ 0.50 and higher cement content (380–420 kg/m³) are required. For non-aggressive environments (inland), w/c ≤ 0.55 is typical.

## Philippine Practice Context

The Philippine National Structural Code (PNSC) requires concrete specifications based on exposure class. Coastal projects and structures in acidic or saline environments must use low w/c ratios and pozzolanic admixtures (fly ash is locally available). Tropical curing conditions—high temperature and humidity—accelerate early hydration but also increase drying shrinkage. Proper curing (keeping concrete wet for at least 7 days) is critical in the tropical climate to prevent early cracking and ensure durability in the humid, corrosive environment.

## How It's Tested

1. **Compressive Strength (ASTM C39):** Standard 150 × 300 mm cylinders are cast, cured, and tested at 28 days. Three cylinders per test date are common. Strength is reported as the average of the three; any specimen more than 15% below average is rejected unless the average of remaining two is at least 85% of the specified _f'_c.

2. **Slump Test (ASTM C143):** A 300 mm tall, 100 mm top/200 mm bottom diameter cone is lifted vertically after being filled with fresh concrete. The vertical distance from the original cone height to the highest point of subsided concrete is the slump. Measured immediately after placement in mm.

3. **Unit Weight and Yield (ASTM C138):** A standard container of known volume is filled with fresh concrete. The mass of concrete is divided by container volume to determine unit weight. Yield (m³ per batch) is calculated to verify mix design proportions.

<Tip>The water-cement ratio is your strongest lever to control concrete strength and durability. Every project in the Philippines should specify w/c ≤ 0.50 for coastal or aggressive environments and w/c ≤ 0.55 for normal exposure. Proper 7-day curing is non-negotiable in tropical climates.</Tip>

## Related Articles
