See also: **Deformed Bars** (lea-strc-006-02) for reinforcement used with concrete, **Concrete Cover** (lea-strc-007-01) for protection requirements, and **Prestressing** (lea-strc-006-04) for an advanced concrete technique.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Confusing w/c ratio with water content. A w/c = 0.50 means 0.5 kg water per 1 kg cement, not 50 kg water per m³. Lower w/c always means stronger concrete if the mix is properly proportioned.", "Assuming 7-day strength equals 28-day strength. Concrete at 7 days is typically 60–75% of 28-day strength. Design is always based on 28-day strength; early testing is for quality control only.", "Using unit weight 2,000 or 2,300 kg/m³ instead of 2,400 kg/m³. This error propagates through load calculations and self-weight estimates. Standard normal-weight concrete is 2,400 kg/m³.", "Neglecting curing in hot, dry conditions. In the Philippines, poor curing in tropical heat causes severe drying shrinkage cracking and reduced long-term durability, even if initial 28-day strength is adequate." ]} />

rows.title: Board Foot Measurement
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Identify Philippine timber species by strength group, density, and common applications, and explain the DENR regulatory framework governing timber sourcing, grading, and documentation for architectural specifications.
## Core Concept

A board foot (BF) is the standard unit of lumber volume in the Philippines and North America. It is defined as a piece of wood measuring 1 foot in length, 1 foot in width, and 1 inch in thickness.

The board foot formula is the foundation of all lumber quantity and cost calculations in construction. Contractors use it to estimate material costs, designers use it to specify structural capacity, and inspectors use it to verify delivered quantities.

## Board Foot Formula

The exact formula is:

**Board Feet (BF) = (T × W × L) / 12**

Where:
- **T** = thickness in inches
- **W** = width in inches
- **L** = length in feet
- **12** = constant (converts cubic inches to board feet)

Note the critical detail: length must be in feet; thickness and width must be in inches. Failure to convert units correctly is the most common error.

<Tip>Always convert length to feet FIRST before applying the formula. If a measurement is given in inches, divide by 12 to convert to feet.</Tip>


<ArticleMedia id="media-lumber-measurement-diagram" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Diagram showing board foot measurement: thickness (T), width (W), and length (L) dimensions on a lumber piece"
  caption="Future diagram: board foot measurement dimensions"
  suggestedAsset="Annotated 3D diagram of lumber with T×W×L callouts"
  placementIntent="Helps learners understand the physical meaning of the board foot formula" />

## Nominal vs. Actual Dimensions

Philippine and North American lumber is sold by _nominal_ dimensions but delivered at _actual_ dimensions, which are smaller to account for drying and finishing.

<WikiExamTable headers={["Nominal Size (in)", "Actual Size (in)", "Usage"]} rows={[["1 × 4", "3/4 × 3.5", "Flooring, siding, shelving"], ["1 × 6", "3/4 × 5.5", "Paneling, deck boards"], ["1 × 8", "3/4 × 7.25", "Deck boards, trim"], ["2 × 4", "1.5 × 3.5", "Framing, studs, joists"], ["2 × 6", "1.5 × 5.5", "Beams, joists, blocking"], ["2 × 8", "1.5 × 7.25", "Beams, joists"], ["4 × 4", "3.5 × 3.5", "Posts, large timbers"], ["6 × 6", "5.5 × 5.5", "Heavy posts, columns"]]} />

When calculating board feet, _always use actual dimensions_ for the most accurate volume. However, many quick-reference tables and some Philippine lumber sellers list board feet using nominal dimensions, which introduces 5—10% error.

## Philippine Lumber Standards and Grading Groups

Philippine timber is classified by specific gravity into grading groups that determine structural capacity and pricing:

- **Group I** (hardest, heaviest): Specific gravity >0.71. Examples: yakal, molave, kamagong. Used for heavy structural applications and fine cabinetry.
- **Group II** (medium-hard): Specific gravity 0.61—0.71. Examples: narra, tanguile, mayapis. Used for general construction and exterior applications.
- **Group III** (medium): Specific gravity 0.51—0.60. Examples: white lauan, red lauan. Used for interior framing and non-structural applications.
- **Group IV** (lightest): Specific gravity ≤0.50. Examples: pine, spruce. Used for temporary construction and non-structural applications in the Philippines (pine is imported).

The DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) specifies minimum grades and species for structural lumber in government projects. NSCP 2015 Section 2401 references Philippine lumber grading through the National Lumber Grading Committee (NLGC).


<ArticleMedia id="media-ph-timber-species-chart" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Reference chart of Philippine timber species: narra, molave, yakal, apitong, mahogany, ipil with strength group, density, and common architectural applications"
  caption="Future chart: Philippine timber species by strength group, density, and application"
  suggestedAsset="Material property comparison table with species identification photos"
  placementIntent="Provides reference for selecting Philippine timber species for construction" />
## Philippine Lumber Grading Classifications

Lumber less than 1 inch in thickness is graded and measured the same as 1 inch lumber. All lumber is graded on the poorer side of the piece.

- **First and Seconds (F&S)**: Highest grade, suitable for visible cabinetry and fine joinery. Few knots or defects allowed.
- **Export Common**: Good structural quality, minor surface defects acceptable. Most export lumber from Philippine mills meets this grade.
- **Merchantable**: Standard construction grade, visible defects acceptable. Most locally sold lumber is Merchantable grade.
- **Culls**: Below Merchantable grade, structural use not recommended. Often rejected at delivery.

## Standard Lumber Lengths in the Philippine Market

Lumber is commonly sold in the following lengths (all in feet):

- 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20 feet

Lumber longer than 20 feet is available but may require special order and premium pricing.

Shorter lengths (4—6 feet) are often called "shorts" or "chairstock" and command a lower price per board foot than longer pieces because they have less structural utility and greater waste potential.

## Worked Examples

<Example title="Example 1: Calculating Board Feet for Standard Framing Lumber">

A construction project requires 20 pieces of 2 × 4 lumber, each 12 feet long. Calculate the total board feet.

**Step 1:** Identify actual dimensions.
- Nominal 2 × 4 = actual 1.5 × 3.5 inches
- Length = 12 feet

**Step 2:** Apply the formula.
- BF = (T × W × L) / 12
- BF per piece = (1.5 × 3.5 × 12) / 12
- BF per piece = (63) / 12 = 5.25 BF

**Step 3:** Calculate total for 20 pieces.
- Total BF = 5.25 × 20 = 105 board feet

**Answer:** The project requires 105 board feet of 2 × 4 lumber.

</Example>

<Example title="Example 2: Philippine Hardwood Decking Calculation">

A residential deck requires 200 linear feet of narra decking boards. The boards are 1 × 6 nominal (3/4 × 5.5 actual) in width. How many board feet are required?

**Step 1:** Identify dimensions.
- Thickness: 3/4 inch
- Width: 5.5 inches
- Total linear length: 200 feet

**Step 2:** Apply the formula (treating total linear footage as the combined length).
- BF = (T × W × L) / 12
- BF = (0.75 × 5.5 × 200) / 12
- BF = (825) / 12 = 68.75 BF

**Answer:** The deck requires 68.75 board feet of 1 × 6 narra.

**Note:** If the narra is Group II hardwood at $3.50/BF (typical 2024 Philippine market price), the total material cost would be approximately 68.75 × $3.50 = $240.63 (before waste and installation allowance).

</Example>

## Quick-Reference Computation Table

Use this table to estimate board feet for common sizes quickly:

<WikiExamTable headers={["Size (Nominal)", "BF per 8-ft Length", "BF per 12-ft Length", "BF per 16-ft Length"]} rows={[["1 × 4", "2.67", "4.0", "5.33"], ["1 × 6", "4.0", "6.0", "8.0"], ["1 × 8", "5.33", "8.0", "10.67"], ["2 × 4", "5.33", "8.0", "10.67"], ["2 × 6", "8.0", "12.0", "16.0"], ["2 × 8", "10.67", "16.0", "21.33"], ["4 × 4", "10.67", "16.0", "21.33"], ["6 × 6", "24.0", "36.0", "48.0"]]} />

These values use actual lumber dimensions and are accurate for Philippine and North American lumber.

## Common Calculation Errors

<WikiMistakeCard
  mistake="Using nominal dimensions in the formula instead of actual dimensions"
  correction="The formula requires actual dimensions. A nominal 2 × 4 is actually 1.5 × 3.5 inches. Using 2 and 4 directly inflates the calculated volume by approximately 10%."
  context="Contractors sometimes use quick nominal-based mental math, which leads to under-ordering lumber or mis-estimating costs." />

<WikiMistakeCard
  mistake="Forgetting to convert length from inches to feet"
  correction="If length is given in inches (e.g., 144 inches), divide by 12 to convert to feet (144 / 12 = 12 feet). Failing to convert results in 144 times too much volume."
  context="A common student error when reading specifications that list dimensions in inches throughout." />

<WikiMistakeCard
  mistake="Adding up board feet from multiple pieces by multiplying piece count × nominal BF, without verifying the actual length of each piece"
  correction="Always confirm the actual length of each piece. A 'standard' 2 × 4 might be 8 feet or 12 feet depending on supplier and grade. Mixing lengths leads to cost overruns or shortfalls."
  context="Real-world deliveries often include mixed lengths; careless counting creates surprises during framing." />

<WikiMistakeList
  title="Other Common Errors"
  items={[
    "Using 12 as a divisor incorrectly: The formula divides by 12 because 1 board foot = 144 cubic inches (12 × 12), and the formula produces cubic inches in the numerator. Do not change the divisor.",
    "Confusing board feet with linear feet or square feet: Board feet measure volume (cubic capacity); linear feet measure length; square feet measure area. They are not interchangeable.",
    "Grading errors: Assuming all Philippine lumber is the same price regardless of species. Group I hardwoods (yakal, molave) cost 2—3 times more than Group IV softwoods. Always verify grade and species.",
    "Waste allowance omission: Cutting, damage, and defects consume approximately 10—15% of delivered lumber. Always order 1.1—1.15 times the calculated board feet.",
    "Mismatching nominal length: A lumber specification might call for 2 × 8 at 16 feet, but the supplier delivers 2 × 8 at 14 feet. Always verify length before final payment."
  ]} />

## Philippine DPWH Specifications for Structural Lumber

The DPWH specifies lumber grading, species, and sizing for government projects:

- **Structural grade requirement:** Minimum F&S or Export Common grade for primary members (beams, columns)
- **Species for structural use:** Group I or II only (yakal, molave, narra approved; pine not approved for main structural members)
- **Moisture content:** 15% maximum at time of delivery (kiln-dried specification)
- **Defect limits:** Knots limited to 1/4 of face width; slope of grain not to exceed 1:15

NSCP 2015 Section 2401 references DPWH standards and allows use of visual grading rules from the Philippine National Lumber Grading Committee (NLGC) or equivalent.

## How It's Tested

The LEA expects you to:

1. Apply the board foot formula correctly with proper unit conversions
2. Distinguish nominal from actual dimensions and choose the correct dimensions for calculations
3. Calculate total board feet for projects with multiple pieces or variable lengths
4. Work backward from a desired board foot quantity to determine piece count or dimensions
5. Identify common grading and species errors in specifications
6. Estimate material cost using market prices and board feet
7. Account for waste and determine minimum order quantities
8. Apply DPWH and NSCP 2015 requirements for Philippine structural lumber

Typical questions present a project scope (deck, framing, cabinetry) and ask you to calculate total board feet, specify appropriate species/grade, and determine delivered cost. Some questions test your ability to recognize when a given dimension set produces an incorrect or unattainable board foot total.

<Tip>Always write out the formula step-by-step on the exam. Show unit conversions explicitly (e.g., "Length = 144 inches ÷ 12 = 12 feet"). This reduces errors and earns partial credit if final answer is incorrect.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also within Wood and Timber Products: **lea-matl-001-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-001-04-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Philippine timber stress groups rank species by bending
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal

By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define Philippine timber stress groups: Group I (highest strength) through Group IV
- Identify which stress group a given species belongs to
- Explain how stress group affects allowable bending and compression values
- State the basis for stress group classification (testing of small clear specimens)

---
## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-009-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Philippine Timber Stress Groups — Bending and Tension/Compression Ratings" description="Reference diagram showing Philippine timber stress groups ranked by bending stress Fb: Group I (highest strength), Group II (intermediate), Group III (lowest). Each group shown with allowable stress values for bending, tension parallel to grain, compression parallel/perpendicular to grain, shear parallel to grain, and modulus of elasticity. Common species listed for each group (e.g., Narra, Yakal, Mahogany, Guijo, Red Lauan)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />
Philippine timber stress groups rank species by bending and compression capacity, with Group I (highest strength) and Group IV (lowest strength) as the extremes. Within each group, species show similar allowable stresses under the Allowable Stress Design method. Timber products fall into three main categories: solid sawn lumber, fiberboard (density >160 but <497 kg/m³), and hardboard (density ≥497 kg/m³). Grading is not cosmetic—it is a mechanical classification tied to defect tolerance, knot size, slope-of-grain limits, and moisture content. A timber element graded as "Select Structural" (best grade) has stricter knot and defect limits than "No. 2 Common" (standard grade), and allowable stresses differ accordingly. Lumber dimensions follow nominal (timber size as marketed) and actual (true milled size) conventions: a nominal 2×4 is actually 1.5" × 3.5" (38 × 89 mm). The distinction is critical in design calculations. Fiberboard and hardboard are engineered products with uniform density and are not interchangeable with solid lumber—they are specified by density range and intended use (sheathing, subflooring, acoustic backing). Unit weight for Philippine hardwood timber ranges from 5–12 kN/m³; fiberboard (1.6–5.0 kN/m³) and hardboard have specified densities for non-structural uses.

## Key Provisions

### Philippine Timber Stress Groups

<WikiExamTable headers={["Stress Group", "Bending Capacity", "Example Species"]} rows={[  ["I (Highest)", "Very High", "Yakal, Molave, Malabayabas, Sasalit"], ["II", "High", "Apitong, Narra, Tindalo, Guijo, Ipil"] ["III", "Moderate", "Lauan, Tanguile, Red Lauan"], ["IV (Lowest)", "Lower", "White Lauan, Almaciga"] ]} />

### Lumber Grade Definitions
- _Select Structural_: Highest quality. Minimal knots, tight grain, tight wane. Used for exposed, high-stress applications.
- _No. 1 Common_: Good quality. Larger knots permitted. Suitable for standard structural use.
- _No. 2 Common_: Standard grade. Defects more visible. Allowable stresses reduced. General-purpose framing and non-exposed use.
- _Construction Grade_: Lowest quality. High knot frequency, larger checks permitted. Limited to temporary or lightly loaded applications.

### Dimension Definitions
- _Nominal_: Timber size as marketed (e.g., 2×4, 4×12). Used for material orders.
- _Actual_: True milled size after surfacing (e.g., 2×4 nominal = 1.5" × 3.5" actual). Used for all design calculations.
- _Adjustment_: Design tables account for moisture content (green vs. dry). Green timber (≥19% moisture) has lower allowable stresses than kiln-dried (≤15%).

### Wood Product Density Classifications
  ["Solid Lumber", "Varies by species", "Beams, joists, columns, primary structure"]
  ]}
/>

### Allowable Stress Selection Logic
- _Step 1_: Identify species and stress group (I, II, III, IV).
- _Step 2_: Identify grade (Select Structural, No. 1, No. 2, Construction).
- _Step 3_: Identify moisture condition (green or dry). Apply adjustment factor if required.
- _Step 4_: Look up allowable bending (Fb) and horizontal shear (Fv) stresses from Philippine timber design manual or NatCor supplement.

## Philippine Practice Context
Philippine lumber grading is governed by the National Timber Code and referenced by the Philippine Building Code. Yakal (Group I) commands premium allowable stresses due to high density and strength; Lauan and Red Lauan (Group III) are more economical and widely available. Fiberboard and hardboard are imported engineered products or locally manufactured; their use in structural design is limited to non-primary-load paths (infill, backing, insulation). Field verification of grade markings is common practice in Philippine construction—unmarked or undocumented timber is often reclassified by visual inspection or reduced to the lowest safe grade by the engineer.

## How It's Tested

### Pattern 1: Stress Group Identification
"A timber lintel is designed from Narra. Which stress group applies?"
- Answer: Group II (Narra is classified as Group II).
- Takeaway: Species determines group; grade refinement comes next.

### Pattern 2: Dimension Conversion
"A beam is specified as nominal 6×12 lumber, actual dimensions 5.5" × 11.5". Which dimension set is used in the section modulus calculation?"
- Answer: Actual dimensions (5.5" × 11.5") are used in all structural calculations.
- Takeaway: Nominal is for purchasing; actual is for design.

### Pattern 3: Product Suitability
"Can fiberboard (density 250 kg/m³) be used as a primary load-bearing beam in a multi-story building?"
- Answer: No. Fiberboard is an infill/backing product, not a primary structural element. Solid lumber or engineered lumber (LVL, glulam) must be used.
- Takeaway: Product category, not just density, determines application scope.

<Tip>Group I = highest capacity (Yakal, Molave); Group IV = lowest (White Lauan, Red Balau). Always verify the specific group from the design manual or code supplement.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Timber Durability** (lea-strc-009-01) for complementary wood properties, **Timber ASD** (lea-strc-009-03) for how stress group values enter design, and **Stress-Strain** (lea-strc-003-01) for the material behavior foundation.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Using nominal dimensions in design calculations. Nominal 2×4 is 1.5×3.5; actual dimensions are required.", "Confusing Narra (Group II) with Yakal or Molave (Group I) and applying wrong allowable stresses.", "Treating fiberboard and hardboard as interchangeable with solid lumber. Density alone does not qualify them for primary structural duty.", "Ignoring moisture adjustment factors. Green lumber (≥19% MC) may have 10–15% lower allowable stresses than kiln-dried.", "Applying allowable stresses from a different species group without re-verifying the table." ]} />

rows.title: Social architecture (also termed socially responsive
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
<Callout>
Social architecture reorients the design process from top-down professional authority to participatory engagement with end-users and affected communities. The LEA tests whether you understand the theoretical shift: architecture as a **solution imposed by experts** versus architecture as a **process negotiated among stakeholders**. You must master participatory methodologies, equity frameworks, and the distinction between superficial "community input" and genuine power-sharing in design.
</Callout>

## Learning Goal

- Distinguish genuine sustainability (reducing total environmental impact across a building's lifecycle) from greenwashing (cosmetic claims without systematic change).
- Define embodied carbon, operational energy, lifecycle assessment, and passive/active system balance.
- Explain how sustainable architecture treats environmental performance as a primary design generator equivalent to program, structure, and aesthetics.

## Core Concept

<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-theo-007-10-social-architecture" type="image" caption="Social Architecture — Community-Engaged Design and Arnstein's Ladder of Participation" alt="Concept diagram showing Arnstein's Ladder (1969) with eight rungs from bottom to top: (1) Manipulation, (2) Therapy, (3) Informing, (4) Consultation, (5) Placation, (6) Partnership, (7) Delegated Power, (8) Citizen Control. Horizontal line at rung 5-6 dividing 'Tokenism' (below) from 'Citizen Power' (above). Callout box: 'Participatory design = genuine power-sharing (rungs 6-8); superficial community input = token consultation (rungs 3-5)'. Philippine bayanihan iconography at top rung." suggestedAsset="Ladder diagram showing levels of community participation in architectural design" status="placeholder" />

Social architecture (also termed socially responsive architecture, community-engaged design, or participatory architecture) treats **the community affected by the building as primary stakeholders in design, not mere end-users**. This represents a fundamental epistemological shift from the modernist model where architects possessed privileged knowledge and communities were passive recipients.

<Tip>
**Arnstein's ladder in three tiers**: (1) Non-participation/tokenism where professionals decide and "consult" after; (2) Genuine participation where professionals and community negotiate decisions together; (3) Community control where community has ultimate authority and professionals advise. Most projects claim #2; many settle for #1. Recognize which level you are operating at and be honest about it.
</Tip>

**The Critique of Professional Autonomy**

Modernism consolidated architectural authority: trained professionals possessed technical knowledge unavailable to the public; design decisions were justified through functional and aesthetic principles legible only to the profession. Post-occupancy evaluation research (widely available by the 1970s) revealed the consequences: buildings designed without user input frequently failed to accommodate actual behavior. Oscar Newman's *Defensible Space* (1972) analyzed how modernist housing designs—intended as democratic, efficient, and rational—created instead unsafe, alienated environments because physical form ignored social and behavioral realities.

Social architecture emerged as ethical corrective: if buildings shape behavior and experience, those affected should have voice in design. This is not merely ethical sentiment but epistemological necessity—communities possess place-based knowledge, experiential understanding, and contextual information that professionals lack.

**Participation Frameworks and Graduated Engagement**

Not all community engagement is equivalent. Sherry Arnstein's "Ladder of Citizen Participation" (1969, still foundational) distinguishes levels:

1. **Non-participation**: Manipulation or therapy masquerading as participation; the "community" is informed of decisions already made. Common in projects where consultation is performative.

2. **Tokenism**: Informing, consulting, placating communities but final authority remains with professionals/authorities. Communities can comment; professionals decide. The gap between input and implementation is not bridged.

3. **Citizen Power**: Partnership, delegation, and control; communities share or hold decision-making authority. Decisions reflect community preferences, even if professionally suboptimal.

Social architecture aspires to the third category but often settles into the second—consultation without power transfer. The LEA tests whether you can identify this distinction and critique inadequate participation.

**Methodological Approaches**

Contemporary social architecture employs multiple engagement methods:

**Participatory Design Workshops**: Communities work with designers in structured sessions—mapping, physical modeling, scenario-building. The designer role shifts from conceiving solutions to facilitating collective imagination. Designers contribute technical feasibility; communities contribute lived experience and priorities.

**Community-Based Planning**: Long-term engagement where professional designers embed in communities for extended periods, developing trust and understanding place-specific dynamics. This contrasts with one-off charrettes that can feel extractive.

**Asset-Based Development**: Rather than needs-assessment frameworks (which position communities as deficient), asset-based approaches inventory existing community resources, skills, relationships, and aspirations. The design builds on strengths, not remediation.

**Co-Design and Co-Production**: In its strongest form, communities participate in design decisions, construction, and ongoing maintenance. This is resource-intensive but creates ownership and sustains buildings long-term. Examples include self-build housing cooperatives and community fabrication workshops.

**Precedent: Participatory Housing and Sennett's Collective Craftsmanship**

Lucien Kroll's housing developments in Belgium (1970s–present) pioneered participatory design in residential architecture. Rather than master-planned housing estates, Kroll involved future residents in design decisions—spatial configurations, material choices, facade treatments. The result: buildings that appear collaged, even chaotic, but are deeply responsive to diverse household requirements. Kroll's theoretical position: **order imposed top-down is alienating; diversity emerging from negotiated decision-making is humanizing**.

Richard Sennett's *The Craftsman* (2008) theorizes that participatory design reconnects people to material making and decision-shaping. When residents participate in construction decisions, they develop tacit understanding—feel for materials, awareness of consequences, investment in stewardship. This contrasts with the modernist separation of designer, builder, and user into sealed professional roles.

**Social Equity and Systemic Justice**

Contemporary social architecture increasingly addresses **systemic inequities**—how design perpetuates or ameliorates class, racial, and gendered injustices.

**Housing as Fundamental Right**: Architecture for displaced populations, informal settlers, and economically marginalized communities treats housing not as commodity but as human right. Leajandro Aravena's Elemental (Chile) designs housing that is intentionally incomplete—half-built structures that families can expand and customize according to resources and needs. This reflects both pragmatic resource constraints and philosophical position: **the community, not the professional, determines final form**. The architecture provides framework (utilities, structure, public space); families provide labor and vision.

**Gentrification and Displacement Resistance**: Where neighborhoods face displacement through development, social architecture shifts from improvement-focused (which can trigger gentrification) to community-controlled development ensuring existing residents benefit. This requires political-economic interventions beyond architecture—community land trusts, anti-displacement covenants, community-controlled developer selection.

**Racialized Space and Inclusive Design**: Design frameworks often encode racial and class assumptions invisibly. Contemporary social architecture explicitly names these—how do design standards reflect particular bodies, abilities, cultural practices? Who is centered in the design brief? Public space design, for example, has historically centered male, able-bodied, white bodies; inclusive design centers women, disabled people, elders, children, and diverse cultural practices (prayer spaces, informal commerce, multigenerational gathering).

**Indigenous Sovereignty and Design Authority**

A crucial contemporary framework: **Indigenous communities should control design decisions affecting Indigenous lands**. This reflects broader decolonization principles and acknowledges that Indigenous place-based knowledge is epistemologically equivalent to (and often superior to) professional technical knowledge.

Examples:

- **Snoqualmie Tribe Housing** (Washington State): Rather than imposing external design standards, projects are co-designed with tribal members, centering Indigenous spatial practices and cosmology.
- **Aboriginal Community Centers** (Australia): Recognition that Indigenous cultural spaces have specific spatial and ceremonial requirements often absent from standard public facility design.

This is more radical than typical participation—it is **design control by the affected community, with professional architects as consultants**, not authorities.

<Note>
Indigenous sovereignty in design represents decolonial principle: communities with millennia of place-based knowledge are not "lacking expertise" but are holders of epistemic authority equivleant to or exceeding professional training. This shift requires professionals to relinquish authority positioning, not merely "involve" Indigenous peoples in professionally-led processes. True decolonial design inverts the hierarchy: Indigenous community leads, professionals support.
</Note>

**Slum Upgrading and Incremental Development**

In the Global South, where formal housing is inaccessible and informal settlements (slums) house majority populations, social architecture engages informal communities in upgrading existing settlements rather than demolition-based redevelopment. Successful models:

**Participatory Slum Upgrading**: Residents of informal settlements identify priority infrastructure (drainage, pathways, water, sanitation) and decide collectively on interventions. Physical improvements (built with community labor) are paired with tenure security, livelihood development, and community organizing. The architecture is modest—pathways, drainage, community facilities—but embedded in genuine community control.

**Philippines Examples**: Barangay-level community development projects often employ participatory budgeting and community engagement. The Port Area Community Development and Housing Project (PACDH) in Tondo involved residents in design and development of relocation housing, though with complex power dynamics.

**Theoretical Risks and Critiques**

**Romantic Idealization**: Social architecture can idealize community wisdom while overlooking internal power asymmetries (patriarchy, elites dominating decisions, marginalization of minorities within communities). Genuine participation requires managing these, not assuming communities are inherently democratic.

**Neoliberal Co-optation**: Community participation can be deployed as neoliberal strategy—downloading responsibility onto communities ("self-help" housing) while withdrawing state resource provision. Aravena's incremental housing reflects genuine constraint but also fits neoliberal logic of minimal public intervention.

**Professional Disempowerment**: Overvaluing community input while undervaluing professional expertise can result in architecturally incoherent or functionally problematic designs. The professional contribution—technical knowledge, aesthetic judgment, systems thinking—remains necessary.

**Time and Resource Burden**: Genuine participation requires extensive time and resources (facilitators, workshops, decision-making processes, multiple revision cycles). Many projects cannot sustain this; participation becomes abbreviated or performed.

Contemporary social architecture increasingly emphasizes **negotiation over romance**: communities and professionals have different knowledge; the process is fundamentally conflictual (desires exceed resources, preferences diverge); the outcome reflects negotiated compromise, not consensus harmony.

<Warn>
Beware romanticization: communities are not inherently unified or democratic. Participatory design can amplify internal power hierarchies—patriarchs override women, elites silence marginalized members, landowners exclude renters. "Community voice" is often whose voice gets heard. Genuine social architecture requires active management of internal power dynamics, not naive assumption that participation automatically produces justice or inclusivity.
</Warn>

## Key Facts and Testable Items

<WikiExamTable headers={["Framework", "Theorist", "Core Principle", "Critique/Limitation"]} rows={[['["Ladder of Participation", "Sherry Arnstein (1969)", "Levels from manipulation to citizen control", "Most projects operate at tokenism, not genuine power-sharing"]', '["Participatory Design", "Lucien Kroll, others", "Communities co-design with professionals", "Time/resource intensive; requires trust-building"]', '["Asset-Based Development", "John Kretzmann, others", "Build on community strengths, not needs", "Can minimize legitimate grievances; may understate material constraints"]', '["Co-Production", "Collective models", "Community labor and decision-making throughout", "Creates ownership; demands volunteer labor (equity issue)"]', '["Incremental Design", "Aravena, others", "Incomplete structures communities complete", "Pragmatic but can normalize inadequate initial provision"]', '["Indigenous Sovereignty", "Decolonization frameworks", "Indigenous communities control design decisions", "Requires redistributing professional authority; politically contentious"]', '["Participatory Slum Upgrading", "UN-Habitat, others", "Existing residents guide incremental improvements", "Often paired with inadequate state investment; can legitimize informal tenure"]']]} />
## How It's Tested on the LEA

<ExamTip>1. **Participation Level Identification**: "A project claims 'community engagement' but residents were invited to comment on designs already completed. Which level of Arnstein's ladder is this?" (Answer: Tokenism; comments are collected but decisions remain with professionals)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>2. **Equity Framework Application**: "Design a housing project for economically displaced residents. What social architecture principles should guide this?" (Answer: Participatory design (not top-down), community control (not professional authority), tenure security (legal rights, not temporary), incrementalism (respecting existing resources and labor), explicit anti-displacement measures)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>3. **Professional Role Negotiation**: "In participatory design, what is the architect's role if the community's preference differs from technical recommendations?" (Answer: Facilitate negotiation, clarify trade-offs, but ultimately defer to community decision-making; professional authority is advisory, not determinative)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>4. **Indigenous Consultation vs. Control**: "A project on Indigenous land consulted with the tribe. Is this genuine social architecture?" (Answer: Consultation alone is insufficient; genuine decolonial architecture requires Indigenous control over design decisions, with professionals as consultants)</ExamTip>

<ExamTip>5. **Philippine Application**: "How should slum upgrading in Metro Manila incorporate social architecture principles?" (Answer: Participatory budgeting, residents determine priorities, tenure security measures, community labor and skill-building, long-term community organizing, not demolition-based relocation)</ExamTip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing Consultation with Participation" correction="Asking community input is not participation if the community cannot influence final decisions." context="Genuine participation requires shared decision-making authority." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Idealizing Communities as Unified and Democratic" correction="Communities contain conflicts, hierarchies, and marginalized members whose voices are suppressed." context="Participation must actively manage internal power dynamics." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Assuming All Community Preferences are Architecturally Desirable. Communities may prefer unsafe, unhealthy, or legally problematic designs. Professionals retain responsibility to ensure standards are met, but this must be negotiated transparently, not imposed.", "Underestimating Time and Resource Requirements. Genuine participation demands extensive facilitation, multiple revision cycles, consensus-building processes. Projects often treat participation as additive without reallocating time/budget.", "Treating Participation as Optional Rather Than Foundational. If participation is afterthought (added late in design), it cannot meaningfully influence form. Genuine participation integrates community perspective from project inception.", "Ignoring Broader Systemic Issues. Architecture cannot solve poverty or systemic racism; social architecture that addresses housing without addressing employment, education, healthcare, and legal systems risks becoming neo-colonial improvement."]} />

## Key Terms

**Participatory Design** — Design methodology where affected communities collaborate with professionals throughout the design process, not merely commenting on completed proposals.

**Community-Centered Design** — Design process where community priorities and preferences guide decisions; professional expertise serves community goals rather than imposing external standards.

**Co-Production** — Model where community members contribute labor, resources, and decision-making alongside professionals; collective ownership and stewardship.

**Asset-Based Development** — Community development approach that inventories existing resources, skills, and relationships rather than emphasizing deficiencies; builds from strengths.

**Incremental Design** — Providing initial structure that communities complete and adapt over time; pragmatic response to resource constraints; respects community agency.

**Slum Upgrading** — Physical and social improvement of informal settlements through resident-led priorities, tenure security, and infrastructure investment; contrast to demolition-based redevelopment.

**Gentrification** — Process where neighborhood improvement increases land/housing values, displacing lower-income residents through rising costs; social architecture resists through community land trusts, anti-displacement covenants.

**Tenure Security** — Legal certainty of housing rights; essential for community investment in housing improvements and long-term wellbeing.

**Decolonial Design** — Framework recognizing Indigenous sovereignty and epistemic authority; non-Indigenous designers operate as consultants, not authorities, on Indigenous lands.

**Tokenism** — Performative community engagement where input is collected but decision-making remains with professionals/authorities; creates appearance of participation without power-sharing.

**Citizen Control** — Highest level of participation where community holds decision-making authority; professionals advise but do not override.

**Collective Craftsmanship** — Engagement in material making and design decision-shaping; develops tacit knowledge, ownership, and stewardship (Sennett concept).

## Related Articles

See also within Contemporary Movements & Discourse: **lea-theo-007-01-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-02-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-09-core-concept**, **lea-theo-007-11-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** overview-theory-of-architecture for the full curriculum structure and study strategy for Theory of Architecture.

rows.title: Philippine Housing Finance Institutions
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Distinguish the four housing finance institutions — Pag-IBIG/HDMF (employed workers), SSS (private sector), GSIS (government employees), NHMFC (secondary mortgage) — by target sector, membership basis, and financial products.

Four primary institutions provide housing finance to different sectors of the Philippine population: **Pag-IBIG/HDMF** finances employed workers (mandatory membership); **SSS** finances private sector workers (insurance + housing); **GSIS** finances government employees (insurance + housing); **NHMFC** operates as the secondary mortgage market, enabling lenders to recycle capital.

## Core Concept

The Philippine housing finance system is _employment-based_ and _segmented by sector_. There is no single national housing bank—instead, four specialized institutions serve different populations.

**Pag-IBIG (Home Development Mutual Fund, HDMF)** is the primary housing finance institution. Membership is mandatory for all employees (private and government). Monthly contributions from employer and employee fund the program. Pag-IBIG offers tiered loans:
- **Socialized housing loan:** Up to ₱580,000 (as of 2024; verify current threshold)
- **Low-cost housing loan:** For units priced ₱1–2 million
- **Open-market housing loan:** Up to ₱6 million for any residential property

**SSS (Social Security System)** and **GSIS (Government Service Insurance System)** are primarily social insurance institutions, but both offer housing loans as ancillary programs:
- SSS housing loans for private sector workers
- GSIS housing loans for government employees

**NHMFC (National Home Mortgage Finance Corporation)** operates the secondary mortgage market. When Pag-IBIG, banks, or other primary lenders originate a housing loan, NHMFC can purchase that loan, returning capital to the lender so they can issue new loans. This recycling mechanism is critical for loan availability.

The critical distinction: These agencies _finance_ housing (they issue loans to end-buyers). They do NOT _build_ housing (that is NHA's role) and do NOT _regulate_ developers (that is DHSUD's role).
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-plan-007-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Housing Finance Institutions — Pag-IBIG, SSS, GSIS, NHMFC Comparison" description="Four-panel comparison of housing finance institutions: Pag-IBIG/HDMF (employed workers, mandatory), SSS (private sector, housing loans), GSIS (government employees), NHMFC (secondary mortgage market, liquidity). Target sector, membership basis, and financial products per institution." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

<WikiExamTable headers={["Institution", "Primary Sector Served", "Membership/Eligibility", "Loan Range", "Ancillary Function"]} rows={[["**Pag-IBIG/HDMF**", "All employed workers (private and government sectors)", "Mandatory for all employees", "Socialized (≤₱580K) to Open-market (up to ₱6M)", "Housing savings accumulation (membership contributions)"], ["**SSS**", "Private sector workers", "Contributors to SSS insurance", "Housing loans for members", "Social insurance for private sector"], ["**GSIS**", "Government employees", "Contributors to GSIS insurance", "Housing loans for government employees", "Life and disability insurance"], ["**NHMFC**", "Lenders and loan portfolio investors", "Buys loans from Pag-IBIG, banks", "Purchases loans from primary lenders", "Secondary mortgage market operation"]} />

## Philippine Context

Pag-IBIG is ubiquitous in Philippine housing—nearly every employed person contributes monthly and has a Pag-IBIG housing loan account. The system has financed millions of housing units for the employed sector. SSS and GSIS housing programs are more modest but serve important constituencies (private and government employees respectively). NHMFC's role is less visible but essential: without secondary mortgage market purchases, primary lenders would exhaust capital and stop issuing new loans.

## How It's Tested

1. **Agency identification by sector:** "Who provides housing loans to private sector workers?" → SSS or Pag-IBIG. "Who provides housing loans to government employees?" → GSIS or Pag-IBIG.
2. **Loan amount identification:** "A teacher on a government salary applies for a ₱2.5 million housing loan. Which institution would typically serve this request?" → GSIS or Pag-IBIG.
3. **System role:** "Who recycles housing loans in the secondary market?" → NHMFC.

<Tip>**Memory aid:** Pag-IBIG = **P**rimary lender for all **employed** (government + private). SSS = private sector workers (extra benefit beyond insurance). GSIS = government employees (extra benefit). NHMFC = secondary market (buys loans so lenders can lend again).</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Pag-IBIG = employed workers (mandatory, 2% EE + 2% ER). SSS = private sector (insurance + housing loan). GSIS = government (insurance + housing). NHMFC = secondary market (buys mortgages from originators, not direct lending).

## Cross-References

See **LEA-PLAN-003-03** (Housing Finance) for Pag-IBIG/SHFC/NHA finance roles, **LEA-PLAN-007-01** (NHA) for non-finance housing production, and **LEA-PLAN-003-01** (Housing Law Framework) for Maceda Law protections.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing Pag-IBIG (finance) with NHA (production)—Pag-IBIG loans; NHA builds", "Stating SSS or GSIS are primary housing lenders—they are ancillary; Pag-IBIG is primary", "Forgetting that NHMFC does not issue loans; it purchases them from primary lenders", "Saying Pag-IBIG is for low-income only—Pag-IBIG serves all employed sectors (including open-market loans up to ₱6M)", "Confusing SHFC (community-based) with Pag-IBIG (individual)—different sectors, different mechanisms"]} />

rows.title: Religious buildings (churches, chapels, mosques, temples)
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

Religious buildings—churches, chapels, and mosques—are classified as **Group C, Division C-2** (Education and Recreation - Institutional), with pew seating at 0.5-0.6 sqm/person, standing at 0.7-1.0 sqm/person, and nave ceiling typically 6.0 m. Mosques require qibla orientation near **289°** (clockwise from north) from Metro Manila, or approximately **19°** clockwise from west and wudu facilities at **1 faucet per 10 worshippers**.

## Learning Goal

Identify religious buildings as Group C occupancy, calculate seating and standing occupancy using pew density factors, determine nave ceiling height and sacristy dimensions, apply mosque-specific qibla orientation and wudu requirements, and verify fire egress compliance.

## Core Concept

Religious buildings (churches, chapels, mosques, temples) are classified as **Group C** (education and recreation) per **RA 9514 2019 Revised IRR Rule 10** (table reference should be verified against current edition; occupancy classification per PD 1096 Rule VII Sec 701). This differs from assembly halls (Group H, used for sports/concerts), which have much larger standing occupancy densities. Pew-based seating in churches accommodates **0.5-0.6 sqm per seated person**; standing areas (narthex, aisles during overflow) use **0.7-1.0 sqm per person**. The nave (main worship space) requires minimum ceiling height of **6.0 m** to achieve adequate acoustics and visual sight lines to altar/pulpit.

Sacristy (preparation room for clergy) is typically **12-18 sqm**, providing robing space and sacramental item storage. Confessionals are compact: **1.0 m × 1.5 m** per booth (priest + penitent separated). Choir lofts allocate **1.0 sqm per choir member**. Acoustic performance targets reverberation time (RT60) of **1.2-2.0 seconds**, achieved through material selection and volume optimization.

Mosque-specific requirements include qibla (prayer direction) oriented approximately **273° from Manila** (adjusted by location). Wudu (ritual ablution) facilities provide *1 faucet per 10 worshippers (recommended practice)rate male/female if applicable), typically with low-height basins (0.6-0.8 m) and floor drainage. Heritage religious buildings often trigger **NHCP (National Heritage Commission of the Philippines) certification**, extending approval timelines but ensuring cultural preservation. Fire egress follows Group C: 45 m travel distance (unsprinklered) or 60 m (sprinklered), **7.6 mm per occupant** exit width (per RA 9514 2019 Revised IRR Rule 10 Table 10.2.5.1.1 for 'All Others' occupancy), dual exits at 50+ persons.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-005-06-core-concept" type="image" caption="Religious Building Design — Mosque and Church Comparative Plans" description="Comparative floor plans showing spatial organization for a mosque (qibla orientation ~289°, wudu at 1 faucet/10 worshippers) and a church (nave at 0.5-0.6 sqm/person, 6.0m ceiling). Annotated with key dimension standards." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

| Element | Requirement | Source |
|---------|-------------|--------|
| **Occupancy Group** | Group C (education/recreation) | PD 1096 |
| **Pew Seating Density** | 0.5–0.6 sqm per person | Standard Practice |
| **Standing Occupancy** | 0.7–1.0 sqm per person | Standard Practice |
| **Nave Ceiling Min.** | 6.0 m | Acoustics/Sight Lines |
| **Sacristy Floor Area** | 12–18 sqm | Standard Practice |
| **Confessional Dimensions** | 1.0 m × 1.5 m per booth | Standard Practice |
| **Choir Space** | 1.0 sqm per member | Standard Practice |
| **RT60 Acoustic Target** | 1.2–2.0 seconds | Acoustics Standard |
| **Mosque Qibla Direction** | ~273° from Metro Manila | Islamic Standard |
| **Wudu Facilities** | 1 faucet per 10–20 worshippers (recommended practice; verify with local authority and faith community) |
| **Fire Travel Distance** | 45 m (unsprinklered) / 60 m (sprinklered) | PD 1096 2004 Revised IRR Rule X |
| **Exit Width** | 7.6 mm per occupant | RA 9514 2019 Revised IRR Table 10.2.5.1.1 |
| **Dual Exit Requirement** | based on occupant load | RA 9514 2019 Revised IRR Sec 10.2.5.2 |
| **Accessible Door Width** | 900 mm minimum | BP 344 §303 |
| **Ramp Slope Maximum** | 1:20 maximum (2024 Revised IRR; supersedes 1:12 from 2013 IRR) | BP 344 §301 |

**Occupancy Calculation (Seating + Standing):**
Seated occupancy = (pew area in sqm) ÷ 0.55 (using midpoint 0.5-0.6)
Standing occupancy = (aisle/narthex area) ÷ 0.85 (using midpoint 0.7-1.0)
Total occupancy = seated + standing

Example: 200 sqm pew area ÷ 0.55 = 364 seated persons; 80 sqm standing ÷ 0.85 = 94 standing persons; total = 458 occupants.

**Wudu Facility Calculation:**
Expected peak worship occupancy ÷ 10 = minimum faucets required

Example: Mosque with 300-person capacity requires 30 wudu faucets minimum.

## Philippine Practice Context

Manila's diverse religious landscape includes centuries-old churches (requiring NHCP compliance alongside fire code), modern non-denominational chapels, and growing mosque complexes serving Muslim communities. Common design tensions: developers want compact layouts (reduced pew spacing, lower ceilings for cost control), but code mandates 6.0 m nave height and 0.5-0.6 sqm minimum pew density. Heritage churches often have existing structures predating modern fire codes; retrofitting dual egress and widening aisles can require structural modifications. Mosque design requires careful qibla alignment; consulting prayer direction resources and verifying with community leadership prevents costly redesigns. Wudu facilities in shared-use buildings (prayer rooms in hospitals, corporate offices) are underutilized and often incorrectly downsized; 1:10 faucet ratio is not negotiable. Confessional privacy is increasingly requested in multi-faith facilities, requiring soundproofing beyond traditional booth design.

## How It's Tested

1. **Occupancy Group Identification:** Confirm religious buildings = Group C (not Group H assembly). This affects fire egress thresholds and parking ratios.
2. **Seating Density Calculation:** A 300 sqm church sanctuary with pew layout. Occupancy = 300 ÷ 0.55 = ~545 seated persons. If standing aisles = 50 sqm, standing = 50 ÷ 0.85 = ~59 persons. Total = 604 occupants; dual exits required.
3. **Wudu Facility Requirement:** A 500-capacity mosque requires 50 wudu faucets. Candidates often underestimate this (providing only 10-15 faucets), creating prayer time delays and non-compliance.

<Tip>**Religious Building Anchors:** Group C occupancy. Pew seating = 0.5–0.6 sqm/person. Standing = 0.7–1.0 sqm/person. Nave ceiling min = 6.0 m. Sacristy = 12–18 sqm. Confessional = 1 × 1.5 m. Mosque qibla ≈273° from Manila. Wudu = 1 faucet/10 worshippers. RT60 = 1.2–2.0 sec.</Tip>

**Exam Tip — ERR-DSGN-023:** Ambulatory surgical centers are Group D with higher egress standards due to patients under sedation. Treatment room minimum = 12 sqm. Travel distance limits apply to all patient areas.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-005-06-core-concept" type="image" caption="Comparative Religious Architecture — Church Nave vs. Mosque Prayer Hall" description="Comparative floor plans: church nave (longitudinal axis, pew seating 0.5 sqm/person, 6.0m ceiling) vs. mosque prayer hall (qibla wall oriented ~289°, carpeted floor 0.7-1.0 sqm/person, wudu facilities at 1 faucet/10 worshippers). Key dimension and orientation differences annotated." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-005-05** (Specialized Health Facilities) for Group D space standards, **LEA-DSGN-008-02** (Fire Separation) for institutional fire ratings, and **LEA-DSGN-007-08** (Human Factors) for accessible exam room layout.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["ERR-DSGN-005: Classifying churches/mosques as Group H (assembly) instead of Group C","Pew density too high (0.4 sqm/person instead of 0.5–0.6)","Nave ceiling undersized (5.0 m instead of 6.0 m minimum)","Wudu faucet ratio incorrect (1 per 20 or 30 instead of 1 per 10)","Qibla direction incorrect or not verified with faith community","ERR-DSGN-019: Exit width at 5 mm/person instead of 7.6 mm/person","ERR-DSGN-021: Single exit for 50+ person worship space"]} />

rows.title: Prestressing
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define prestressing and explain why it is used in concrete
- Distinguish between pre-tensioning (strands tensioned before casting) and post-tensioning (tensioned after curing)
- Explain how prestressing creates compressive stress that offsets tensile service stresses
- Identify common applications: bridge girders, prestressed slabs, and beams

Prestressed concrete applies permanent compression to concrete before or during service loads to reduce or eliminate tensile stresses that would otherwise cause cracking. The two methods are fundamentally different in application timing: pre-tensioning applies compression before concrete is cast, while post-tensioning applies compression after concrete has hardened. Understanding this distinction and the resulting structural behaviors is essential for recognizing when each method is appropriate.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-006-04-core-concept" type="image" caption="Prestressing — Pretensioning vs Post-Tensioning Comparison" description="Side-by-side comparison of pretensioning and post-tensioning: (1) Pretensioning — strands tensioned before concrete pour, bond transfer after curing, shown in precast bed; (2) Post-tensioning — ducts placed in concrete, strands tensioned after curing, anchored at ends. Stress distribution comparison: full section compression vs eccentric compression. Tendon profile diagrams for simply supported and continuous beams." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

**Prestressing** is the application of deliberately induced internal compression to a concrete member to counteract tensile stresses that would develop from external loads. Instead of relying entirely on reinforcing steel to resist tension (as in ordinary reinforced concrete), prestressed concrete uses high-strength steel tendons—either wires or strands—to apply sustained compression. This reduces or eliminates cracks, improves serviceability, and increases the effective load-carrying capacity of the member.

**Pre-tensioning** is the process of tensioning the steel tendons _before_ concrete is placed. The sequence is:
1. Steel tendons (wires or seven-wire strands, typically _F_y ≈ 1,770–1,960 MPa) are stretched to a specified stress (typically 60–75% of breaking strength) and held in tension on a form or frame (the "casting bed").
2. Concrete is cast around the tensioned tendons.
3. After concrete reaches sufficient strength (typically 3–7 days), the tendons are released from the external holding devices.
4. The tendons, now bonded to the concrete, attempt to retract but are prevented by concrete friction and mechanical anchorage. This creates a compressive force on the concrete.
5. The concrete is permanently compressed from the inside by the tendons.

**Characteristics of Pre-tensioning:**
- Tendons are _bonded_ to concrete from casting onward.
- Transfer of stress from tendon to concrete occurs gradually as the tendon tries to shorten (frictional transfer).
- Pre-tensioning is commonly used in factory-controlled environments (precasting plants) because it requires long bed frames and repeated casting/release cycles.
- Typical products: precast I-beams, double-T slabs, hollow core slabs, and box beams.
- Once released, the member immediately carries its own weight (self-weight compression) and remains compressed throughout service.

**Post-tensioning** is the process of tensioning the steel tendons _after_ concrete has hardened. The sequence is:
1. Concrete is cast with ducts (conduits) left empty for later tendon placement.
2. Concrete hardens and reaches full strength (28 days or later).
3. Steel tendons are placed through the ducts.
4. Tendons are tensioned (pulled) by hydraulic jacks at one or both ends, applying force to the concrete.
5. Tendons are anchored at the ends (typically with wedge anchors), locking in the compression.
6. Ducts are grouted (filled) to bond the tendons to concrete and protect them from corrosion.

**Characteristics of Post-tensioning:**
- Tendons may be unbonded (not grouted into the ducts) during the testing phase, but are typically grouted for final service.
- Stress transfer is _instantaneous_ when jacks release (unlike pre-tensioning, which is gradual).
- Post-tensioning is used in cast-in-place construction because it does not require external holding frames or precasting facilities.
- Typical applications: parking structures, bridges, buildings with long spans, and foundation slabs.
- The member carries its own weight _without_ compression (the concrete is uncompressed when the tendons are placed); compression is applied only after the concrete has developed sufficient strength and cured.
- Compression can be applied at multiple stages (e.g., after deck placement in bridge construction) and can be partially or fully locked in.

**Key Differences:**

| Aspect | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|
| **Timing of Tension** | Tendons tensioned BEFORE concrete placed | Tendons tensioned AFTER concrete hardened |
| **Bonding** | Bonded from casting | Typically bonded after tensioning (grouted) |
| **Stress Transfer** | Gradual (friction transfer) | Instantaneous (jacks release) |
| **Common Uses** | Precast/precasting plants | Cast-in-place construction, bridges |
| **Tendon Type** | Wires, strands; continuous | Strands in ducts; can be individual tendons |
| **Anchorage** | Mechanical bond to concrete, friction | Wedge anchors at ends |
| **Cost Sensitivity** | Economical for mass production | Economical for long spans, unique shapes |
| **Self-Weight** | Member compressed from release onward | Self-weight resisted by uncompressed concrete until tensioning |

**Tendon Materials:**
High-strength steel is essential to prestressing because:
- High yield strength (_F_y ≈ 1,770–1,960 MPa for strands vs. 414 MPa for ordinary bars) allows large compression forces with small cross-sectional area.
- Modulus of elasticity _E_ = 200,000 MPa (same as ordinary reinforcing steel).
- Relaxation (loss of stress over time under sustained loading) is a concern; prestress is typically applied at 60–75% of breaking strength to minimize long-term relaxation losses.

**Prestress Losses:**
Both pre-tensioned and post-tensioned members experience stress losses over time due to:
- Elastic deformation (instantaneous loss in post-tensioning; gradual in pre-tensioning)
- Concrete creep and shrinkage (time-dependent, referenced in Article LEA-STRC-003-02)
- Steel relaxation (stress loss under sustained load)
- Friction losses in ducts (post-tensioning only)

The initial prestress must be higher than the final required compression because of these losses. Typical final compression is 60–80% of initial prestress.

## Key Provisions

| Parameter | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|
| **Steel Yield Strength** | 1,770–1,960 MPa (typical strand) | 1,770–1,960 MPa (typical strand) |
| **Initial Stress** | 60–75% of breaking strength | 60–75% of breaking strength |
| **Bonding Method** | Mechanical grip + friction | Grouted ducts + wedge anchors |
| **Transfer Length** | Requires development (0.5–2 m typical) | Instantaneous at anchors |
| **Duct Grouting** | Not applicable (fully bonded) | Required for final service |
| **Typical Span** | 15–30 m (precast beams) | 20–60+ m (cast-in-place, bridges) |

**Concrete Cover Requirements for Prestressed Concrete (Simplified):**
Cover is measured from the outer surface to the tendon duct or strand surface and varies by exposure:
- Cast against earth: 75 mm
- Exposed to weather (walls/slabs): 25 mm
- Exposed to weather (beams/columns): 40 mm
- Not exposed (slabs/walls): 20 mm
- Not exposed (beams/columns): 40 mm

These values protect tendons from corrosion, especially important in coastal environments and aggressive exposures.

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, precast prestressed members (pre-tensioned I-beams, double-T slabs, hollow-core slabs) are widely used in housing projects and bridge construction because of high production efficiency and consistent quality. Post-tensioning is less common but is used in large-span bridges (e.g., across major rivers), long-span parking structures, and high-rise buildings with long cantilevers. Coastal regions, where chloride corrosion is a concern, require high-quality grouting of post-tensioned ducts and adequate concrete cover to protect the high-strength tendons. The PNSC Chapter 7 specifies prestress design requirements and cover requirements specific to Philippine construction and exposure classes.

## How It's Tested

1. **Prestress Transfer Test (ASTM E8 / Philippines Custom):** In a precasting plant, strand samples are tested for ultimate tensile strength and stress-strain properties. Tendons must reach the specified yield strength without failure; typical test values are _F_u_ ≈ 1,860 MPa or higher.

2. **Prestress Loss Measurement (ASTM A416 / Technical Tests):** Strain gauges are placed on a sample member to measure prestress loss over time. Losses due to elastic deformation, creep, and shrinkage are recorded at key ages (1 day, 7 days, 28 days, 90 days, 1 year). Engineers use these measurements to refine prestress loss estimates for design.

3. **Duct Grouting Verification (Post-Tensioning Only):** After grouting ducts, cores are extracted to verify complete grouting (no voids) and proper adhesion to the tendon. Poor grouting allows water infiltration and corrosion.

4. **Residual Prestress Verification:** After all curing and service, or after removal of temporary loads (in bridges), the residual compression is verified by ultrasonic methods or other non-destructive testing to confirm that design prestress levels are maintained.

<Tip>The defining distinction: Pre-tensioning = tendons tensioned BEFORE concrete placed. Post-tensioning = tendons tensioned AFTER concrete hardened. This timing difference determines the structural system, production method, and field application. Memorize this clearly to avoid the common reversal error (ERR-STRC-016).</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Concrete Materials** (lea-strc-006-01) for the basic concrete properties, **Flexural Theory** (lea-strc-006-03) for how reinforced sections work without prestress, and **Precast Concrete** (lea-strc-006-05) for how precasting relates to prestressing.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Reversing pre-tensioning and post-tensioning definitions. Pre = tendons tensioned BEFORE concrete placed. Post = tendons tensioned AFTER concrete hardened. This is the opposite of the common error; verify by physical logic: 'pre' comes before, 'post' comes after.", "Assuming pre-tensioning and post-tensioning have identical structural behavior. Pre-tensioning provides immediate compression (from release onward); post-tensioning requires the concrete to develop strength before compression is applied. The timing affects serviceability, deflection, and crack control.", "Forgetting that post-tensioned ducts must be grouted after tensioning. Ungrouted tendons do not provide full composite action and allow corrosion risk. Grouting bonds the tendon to concrete and protects against corrosion—non-negotiable for permanent service.", "Using ordinary reinforcing bar yield strength (414 MPa) instead of prestressing tendon strength (1,770–1,960 MPa) in calculations. Prestressing relies on the much higher strength of special steel; using lower strength numbers makes the system uneconomical and underperforming." ]} />

rows.title: Moment-resisting frame (MRF)
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define a moment-resisting frame (MRF) and explain its load path
- Distinguish between ordinary, intermediate, and special MRFs
- Explain why rigid beam-column connections are essential for MRF behavior
- Describe the advantages and disadvantages of MRFs compared to shear walls

Moment-resisting frames are classified into three categories based on their seismic design level: Ordinary (OMRF), Intermediate (IMRF), and Special (SMRF). Each category has specific detailing requirements and a seismic response modification factor (R factor). Understanding these categories is critical for seismic design in the Philippines.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-002-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Moment-Resisting Frame — Rigid Connection Behavior" description="Diagram showing a moment-resisting frame under lateral load with: (1) rigid beam-column connections with moment diagrams at joints; (2) deflected shape showing double curvature in beams and columns; (3) comparison of OMRF (R=3), IMRF (R=4.5-5.5), and SMRF (R=8-8.5) detailing requirements including connection reinforcement and confinement zones." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

A **moment-resisting frame (MRF)** is a structural system in which beams and columns are rigidly connected, allowing the frame to resist lateral loads through bending moments at the joints. Unlike braced frames (which use diagonal members), moment-resisting frames rely on the rigidity of connections to develop moment capacity.

The three MRF categories are defined by the NSCP based on seismic hazard and design philosophy:

**Ordinary Moment-Resisting Frames (OMRF, R = 3 for steel OMF per NSCP Table 208-11A)** are designed for regions with lower seismic demand or for use in non-critical structures. OMRF connections are not specially detailed for ductility—they may be welded or bolted, but without enhanced confinement or reinforcement. OMRF provides moderate lateral stiffness and limited energy dissipation. R = 3.5 reflects this lower capability.

**Intermediate Moment-Resisting Frames (IMRF/IMRF, R = 5.5 concrete / 4.5 steel per NSCP Table 208-11A/Sec 418)** are designed with intermediate seismic detailing. Connections are more robust than OMRF, with some reinforcement requirements and welding controls. IMRF is used in moderate seismic zones. R = 5.5 reflects improved ductility and strength.

**Special Moment-Resisting Frames (SMRF, R = 8.0)** are designed for high seismic demand regions like Seismic Zone 4 in the Philippines. SMRF requires extensive detailing: full-penetration welds at beam-column connections, restricted steel grades, confining transverse reinforcement in concrete columns, and plastic hinge detailing in beams. R = 8.0 reflects high ductility, capacity for energy dissipation, and predictable inelastic behavior.

The R factor (response modification factor) represents how much the frame can be designed for reduced forces compared to elastic response, because the frame is allowed to deform inelastically and dissipate energy. Higher R values mean more ductility and greater lateral flexibility are accepted.

## Key Provisions

| Frame Type | R Factor | Connection Detailing | Seismic Zone Typical | Ductility | Lateral Stiffness |
|----------|----------|----------------------|----------------------|-----------|-------------------|
| **OMRF** | 3.5 | Minimal; may lack enhancement | Low-moderate | Limited | Moderate |
|IMRF | 5.5 (concrete) / 4.5 (steel) | Intermediate; some reinforcement | Moderate | Good | Moderate-High |
| **SMRF** | 8.0 | Extensive; full-penetration welds, confined reinforcement | High (Zone 2) | Excellent | Can be tuned |

**R Factor Definition:** The response modification factor allows the design force to be reduced from the elastic (full-strength) demand. A structure with R = 8.0 may be designed for 1/8 the elastic shear force if it meets SMRF detailing requirements and accepts larger inelastic deformations.

**Seismic Zone 2 (Most Severe):** In the Philippines' most seismic zone, SMRF is the standard for moment-resisting frame design in buildings where lateral system is a moment frame.

## Philippine Practice Context

NSCP 2015 Table 208-11A (R factors), Sec 408 (steel general), Sec 418 (concrete MRF) define these frame types explicitly. In Seismic Zone 4 (covering most of the Philippines except Palawan except Busuanga, Tawi-Tawi, and Sulu which are Zone 2), SMRF is required for multi-story buildings relying on moment resistance. Office towers, commercial buildings, and high-occupancy structures use SMRF. OMRF is rarely used in the Philippines due to the high seismic hazard nationally.

## How It's Tested

**Remember-level:** Identify the R factor for OMRF, IMRF, and SMRF from a frame description.

**Understand-level:** Explain why SMRF detailing is more stringent than OMRF, and how this relates to energy dissipation.

**Apply-level:** Given a 8-story office building in Seismic Zone 2, justify why SMRF is required and what design force reduction is allowed due to the R factor.

<Tip>**Memory aid:** O=3.5, I=5.5, S=8.0. SMRF (Special) gets the highest R because it's **specially** detailed for maximum ductility. Think: "Special demands special detailing."</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Bearing Wall Systems** (lea-strc-002-01) for comparison with wall systems, **Trusses** (lea-strc-002-05) for a different lateral system, and **Static Determinacy** (lea-strc-001-06) for how rigid frames affect determinacy.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing R factor with safety factor—R is a reduction factor allowing smaller design forces due to ductility, not a safety multiplier","Assuming IMRF and SMRF are equivleant; IMRF has less stringent detailing and lower R (5.5 vs 8.0)","Using OMRF (R=3.5) in Seismic Zone 2 because it is cheaper—NSCP requires SMRF in high-seismic areas"]} />

rows.title: Base shear (V)
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define base shear (V) as the total design lateral force at the base of a structure
- Identify the variables in the base shear formula: V = (Z × I × C × W) / R
- Explain how each variable (Z, I, C, W, R) affects the design seismic force
- State the relationship between building period (T) and seismic response coefficient (C)

A soft story and a weak story are not synonyms. Soft story is a lateral stiffness deficiency (< 70% of story above); weak story is a lateral strength deficiency (< 80% of story above). Both create seismic vulnerability and are regulated by design codes. The LEA distinguishes them clearly.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-004-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Base Shear — Seismic Force Distribution" description="Building elevation diagram showing: (1) Total base shear V calculated from V=(ZIC/RW)W applied at base; (2) Vertical distribution of lateral forces (Fx) increasing from bottom to top following Fx = (Wxhx^k/ΣWihi^k)V; (3) Story drift and overturning moment diagram. Key parameters labeled: Z (zone), I (importance), C (response), R (ductility), W (weight)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

_Base shear_ (V) is the total lateral (seismic) force at the building base, calculated as V = Z × I × C × W. It represents the maximum expected seismic demand that the foundation must resist. The base shear is distributed up the height of the building according to the code formula.

_Story drift_ (Δ) is the lateral displacement of one story relative to the story below. It is measured in the same seismic direction and is a primary check for building adequacy. Code limits story drift to no more than 0.02 × story height (sometimes 0.025 for very tall flexible buildings, but 0.02 is the standard). Excessive story drift causes non-structural damage (cracking in partitions, breaking of windows) and can initiate P-delta (second-order) effects.

A _soft story_ is one where the lateral stiffness is less than 70% of the story immediately above it. Lateral stiffness is the lateral force required to produce unit displacement (kips/inch or kN/mm). A soft story leads to disproportionate lateral displacement in that one story—the deformation concentrates there. This is a stiffness deficiency.

A _weak story_ is one where the lateral strength (shear capacity) is less than 80% of the story immediately above it. Lateral strength is measured as the shear force (in kN) that the story can resist before yielding or shear failure. A weak story is the first to fail during an earthquake. This is a strength deficiency.

Both conditions are _irregular_ in the code sense. The NSCP requires that buildings avoid these irregularities. If a soft or weak story exists, special detailing, increased member capacities, or nonlinear analysis is required.

_Collectors_ and _diaphragms_ (defined in LEA-STRC-002-02) transfer seismic forces from the lateral load-resisting system (LLRS) to the foundation. Seismic column confinement (defined in LEA-STRC-007-04) ensures ductile behavior in columns at soft or weak stories.

## Key Provisions

| Parameter | Definition | Limit/Typical Value |
|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| Base Shear (V) | Total lateral seismic force at base | V = Z × I × C × W (calculated, not limited a priori) |
| Story Drift (Δ) | Lateral displacement of story relative to floor below | ≤ 0.02 × story height |
| Soft Story | Lateral stiffness < 70% of story above | Irregular; avoid or provide special design |
| Weak Story | Lateral strength < 80% of story above | Irregular; avoid or provide special design |

The soft/weak story check is performed for every story pair in a building. If any story fails the check, the entire building is flagged as irregular and must be analyzed with additional scrutiny or redesigned.

Story drift control prevents both non-structural damage and P-delta amplification. In a 4 m tall story, Δ must not exceed 0.02 × 4000 mm = 80 mm. If seismic demand produces 100 mm drift, the system is undersized and must be stiffened (larger columns, shear walls, bracing).

## Philippine Practice Context

Soft stories are common in Philippine commercial buildings where ground floors are designed open for retail or lobby space, and upper floors are column-grid office/residential. The transition from open ground to enclosed upper stories creates a stiffness discontinuity. Weak stories can occur where a story loses shear wall area (common when a shear wall terminates at mid-height). The 1990 Luzon and 2013 Bohol earthquakes caused significant damage to structures with soft or weak stories; post-earthquake surveys identified these irregularities as primary failure modes. Modern NSCP enforcement requires detection and mitigation at the design phase.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Definition distinction.** "A story with lateral stiffness less than 70% of the story above is called a..." → Soft story (not weak). Stiffness → soft.

**Pattern 2: Threshold identification.** "A weak story is defined as one where lateral strength is less than ___ percent of the story above." → 80% (not 70%).

**Pattern 3: Consequence analysis.** "A building has a soft story at the ground level. What is the likely effect?" → The ground story experiences disproportionately large lateral displacement; story drift concentrates at the weak stiffness point; non-structural damage and P-delta effects increase. The design is irregular and requires special attention.

<Tip>_Soft_ = stiffness (S.S. = Same Sound). _Weak_ = strength (starts with W). Soft < 70%; Weak < 80%. Remember: 70 (soft) comes before 80 (weak) numerically and alphabetically (Soft, Weak).</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Seismic Zones** (lea-strc-004-02) for zone factor Z, **Earthquake Fundamentals** (lea-strc-004-01) for the science behind seismic demand, and **Required Strength** (lea-strc-005-01) for how base shear combines with other loads.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating soft and weak as synonyms. They are distinct: soft = stiffness; weak = strength. Different definitions, different thresholds (70% vs. 80%).","Using 80% for soft story threshold. Soft story threshold is 70% of story above (stiffness). Weak story is 80% (strength).","Confusing story drift (displacement) with soft/weak (stiffness/strength). Drift is the lateral movement; soft/weak are structural deficiencies that can cause excessive drift.","Thinking soft/weak stories only matter for tall buildings. Any building with a stiffness or strength discontinuity (e.g., ground floor retail below office) is subject to the check.","Ignoring the story-pair nature of the check. A soft story is 70% of the story ABOVE, not an absolute value. Compare each story to its upper neighbor.","Assuming P-delta effects are automatically accounted for.
