rows.title: Non-Ferrous Metals
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Identify structural steel sections (W-shapes, channels, angles, HSS, plates) by their cross-section geometry, standard designations, and typical applications in building frames, and recall standard yield strengths for A36 and A572 Grade 50 steel.
## Core Concept

Non-ferrous metals are metallic elements or alloys that contain little or no iron. Unlike ferrous metals (iron-based), they do not corrode through rust oxidation in the same manner, making them ideal for exposed architectural elements, coastal environments, and wet areas. Aluminum dominates Philippine construction due to its lightweight, excellent corrosion resistance, ease of extrusion, and aesthetic versatility.

Aluminum alloys are designated by a four-digit system (XXXX) established by the Aluminum Association. The first digit identifies the alloy group, and the three subsequent digits distinguish individual alloys within that group.


<ArticleMedia id="media-steel-section-cross-sections" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Cross-section profiles of standard structural steel sections: W-shape, channel (C), angle (L), HSS rectangular, HSS round, and plate with dimension callouts"
  caption="Future diagram: structural steel section profiles — W-shape, channel, angle, HSS, and plate"
  suggestedAsset="Cross-section drawing set with standard designations and nominal dimensions"
  placementIntent="Helps learners recognize steel section types by cross-section geometry" />

### Aluminum Alloy Series (1xxx–7xxx)

_1xxx Series (Commercially Pure)_ — 99.0% purity aluminum. Used for electrical applications and decorative elements. Limited structural use.

_2xxx Series (Al-Cu)_ — Copper-bearing alloys. Higher strength, lower corrosion resistance. Rarely used in exposed outdoor architectural applications.

_3xxx Series (Al-Mn)_ — Manganese-bearing alloys. Good workability, moderate strength. Used in interior components and decorative trim.

_4xxx Series (Al-Si)_ — Silicon-bearing alloys. Excellent for casting and brazing. Limited extrusion use in architectural work.

_5xxx Series (Al-Mg)_ — Magnesium-bearing alloys. Superior corrosion resistance, high strength-to-weight ratio. Marine and coastal applications.

_6xxx Series (Al-Mg-Si)_ — Magnesium-silicon alloys. **The most common for architectural extrusions**. Alloy 6063 dominates window frames, curtain wall systems, door frames, roofing systems, and visible trim throughout the Philippines.

_7xxx Series (Al-Zn)_ — Zinc-bearing alloys. Highest strength but lower corrosion resistance. Aerospace applications, rarely used in building construction.

### Alloy 6063: The Architectural Standard

Alloy 6063 provides exceptional extrudability—the ability to form complex shapes with smooth, highly anodizable surfaces. Ultimate tensile strength differs by temper: 6063-T5 achieves minimum 140 MPa with yield strength of 110 MPa, while 6063-T6 reaches minimum 190 MPa with yield strength of 160 MPa. T6 temper offers superior strength and is specified when higher loads or smaller cross-sections are required. T5 provides cost savings for non-structural or lightly loaded architectural members.

### Surface Finishing Systems

Unprotected aluminum oxidizes spontaneously, forming a thin, naturally adherent aluminum oxide layer that protects against further oxidation. However, this passive film is vulnerable to chloride attack in coastal environments and acidic/alkaline solutions in wet areas.

_Anodizing_ is an electrochemical process that accelerates and thickens the oxide film, creating a durable protective surface available in natural and dyed colors.

- **Type I (Chromic Acid Anodize)** — Produces thin (0.5-7.5 µm) oxide film per MIL-A-8625. Limited corrosion protection. Rarely specified for architectural work.
- **Type II (Sulfuric Acid Anodize)** — Produces medium thickness (5-25 µm) film per MIL-A-8625. Standard choice for architectural extrusions. Provides excellent corrosion resistance and aesthetic appearance in natural and dyed finishes.
- **Type III (Hard Coat Anodize)** — Produces thick (25-75 µm), extremely hard film per MIL-A-8625. Specified when enhanced abrasion resistance or high corrosion protection is critical, such as high-traffic areas or severe coastal/industrial environments.

_Powder Coating_ applies thermosetting polymers electrostatically and cures through heat. Superior adhesion, durability, color retention, and uniform coverage compared to spray painting. Commonly applied to aluminum architectural components in Philippine buildings to achieve custom colors and improved weather resistance.

### Non-Ferrous Metals in Philippine Construction

_Copper_ and its alloys appear as roofing material, gutters, downspouts, and decorative elements. Copper develops a protective patina (green or brown oxide) that provides long-term corrosion protection.

_Brass_ (copper-zinc alloy) and _Bronze_ (copper-tin alloy) are reserved for decorative hardware, door frames, and aesthetic trim.

_Zinc_ galvanizing protects ferrous steel. Pure zinc also serves specialized applications including roofing flashings and cladding.

_Lead_ is obsolete in new construction due to health hazards, though it may be encountered in renovations of older structures.

## Key Provisions

| Alloy Series | Typical Temper | Tensile Strength (Min.) | Primary Architectural Use | Corrosion Class |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6063 | T5 | 140 MPa | Curtain walls, window frames, non-structural trim | Moderate |
| 6063 | T6 | 190 MPa | Structural extrusions, load-bearing members | Moderate |
| 5005 | H34 | 170 MPa | Cladding, siding, high-corrosion environments | High |
| 3003 | H24 | 110 MPa | Interior decorative elements, non-exposed trim | Low |
| 1100 | H14 | 90 MPa | Electrical, specialized decorative work | Moderate |

| Anodizing Type | Film Thickness (µm) | Typical Application | Corrosion Protection | Abrasion Resistance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type I | 5–10 | Minimal; rarely specified | Poor | Poor |
| Type II | 10–25 | Standard architectural extrusions | Excellent | Moderate |
| Type III | 25–75 | High-traffic areas, severe environments | Excellent | Excellent |

## Philippine Construction Context

Philippine suppliers including Aluminium Bahay, Hydro Philippines, and regional fabricators stock 6063-T5 and T6 extrusions for curtain wall systems, sliding window frames, and entrance systems. Coastal regions and high-humidity lowland areas demand Type II or Type III anodizing to prevent corrosion failure within the 50-year service life expected by NSCP 2015 durability provisions.

Aluminum alloy curtain wall systems manufactured to ASTM B221 (Standard Specification for Aluminum and Aluminum-Alloy Extruded Bars, Rods, and Profiles) dominate mid-rise residential and commercial construction. Pre-fabricated modular systems from suppliers like Phividec-based manufacturers simplify installation and ensure consistent material certification.

Copper roofing and brass hardware appear in heritage structures and premium projects. Understanding alloy composition prevents galvanic corrosion when dissimilar metals—such as aluminum framing adjoining copper roofing or stainless steel fasteners connecting aluminum members—contact each other in wet environments.

## Galvanic Corrosion

When two dissimilar metals contact in the presence of an electrolyte (water containing dissolved salts or minerals), electron flow between metals creates a galvanic cell. The more active metal (anodic) corrodes preferentially while the less active metal (cathodic) remains protected. The _galvanic series_ ranks metals by activity.

In Philippine coastal projects, aluminum window frames in contact with stainless steel fasteners or copper gutters risk accelerated corrosion at the interface. Prevention requires isolation using EPDM gaskets, nylon washers, or non-conductive spacers. Sealants like polyurethane or silicone prevent water entrapment at joints.


<ArticleMedia id="media-galvanic-series-chart" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Galvanic series chart ranking metals from anodic to cathodic with examples of compatible and incompatible metal pairs for construction"
  caption="Future chart: galvanic series — metal compatibility for architectural assemblies"
  suggestedAsset="Galvanic series infographic or compatibility table"
  placementIntent="Helps learners prevent galvanic corrosion when specifying dissimilar metals" />
## How It's Tested

The LEA evaluates non-ferrous metals knowledge through:

1. _Alloy identification and temper selection_ — Given a project requirement (e.g., "architectural extrusion for a thermally broken curtain wall system"), select appropriate alloy and temper.
2. _Finishing system specification_ — Match anodizing type to environmental severity and expected service life.
3. _Corrosion prevention_ — Identify galvanic risks when dissimilar metals connect and specify isolation methods.
4. _Philippine code alignment_ — Confirm material selections against NSCP 2015 Sections 1402–1405 (Aluminum Structures) and durability criteria in Section 402.

<Tip>Alloy 6063 is the undisputed standard for Philippine architectural extrusions because of its exceptional extrudability, smooth anodizable surface, and cost-effectiveness. When you see "aluminum curtain wall" on the LEA, assume 6063-T6 unless context suggests otherwise. Type II anodizing is the default for standard architectural applications; only upgrade to Type III if the question emphasizes high-traffic, severe corrosion, or abrasion resistance.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard title="Confusing Alloy Number with Strength" body="A candidate specifies 3003-H14 for a structural member because the number looks stronger. In reality, 3003 is a decorative alloy with only 110 MPa tensile strength—insufficient for any structural role. 6063-T6 (190 MPa) is the minimum architectural structural alloy." />

<WikiMistakeCard title="Anodizing as a Standalone Corrosion Barrier" body="A design relies on Type I anodizing (5 µm film) for a coastal residential building. Type I provides only minimal protection; Type II (10–25 µm) is the minimum standard for architectural exposure, and Type III (25–75 µm) is required for harsh marine environments. The building faces premature corrosion failure." />

<WikiMistakeList items={["Assuming all non-ferrous metals are 'corrosion-proof'—copper oxidizes (patina), zinc can corrode, and unprotected aluminum is vulnerable in wet/coastal conditions.", "Omitting isolation methods when dissimilar metals contact—a stainless steel bolt connecting an aluminum extrusion to a copper component risks galvanic corrosion without EPDM or nylon separation.", "Specifying 6063-T5 for load-bearing members when T6 strength is required, or over-specifying T6 when T5 cost savings are acceptable for non-structural trim.", "Failing to account for Philippine coastal or high-humidity environments when selecting anodizing type—tropical climates demand more aggressive surface protection than temperate regions."]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Metals, Glass, and Glazing: **lea-matl-003-05-core-concept**, **lea-matl-003-07-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: CHB quantity
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Calculate CHB quantities by wall area, accounting for openings (doors, windows), bond pattern, and waste factor, and compute mortar volume and reinforcing steel requirements for reinforced masonry walls.
## Core Concept

CHB quantity is determined by wall surface area and block size. In the Philippines, standard CHB sizes are 4 inches (100 mm), 6 inches (150 mm), and 8 inches (200 mm) in thickness, with a consistent nominal height of 8 inches (200 mm) and length of 16 inches (400 mm). Each block occupies approximately 0.16 m² of wall face area (including the 10 mm mortar joint).

The fundamental formula is: _Number of CHB = Wall area (m²) ÷ 0.16 m² per block_. However, practical estimation uses a shortcut: approximately 12.5 blocks per square meter for standard 6-inch (150 mm) or 8-inch (200 mm) CHB. This accounts for the mortar joint thickness (10 mm standard). When openings (windows, doors) exist, subtract their area from the gross wall area before calculating.

Mortar volume (cement-sand mix for bedding and joints) is estimated at 0.03 to 0.05 m³ per cubic meter of masonry wall, or approximately 1 bag of cement (40 kg) and 0.12 m³ of sand per 100 blocks. Grout (for cavity fill or solid grouting) is calculated separately based on wall thickness and grout design.


<ArticleMedia id="media-chb-estimation-diagram" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Diagram showing CHB wall area calculation, opening deductions, and block layout with bond pattern illustration"
  caption="Future diagram: CHB quantity estimation — wall area, openings, bond pattern, and layout"
  suggestedAsset="Wall elevation diagram with block count calculation steps"
  placementIntent="Visualizes CHB estimation methodology" />

## Key Provisions

| Parameter | Value / Standard | LEA Relevance |
|-----------|------------------|------------------|
| Standard CHB thickness | 4" (100 mm), 6" (150 mm), 8" (200 mm) | Affects wall thermal and acoustic properties; impacts cost |
| CHB nominal height | 8" (200 mm) | With 10 mm joint = 210 mm per course |
| CHB nominal length | 16" (400 mm) | With 10 mm joint = 410 mm per block face |
| Blocks per m² (standard) | ~12.5 pcs/m² | Used for quick estimation across all sizes |
| Mortar joint thickness | 10 mm (standard) | Included in block spacing calculations |
| Mortar requirement | ~0.04 m³ per m³ of masonry OR 1 bag + 0.12 m³ sand per 100 blocks | Scales with block count |
| Minimum compressive strength (PH) | 2.0 MPa (loadbearing) | Per PNS ASTM C90:2019 |
| DPWH Item 1046 | Standard Specification for Masonry Works | Governs public work specifications |
| Wall opening deduction | Full area of window/door openings | Subtract openings from gross wall area |

## Worked Examples

<Example>
**Scenario 1: Residential wall, 6-inch CHB, 30 m² gross area with two 1.5 m × 1.2 m windows and one 1.0 m × 2.1 m door**

**Step 1: Calculate net wall area**

Gross wall area = 30 m²

Window opening 1: 1.5 m × 1.2 m = 1.8 m²

Window opening 2: 1.5 m × 1.2 m = 1.8 m²

Door opening: 1.0 m × 2.1 m = 2.1 m²

Total openings = 1.8 + 1.8 + 2.1 = 5.7 m²

Net wall area = 30 – 5.7 = 24.3 m²

**Step 2: Calculate CHB quantity**

CHB quantity = 24.3 m² × 12.5 pcs/m² = 303.75 pcs

Round up to 304 blocks (add 5% waste: 304 × 1.05 = 319.2 ≈ 320 blocks)

**Step 3: Estimate mortar (1 bag cement + 0.12 m³ sand per 100 blocks)**

Mortar bags: (320 blocks ÷ 100) × 1 bag = 3.2 bags ≈ 4 bags cement

Mortar sand: (320 blocks ÷ 100) × 0.12 m³ = 0.384 m³ ≈ 0.4 m³ sand

**Answer: 320 CHB, 4 bags cement, 0.4 m³ sand**
</Example>

<Example>
**Scenario 2: Commercial building, 4-story structure with 8-inch (200 mm) CHB on ground floor, 45 m² per floor (multiple walls) with 3 doors (1.0 m × 2.1 m each) and 6 windows (1.2 m × 1.5 m each)**

**Step 1: Calculate total gross area for ground floor walls**

Total wall area: 45 m² (given for floor perimeter)

Door openings: 3 × (1.0 × 2.1) = 3 × 2.1 = 6.3 m²

Window openings: 6 × (1.2 × 1.5) = 6 × 1.8 = 10.8 m²

Total openings: 6.3 + 10.8 = 17.1 m²

Net area: 45 – 17.1 = 27.9 m²

**Step 2: Calculate CHB (same formula applies regardless of thickness)**

CHB quantity: 27.9 m² × 12.5 pcs/m² = 348.75 pcs

Add 5% waste: 348.75 × 1.05 = 366.1 ≈ 367 blocks

**Step 3: Mortar estimation**

Mortar cement: (367 ÷ 100) × 1 bag = 3.67 ≈ 4 bags

Mortar sand: (367 ÷ 100) × 0.12 m³ = 0.44 m³

**Step 4: For 4 floors (if same configuration)**

Total CHB: 367 blocks × 4 floors = 1,468 blocks ≈ 1,470 blocks

Total mortar: 4 bags × 4 floors = 16 bags cement

Total sand: 0.44 m³ × 4 floors = 1.76 m³ sand

**Answer: 1,470 CHB for 4 floors, 16 bags cement mortar, 1.76 m³ sand**
</Example>


<ArticleMedia id="media-chb-estimation-example" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Step-by-step CHB quantity estimation example showing wall area calculation, opening deduction, block count, mortar volume, and steel reinforcement"
  caption="Future diagram: CHB estimation worked example — wall area, openings, block count, and reinforcement"
  suggestedAsset="Step-by-step illustrated calculation example"
  placementIntent="Provides practical example of masonry quantity estimation" />
## Quick Reference: CHB Estimation Table

| Wall Thickness | Net Area (m²) | CHB per m² | Total CHB (5% waste) | Mortar Bags | Mortar Sand (m³) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4" (100 mm) | 25 | 12.5 | 329 | 3 | 0.40 |
| 6" (150 mm) | 30 | 12.5 | 394 | 4 | 0.47 |
| 8" (200 mm) | 40 | 12.5 | 525 | 5 | 0.63 |
| Combined (100m² net) | 100 | 12.5 | 1,313 | 13 | 1.58 |

## Philippine Construction Context

In the Philippines, the most common CHB type is the 6-inch hollow block (150 mm), used extensively in residential and light commercial construction. Major manufacturers include Holcim Philippines (Auro brand), Vulcan Products, Filinvest Concrete, and Allied Concrete Products. All products must comply with PNS ASTM C90:2019 for structural performance.

Standard mortar in the Philippines uses 1 part cement to 4-5 parts sand (1:4 to 1:5 by volume), with the ratio depending on exposure conditions. For wet environments (kitchens, bathrooms), 1:3 mortar is preferred. The DPWH Blue Book specifies Item 1046 requirements for public works masonry, including testing and workmanship standards.

Climate consideration: In high-humidity coastal areas and regions with heavy rainfall, moisture-resistant CHB (with reduced water absorption) may be specified. Alternatively, mortar may include hydrophobic admixtures.

## How It's Tested

On the LEA, masonry questions focus on:

1. **Straight quantity calculation**: Given wall area and openings, calculate blocks needed using the 12.5 pcs/m² factor.

2. **Waste adjustment**: Quantity × (1 + waste %) for typical 5–10% site waste.

3. **Mortar scaling**: Number of blocks ÷ 100 × 1 bag (or equivalent) for mortar cement and sand.

4. **Multi-story scaling**: Same per-floor calculation, then multiply by number of floors.

5. **Mixed opening types**: Subtract doors, windows, and other voids from gross area; calculate net area cleanly.

6. **Cost per unit**: CHB cost/block × total blocks for material budgeting.

<Tip>
**Memory aid**: For any wall thickness and opening arrangement, use 12.5 blocks per m² as your standard. Always subtract openings FIRST, then multiply by 12.5. Always add 5% waste unless otherwise specified.
</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Using 16 blocks per m² instead of 12.5 blocks per m²" correction="The standard 12.5 pcs/m² accounts for the 10 mm mortar joint and is universal across 4-inch, 6-inch, and 8-inch CHB. Using 16/m² over-estimates." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Forgetting to subtract window and door openings from the gross wall area" correction="Always calculate net wall area = gross area – total opening area. Then apply 12.5 pcs/m² to the net area only." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Not adding waste percentage" correction="Site waste is typically 5–10%; multiply the block count by 1.05 or 1.10 unless the problem specifies zero waste." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Using different CHB pcs/m² for different thicknesses (4\", 6\", 8\")" correction="All standard CHB sizes have the same face area (16\" × 8\" = 0.16 m² per block). Thickness does not affect quantity per m² of wall face." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Mixing net area and gross area—always subtract openings before multiplying by 12.5", "Calculating mortar based on weight instead of volume (use m³ for sand, bags for cement)", "Double-counting openings or including the same opening twice", "Forgetting that CHB mortar requires both cement AND sand (do not calculate cement only)"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Estimating Quantities and Material Computation: **lea-matl-010-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-04-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-05-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Daylighting
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Apply daylighting strategies beyond NBC 1:10 minimum window-to-floor ratio, calculate daylight penetration depth (typically 2.5× window head height), specify glare control devices, and integrate daylight with artificial lighting controls.

Natural lighting design extends beyond the National Building Code's minimum window-to-floor ratio. The LEA tests whether candidates can optimize daylighting depth, glare control, and visual comfort while maintaining or exceeding code minimums. The NBC standard (**1:10 for light**, **1:20 for ventilation**) is a legal _baseline_, not a design target.

## Core Concept

Daylighting provides illumination, psychological benefits, and energy savings. However, light penetrates only so far into a building's interior.

### The Rule of Thumb: Daylighting Depth

The **daylighting depth**—the distance from a window at which daylight becomes insufficient (typically <50 lux)—is approximately **2.5 times the floor-to-ceiling height**.

- **Example:** A 3.0 m tall office space gains adequate daylight up to 7.5 m from the facade.
- **Note:** This is an international design guideline (IESNA) used for high-performance buildings; it is not a prescriptive limit in PD 1096, but it is frequently tested as a "best practice" metric in the LEA.

### Statutory Minimums: Window-to-Floor Ratio (WFR)

The **Window-to-Floor Ratio (WFR)** is the total window area divided by the floor area served.

- **PD 1096 Rule VIII, Section 808:** Specifies **1:10 (10%)** window area minimum for light.
- **PD 1096 Rule VIII, Section 808:** Specifies **1:20 (5%)** window area minimum for natural ventilation.
- **Critical Error:** Do not use 1:5 (20%). This is a common mistake (ERR-DSGN-034).
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-009-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Daylighting Strategy — Window-to-Floor Ratio and Light Penetration Depth" description="Building section showing daylight penetration: minimum 1:10 window-to-floor ratio, light penetration depth (2.5× window head height), glare control devices (lightshelves, louvers, fins), and integration with artificial lighting controls." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

| Design Goal | Metric | Standard | Source |
|:---------------------- |:------------------------- |:----------------------- |:------------------------------ |
| **Minimum Daylighting** | Window-to-floor ratio | **1:10 (10%)** | PD 1096 Sec. 808 |
| **Minimum Ventilation** | Operable window ratio | **1:20 (5%)** | PD 1096 Sec. 808 |
| **Daylighting Depth** | Effective penetration | **2.5 × ceiling height** | IESNA Guideline |
| **Glare Control** | Visible Transmittance (VT) | <40% (South/West) | Design Best Practice |

## Philippine Practice Context

Philippine buildings use daylight to reduce high operational costs from air-conditioning. High-performance designs (aiming for BERDE or LEED certification) often achieve **1:6 to 1:8 WFR** in office zones to deepen light penetration.

However, designers must balance this against **Solar Heat Gain**. In the tropics:

- **North/South Facades:** Preferred for maximum glazing due to lower solar loads.
- **East/West Facades:** Require moderate WFR and heavy shading (overhangs/louvers) to prevent afternoon heat gain and glare.

## How It's Tested

**Test Pattern 1: Compliance Calculation**
A 2,000 m² floor plate has 180 m² of exterior windows. Is it compliant for light?

- **Calculation:** $180 / 2,000 = 0.09$ (or 1:11.1).
- **Answer:** **No.** 1:11.1 is less than the required 1:10 (10%).

**Test Pattern 2: Depth Application**
An office has a 3.0 m ceiling. How deep does "effective" daylight reach?

- **Calculation:** $2.5 \times 3.0 = 7.5\text{ m}$.
- **Application:** Beyond 7.5 m, artificial lighting or "secondary zones" are required.

**Test Pattern 3: The "20%" Trap**
The exam asks for the minimum window area for a 100 m² room.

- **Answer:** 10 m² (1:10).
- **Warning:** If you select 20 m² (1:5), you are applying a common misconception not supported by the NBCP.

**Exam Tip:** NBC minimum = 1:10 window-to-floor ratio for light, 1:20 for ventilation. Daylight penetration depth ≈ 2.5× window head height. A 2m high window provides useful daylight ~5m into the room.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-009-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Daylight Penetration — Section Showing Light Shelf and Glare Control" description="Section diagram showing daylight penetration depth (2.5× window head height), light shelf positioning (above eye level at 2.0m minimum), glare control devices (horizontal louvers, vertical fins), and minimum window-to-floor area ratio (1:10 per NBC). Interior daylight distribution zones labeled." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-009-01** (Passive Design) for solar control strategies, **LEA-DSGN-009-04** (Green Building) for daylight credit requirements, and **LEA-DSGN-011-02** (Elevations and Sections) for fenestration documentation.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
 mistakes={[
 'ERR-DSGN-034: Using 1:5 (20% WFR) instead of the correct 1:10 (10% WFR) for daylighting minimums.',
 "Treating the 2.5× height rule as a legal 'limit' rather than a design optimization tool.",
 'Confusing the 1:10 light requirement with the 1:20 ventilation requirement.',
 'Ignoring glare control; assuming more glass always equals better design (excessive glass leads to solar heat gain).',
 'Applying code minimums as the final design goal rather than the starting baseline.',
 ]}
/>

rows.title: Funeral Homes
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Classify funeral homes as dual-occupancy (Group E mercantile + Group H assembly), calculate separate occupant loads for business vs. chapel components, apply egress for mixed-use, and verify BP 344 accessibility.

Funeral homes and memorial chapels are mixed-use facilities requiring dual occupancy classification: **Group E (Business and Mercantile)** for the commercial funeral home business area (office, embalming, storage), and **Group H (Assembly)** for the chapel component depending on chapel capacity and seating configuration.

---

## Core Concept

A funeral home operates as a hybrid facility with distinct functional zones, each having separate occupancy implications.

- **Business Administrative Area**: Including the funeral director's office, reception desk, and back-office functions, this is classified as **Group E (Business and Mercantile)**.
- **Commercial Support Spaces**: The viewing room and embalming room support the Group E-classified commercial operation.
- **Chapel Component**: This is where the public assembles for funeral services and memorial rites. When the chapel has fixed seating and functions as a dedicated assembly space, it is classified as **Group H (Assembly)** Division 1. A typical funeral chapel with 200–400 seated capacity falls under **Group H Division 1**.

### Specialized Infrastructure

- **Embalming Room**: Requires 12–20 square meters with a separate HVAC system serving only that space, chemical storage, and plumbing with a floor drain and backflow prevention. It must have direct external access for receiving deceased persons.
- **Cold Storage (Morgue)**: Must be temperature-controlled (2–4°C), typically 6–12 square meters for 2–4 body capacity, with separate access and no public circulation.
- **Viewing/Visitation Room**: Occupant load is calculated per NBC Table II-2 (0.5 sqm/person for assembly), though actual design area may be increased (typically 1.1–1.5 sqm/visitor) for functional circulation.

### Safety and Egress

- **Fire Separation**: Fire separation between the Group E business office and the Group H assembly component requires a **1-hour minimum** rated wall or door assembly per NBC Rule VI.
- **Chapel Exit System**: Must be sized separately from the commercial office area. It requires 2 separate exits at a capacity of 50+ persons.
- **Travel Distance**: Maximum of 60m (sprinklered) or 45m (unsprinklered).
- **Accessibility**: Accessible routes to chapel seating must follow **BP 344** standards, including a **1:12 maximum ramp slope** per the 2024 Revised IRR and 900mm minimum clear door width.

---

## Key Provisions

**Functional Space Requirements:**

| Function | Minimum Area | Notes |
|:---------------------- |:----------------------------- |:--------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Embalming Room | Size per functional needs | Separate HVAC, drainage, chemical storage |
| Cold Storage | Size per operational needs | Temperature controlled (2-4°C), separate access |
| Viewing Room | Use NBC Table II-2 load factor | Includes standing circulation |
| Funeral Director Office | 9–12 sqm | Administrative, **Group E** |
| Reception/Waiting | 8–15 sqm | Public interface, **Group E** |
| Chapel (seated) | 200–400 sqm typical | **Group H Division 1** (200–400 persons) |

**Occupancy Classification Summary:**

- **Business/Commercial area**: Group E (Business and Mercantile).
- **Chapel component**: **Group H Division 1 (Assembly)**.
- **Fire separation**: Minimum 1-hour rated wall between **Group E and Group H**.

**Specialized Systems:**

- **Embalming Room HVAC**: Separate negative-pressure system to prevent odor transmission.
- **Cold Storage**: Dedicated unit with separate mechanical system.
- **Sanitary Drainage**: Indirect waste piping from the embalming room and floor drain with trap seal.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-005-11-core-concept" type="image" caption="Funeral Home — Dual-Occupancy Space Layout" description="Floor plan diagram of a funeral home showing dual-occupancy zones: Group E mercantile (viewing rooms, selection area) and Group H assembly (chapel, memorial service area). Separate occupant load calculations for each zone with mixed-use egress." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

---

## Philippine Practice Context

Funeral homes are licensed commercial establishments regulated by local health authorities and the Bureau of Internal Revenue. A typical Filipino funeral home includes a viewing room for the _likha_ (wake) and a chapel for formal religious rites. While the viewing room accommodates multi-day informal family visits, the chapel hosts formal services. Embalming rooms must comply with **Republic Act 4167** (Funeral Services Board) regarding chemicals and cross-infection control.

---

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Mixed Occupancy**
"A funeral home's business office area is **Group E**, while the chapel is **Group H**. Fire separation between them requires a minimum **1-hour** rated wall." 

**Pattern 2: Space Sizing**
"A funeral home expects 60 simultaneous visitors in the viewing room. Using a design factor of 1.1–1.5 sqm/person, calculate the minimum required viewing room area." 

**Pattern 3: Exit Capacity**
"A funeral home chapel seats 300 persons. Calculate the minimum combined exit width and the required number of exits (Note: 2 exits are required for 50+ persons)." 

> <Tip>**Funeral Home Anchors:** Mixed occupancy of **Group E (Business)** + **Group H Division 1 (Chapel)**. Embalming = 12–20 sqm. Viewing Room = 1.1–1.5 sqm/visitor. Chapel Exit Width = 7.6mm/person. Fire separation E–H = 1-hour minimum.</Tip>

---

**Exam Tip — ERR-DSGN-027:** Funeral homes are dual occupancy: Group E (mercantile for business areas) + Group H (assembly for chapel). Verify fire-rated separation between occupancies per RA 9514 Section 7.2.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-005-11-core-concept" type="image" caption="Funeral Home — Mercantile and Assembly Zone Separation" description="Floor plan of a funeral home showing: Group E mercantile zone (viewing rooms, casket selection), Group H assembly zone (chapel, memorial service), and service zone (preparation, storage). Fire-rated separation between occupancy groups and dual-egress paths annotated." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-004-07** (Theaters) for Group H chapel classification, **LEA-DSGN-008-01** (Fire Egress) for dual-occupancy egress, and **LEA-PLAN-003-06** (Informal Settlements) for community funeral service context.

## Common Mistakes

- **ERR-DSGN-005**: Classifying the entire funeral home as Group H instead of mixed Group E (Business) + Group H (Chapel).
- Underestimating viewing room area; it should be sized at **1.1–1.5 sqm/visitor** for circulation, not just the 0.5 sqm load factor.
- Failing to apply a 1-hour fire separation between the Group E office and the **Group H** chapel.
- Sizing the embalming room without functional justification (Note: there is **no NBC minimum** specified).
- Designing the embalming room without backflow prevention on the drain system.
- Specifying exit width for the chapel at 5mm/person instead of the assembly factor of **7.6mm/person** (stair/unit factor) per NBC standards.

---

rows.title: Site development planning
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Determine buildable area from site constraints and setbacks, organize site access and circulation, coordinate utility routing and easements, apply zoning and subdivision regulations, and produce site development plans showing land use allocation.

Site development planning is the systematic process of organizing land use, access, and infrastructure to create a functional, safe, and efficient site. Understanding how to determine buildable envelopes, manage site access, and coordinate utilities is essential to laying the foundation for any architectural project. 

## Core Concept

Site development planning transforms raw land into organized, developable space through a methodical approach that balances regulatory constraints, infrastructure logistics, and design intent. 

### The Buildable Envelope

The buildable envelope is the three-dimensional area where structures may legally be placed. It is determined by setback distances from property lines and easements. 

- **Front Setback:** Typically 3–6m depending on the road Right-of-Way (RROW). 
- **Side/Rear Setbacks:** Vary based on the occupancy group and whether the wall has openings (firewall vs. windowed wall). 

### Site Metrics and Formulas

- **PSO (Percentage of Site Occupancy):** The maximum percentage of the Total Lot Area (TLA) that can be occupied by the building footprint. 
- **AMBF (Allowable Maximum Built-up Floor):** The actual area of the footprint. $AMBF = TLA \times PSO$. 
- **TGFA (Total Gross Floor Area):** The sum of all floor areas. $TGFA = AMBF \times \text{number of floors}$. 

### Site Access and Utilities

Access is organized hierarchically—major arterial roads connect to local streets. 

- **Ramps:** Must have a maximum gradient of **1:12** per BP 344 2024 IRR to be considered accessible. 
- **Water Easements (PD 1067):** The "Rule of 3-20-40" applies to the banks of rivers, streams, and seas: 
 - **3 meters:** Urban areas.
 - **20 meters:** Agricultural areas.
 - **40 meters:** Forest areas.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Buildable Area Analysis — Setback, Easement, and Site Constraints" description="Site plan diagram showing buildable area calculation: total site minus setback zones (front 4.5m, sides 2.0m, rear 2.0m for R-1), easement strips (3m utility, water body), and slope constraints. Resulting development footprint with FAR and lot coverage annotation." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

| Control | Requirement / Standard | Source |
|:---------------------------- |:------------------------------------------ |:---------------------- |
| **Open Space (Subdivisions)** | 30% of Gross Area (Total non-sleaable area) | PD 957 |
| **Major Road RROW** | Minimum **12.0 m** | BP 220 / PD 1096 |
| **Secondary Road RROW** | Minimum **10.0 m** | BP 220 / PD 1096 |
| **Local Road RROW** | Minimum **8.0 m** | BP 220 / PD 1096 |
| **Alley / Service Road** | Minimum **3.0 m** | BP 220 / PD 1096 |

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, site development is a layered process. Beyond the NBC, local **Zoning Ordinances** often dictate the specific FAR and PSO for a given block. Due to the monsoon climate, drainage and flood resilience (integrating detention ponds or bioswleas) are now critical components of a site plan, often cross-referenced with the **BERDE** or **EDGE** green building frameworks. 

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Footprint Calculation**
A 1,000 m² lot has a 60% PSO. What is the AMBF?

- **Answer:** 600 m². 
- **Note:** Always check if setbacks restrict the footprint further than the PSO does. The buildable area is the _smaller_ of the two. 

**Pattern 2: Road Hierarchy**
Which road type requires a minimum 12m RROW?

- **Answer:** Major Roads. 

**Pattern 3: Waterway Easements**
A project is located in an **urban** district bordering a river. What is the required easement?

- **Answer:** 3 meters. 

<Tip>
 **Memory Aid:** Remember **3-20-40** for rivers. For roads, it's
 **12-10-8-3**. PSO is your footprint limit; FAR is your total volume limit.
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Buildable area = site area − (setbacks + easements + flood hazard areas + steep slopes + water body buffers). A 2,000 sqm lot with 3m setbacks on all sides yields ~1,200 sqm buildable area.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-012-02-core-concept" type="image" caption="Site Development Plan — Buildable Area, Access, and Utility Routing" description="Master site plan showing: buildable area calculated from setbacks and easement constraints, vehicular access and parking layout, pedestrian walkway circulation, utility routing (water main, sewer line, stormwater, power, telecom), and phased development boundaries." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-012-01** (Site Analysis) for input conditions, **LEA-DSGN-012-03** (Grading and Drainage) for site grading, and **LEA-PLAN-004-07** (Zoning Analysis) for regulatory compliance in site plans.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
 mistakes={[
 'ERR-DSGN-006: Applying a flat 60% PSO to all residential lots (R-1 is typically 50%).',
 'ERR-DSGN-007: Calculating TGFA using TLA instead of the allowed AMBF footprint.',
 'Using waterway width to determine PD 1067 easements (Correct: Use Land Use—Urban, Agri, or Forest).',
 'Specifying a 1:24 ramp slope as the code maximum (Correct: 1:12).',
 "Confusing 'Open Space' (parks/playgrounds) with the 'Total Non-Sleaable Area' (roads + parks) in PD 957 projects.",
 ]}
/>

rows.title: Architectural Drawing Communication
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA

## Learning Goal
Identify and interpret standard architectural symbols for materials (section, elevation), fixtures, doors, windows, and mechanical/electrical elements, read dimension and annotation systems, and apply consistent notation across plan, elevation, and section views.

Architectural symbols and notations are the standardized graphical language used on drawings to communicate building components, materials, and design intent to builders and regulators. The LEA expects you to recognize and interpret these symbols accurately and to understand their use across plan, elevation, and section views.

## Core Concept

Architectural drawings communicate through two primary means: **dimensions and annotations** (text) and **symbols and notation** (graphical marks). Symbols allow complex information to be conveyed quickly and consistently across large drawings. Standardized symbols ensure that anyone—builder, inspector, engineer—can interpret the drawing without ambiguity.

**Categories of architectural symbols:**

1. **Plan symbols** (viewed from above):
   - **Doors**: Single-swing, double-swing, pocket, bifold, accordion. Shown with an arc indicating swing direction. Symbol includes a solid line representing the door leaf and a dotted line showing the swing arc.
   - **Windows**: Shown as an opening in the wall with a break or mark indicating the window type (double-hung, casement, fixed, etc.). Size and type are noted in a schedule or on the drawing.
   - **Stairs**: Shown as a series of parallel lines representing treads, with an arrow indicating the "UP" direction. Number of risers is often noted.
   - **Elevators**: Shown as a rectangle with "ELV" or "E" designation. **Minimum inside cab dimensions per NBC Rule XVIII (Mechanical Regulations) Section 1801: 1,100 mm width x 1,400 mm depth.**
   - **Walls**: Shown as lines of varying thickness. Exterior walls are typically thicker lines (150–200 mm drawn width); interior walls are thinner. Fire-rated walls may be shown with a dotted or dashed line and labeled "1-HR" or "2-HR".

2. **Section/elevation symbols**:
   - **Material hatching**: Standardized patterns indicate material type:
     - **Concrete**: Dotted or speckled pattern.
     - **Masonry**: Diagonal hatching (45°) with regular spacing.
     - **Earth**: Organic, irregular speckled pattern.
     - **Wood**: Diagonal lines (typically 45° at a steeper angle than masonry).
     - **Steel**: Cross-hatching in perpendicular directions.
     - **Insulation**: Wavy or diagonal lines indicating thermal break.
   - **Section cut symbols**: A heavy line on a plan with endpoints and arrows indicating viewing direction (e.g., "Section A-A"). The corresponding section elevation is drawn and labeled with the same letter pair.

3. **Detail markers**: Small symbols placed on plan or elevation indicating where a detail drawing exists at a larger scale. Typically shown as a circle with a number or letter (e.g., "Detail 3" or "Detail A").

4. **Electrical & Plumbing symbols**: Outlets, switches, water lines, and drains. These are typically shown in a dedicated legend on their respective specialty plans.

**Notations and annotations:**

- **Dimension lines**: Thin lines with arrows or tick marks at endpoints, showing distances. Critical dimensions include floor-to-floor heights, room widths, and setbacks.
- **Leader lines**: Thin lines with arrows or dots pointing to a feature, with text annotation (e.g., "FFL +0.00 m").
- **Title blocks**: Located at the bottom right of each sheet, showing project name, scale, and date.
- **Legends and schedules**: Lists defining abbreviations, symbols, materials, and specifications.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-011-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Architectural Symbols — Material, Fixture, and Notation Standards" description="Reference chart of standard architectural symbols: material symbols (brick, concrete, wood in plan/section/elevation), door/window types, plumbing fixtures, electrical outlets, and notation system for room names, dimensions, and finish schedules." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Key Provisions

| Symbol Type              | Representation                                            | Standard Use                                                                              |
| :----------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Doors (single-swing)** | Arc from hinge, solid line at leaf                        | Plan view; indicates swing direction and clearance                                        |
| **Doors (double-swing)** | Two arcs, one in each direction                           | Barn doors, accordion; allows swing either way                                            |
| **Windows**              | Break in wall line; type noted in schedule                | All views; detailed in elevation and section                                              |
| **Stairs**               | Parallel lines with up arrow; number of risers noted      | Plan; direction of ascent; NBC minimum tread/riser noted                                  |
| **Elevators**            | Rectangle labeled "ELV"; **min 1.1 m × 1.4 m inside cab** | All views; **required for buildings 4 storeys and above per NBC Rule XVIII Section 1801** |
| **Concrete hatching**    | Dotted or fine speckled pattern                           | Section/detail views                                                                      |
| **Masonry hatching**     | Diagonal 45° lines                                        | Section/detail views; clarifies unit assembly                                             |
| **Wood hatching**        | Diagonal lines (steeper or finer than masonry)            | Section/detail views; interior finishes                                                   |
| **Steel hatching**       | Cross-hatching (perpendicular lines)                      | Section/detail views; columns, beams                                                      |
| **Insulation**           | Wavy or diagonal lines                                    | Section/detail views; energy code requirements                                            |
| **Fire-rated wall**      | Dotted/dashed line or special notation ("1-HR", "2-HR")   | Plan and section; specifies duration of fire resistance                                   |
| **Section cut**          | Heavy line with arrows and letter labels (e.g., "A-A")    | Plan; references corresponding section elevation                                          |
| **Detail marker**        | Circle with number (e.g., ⊙ 3)                            | Plan or elevation; references enlarged detail drawing                                     |

**Philippine-specific notations:**

- Dimensions in millimeters (mm) or meters (m), with metric units standard.
- Fire ratings noted per **RA 9514** (Fire Code) and **PD 1096** (NBC).
- **Accessible** symbols for ramps, parking, and facilities per **BP 344**.

## Philippine Practice Context

In the Philippines, architectural drawings follow NBC standards. The use of symbols is essential for multi-disciplinary coordination between architects and engineers. Material hatching conventions help builders quickly identify concrete, masonry, or timber—crucial for cost estimation and constructability in a tropical climate.

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Symbol identification and interpretation**
A floor plan section is shown with various symbols. The candidate must identify each correctly (e.g., distinguishing between a casement and a sliding window symbol).

**Pattern 2: Section cut and detail reference**
A plan shows a section cut line. The candidate must determine the viewing direction based on the arrow orientation and locate the correct corresponding elevation.

**Pattern 3: Code-Mandated Symbols**
The exam may ask for the minimum interior dimensions of an elevator cab or the threshold at which an elevator is required.

- **Answer:** Required at **4 storeys and above**; minimum inside cab is **1.10 m x 1.40 m** (Rule XVIII Sec 1801).

<Tip>
  **Memory aid:** "Door-Direction-Arc Rule" — The arc always shows the path of
  the door. If a door swings into a required egress corridor and reduces the
  width, it is a code violation!
</Tip>

**Exam Tip:** Material symbols: diagonal lines = concrete/brick/masonry (spacing indicates material), random squiggles = earth/gravel, dots = sand/cement. Section marks show cut location + view direction.
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-dsgn-011-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Architectural Symbol Library — Plan, Elevation, and Section Graphics" description="Reference chart of standard architectural symbols organized by category: doors and windows (plan, elevation, schedule), materials (section hatch patterns), plumbing fixtures (plan symbols), electrical (plan symbols), and structural (column grid system). Consistent notation conventions per PD 1096." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

## Cross-References

See **LEA-DSGN-011-01** (Floor Plans) for plan symbols, **LEA-DSGN-011-02** (Elevations and Sections) for elevation/section symbols, and **LEA-DSGN-011-03** (Site Plans) for site plan symbols and notation.

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
  mistakes={[
    'Drawing door swings incorrectly; arcs must start at the hinge and represent the actual path of the leaf.',
    'Failing to distinguish between drawn wall thickness and clear interior cab dimensions for elevators.',
    'Inconsistent material hatching (e.g., using masonry hatching for a concrete section).',
    "Using 'Rule XIV' or 'Rule XI' for elevator requirements (Correct: Rule XVIII Section 1801).",
    "Forgetting the 'UP' arrow on stairs; without it, the direction of travel is ambiguous for the builder.",
    'Missing fire-rating notations on critical compartmentation walls.',
    "Misinterpreting the 4-storey rule as requiring 'multiple' elevators (Code requires at least one).",
  ]}
/>

rows.title: Finish schedule
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Identify the purpose and structure of a finish schedule as a specification document that coordinates floor, wall, and ceiling finishes across all rooms, and create a sample finish schedule entry applying correct material codes, locations, and installation notes.
## Core Concept

A finish schedule is a matrix table in construction documents that lists each room/space, identifies wall, floor, ceiling, and sometimes door and window finishes, and cross-references them to larger detail drawings. This document prevents field interpretation and rework. Three interrelated schedules exist: room finish schedules, door schedules, and window schedules.

Room finish schedules typically organize by room number and list finishes for walls (north, south, east, west), floor, ceiling, base, and trim. Format follows CSI (Construction Specifications Institute) standards, with specification callouts like "2.0.5 Semi-gloss Enamel, Boysen Permacoat, Color: Safety Orange per Pantone 151C."

Door schedules list door type (code: A, B, C, etc.), frame material, width×height, swing direction, hardware group, and finish. Example: "Door Type A: 900×2100mm, wood composite, left-hand swing, Hardware Set 1, finish: pre-finished maple stain per 2.0.8."

Window schedules specify type (casement, sliding, fixed), frame material (aluminum, UPVC, wood), glass type (clear, tinted, tempered), size, and finish. These cross-reference structural sections and ensure consistency across the building.

Philippine practice per RA 9266 (Architecture Act of 2004) and DPWH standards emphasizes clarity and traceability. Finish schedules must reference specification sections (e.g., Section 2.0 "Interior Finishes") and product standards (e.g., ASTM C373 for floor tile). Vague finishes like "paint TBD" or "ceramic tile—to be determined" are construction non-starters and cause delays.

Key information in schedules includes paint color codes (matched to approved color chips or Pantone numbers), floor material and size (e.g., "Mariwasa porcelain tile 600×600mm, Pattern #X-101, grout color: light gray"), ceiling type with acoustic rating if applicable, and baseboard/trim material with height and finish.


<ArticleMedia id="media-finish-schedule-example" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Example finish schedule showing room-by-room matrix of floor, wall, and ceiling finishes with material codes, locations, and installation notes"
  caption="Future diagram: sample finish schedule — room-by-room matrix with material codes and installation notes"
  suggestedAsset="Table or matrix template showing finish schedule format"
  placementIntent="Provides visual example of finish schedule document structure" />

## Key Provisions

| Element | Schedule Field | Required Information | Standard | LEA Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Room/Space Identification | Room Name and Number | Unique ID per floor plan | PD 1096 (National Building Code) | Cross-references plans and elevations |
| Wall Finish (Each Orientation) | North/South/East/West Wall | Material, color, thickness, application standard | CSI format | Prevents ambiguity; specifies exact product |
| Floor Finish | Floor Material | Tile type/size, concrete stain, vinyl, wood; grout color if applicable | ASTM C373, ANSI A108.02 | Directs sourcing and installation |
| Ceiling Finish | Ceiling Type | Suspended tile NRC rating, gypsum DFT, paint; grid type if applicable | ASTM C635, ISO 354 | Determines cost and timeline |
| Base/Trim | Baseboard and Trim | Material, height (75mm, 100mm typical), finish/color; riser finish if stairs | CSI format | Visual continuity, maintenance access |
| Door Schedule | Door Type Code | Material, size (W×H), swing, hardware set, finish | CSI format | Replicability across building |
| Door Finish | Veneer/Paint | Wood stain, paint color, hardware finish (brass, stainless, etc.) | CSI format, paint standards | Brand/color uniformity |
| Window Schedule | Window Type Code | Frame material (aluminum, UPVC, wood), glass (clear, tinted, tempered), size | CSI format | Structural and thermal performance |
| Specification Cross-Reference | Section Reference | e.g., "Section 2.0.5—Paint Systems" | CSI MasterFormat | Links schedule to detail specifications |
| Product Callout | Brand and Product | e.g., "Boysen Permacoat, Color #B247" or "Mariwasa Porcelain #X-101" | CSI format | Quality assurance; prevents substitution |
| Quantity/Area | Finish Extent | e.g., "Walls: 1200 m² painted; Floor: 450 m² tile" | Project planning | Material estimation; cost control |

## Philippine Construction Context

Philippine architects and engineers follow CSI MasterFormat conventions, aligned with international practice but adapted to local materials. DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) standard specification compliance is mandatory for government infrastructure projects. Private construction follows the specifications agreed upon in the contract documents, though DPWH specs often serve as the baseline reference.

Local brands (Boysen, Davies, Mariwasa, Niro Granite) are named explicitly in schedules, with color codes referenced to approved color chips or Pantone numbers. Generic references like "paint—light color" cause rework when 20 similar products exist on-site. Finish schedules in Philippine projects often include a key/legend sheet that displays color samples and material samples, reducing field ambiguity.

For high-rise residential projects (dominant in Metro Manila), finish schedules are critical for unit standardization. Developer contracts typically specify standard finishes for all units (e.g., "All residential units: walls—Boysen Permacoat, Color #B150; floor—Mariwasa porcelain 600×600, Pattern #S-02; ceiling—gypsum + latex paint, White). Custom finishes require a change order.

Accessibility compliance (BP 344) is documented in schedules where applicable. Slip-resistant finishes on ramps and level paths are called out separately. Finish schedules serve as compliance documentation for inspectors.


<ArticleMedia id="media-finish-schedule-template" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Template of a finish schedule showing room-by-room entries for floor, wall, ceiling, and base finishes with material codes and installation notes"
  caption="Future diagram: finish schedule template — room-by-room material specification"
  suggestedAsset="Template or example finish schedule document"
  placementIntent="Provides practical template for finish schedule creation" />
## How It's Tested

**Question Type 1 (Schedule Interpretation):** A finish schedule shows "Room 201: North Wall—Paint, Boysen Permacoat, Color #B150." What additional information is unclear that might prevent accurate execution? Answer: DFT (dry film thickness), primer type, sheen level (matte, satin, gloss), and surface prep standard should be cross-referenced to the paint specification section. The color code is clear but other details are implicit, risking substitution.

**Question Type 2 (Schedule Creation):** A lobby requires marble veneer walls, porcelain floor tile, suspended ceiling with NRC 0.80, and wood trim. Create a finish schedule entry. Answer: format should list: walls (marble type, size, finish), floor (porcelain tile, size, grout color), ceiling (suspended tile, NRC 0.80, grid type), and base (wood trim, height, stain color), each cross-referenced to specification sections.

**Question Type 3 (Cross-Reference):** A door schedule shows "Door Type A: wood composite, finish—per 2.0.10." What does "per 2.0.10" refer to? Answer: Specification Section 2.0.10, which details door finish standards (primer, topcoat, sanding sequence, hardness test). The schedule abbreviation directs builders to detailed specifications.

**Question Type 4 (Consistency):** A multi-story residential project specifies different paint colors for Units 201 and 301 in the same location. A finish schedule shows Unit 201: Boysen Permacoat #B150, but Unit 301 shows only "light beige paint." What is the issue? Answer: Lack of consistency and product specification prevents bulk purchasing and creates quality variance. All standard units should use identical finishes; deviations require explicit custom-finish callout and cost tracking.

<Tip>Memory aid: Finish schedules are the builder's contract. Every finish must be specific: product name, color code, size, and cross-reference to specification section. Vague entries ("paint TBD," "tiles to match existing") cause rework and disputes. Use CSI format. Include color/material samples on a separate key sheet.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Creating finish schedules with vague entries like 'paint—light color' or 'ceramic tile—standard'" correction="Every finish must be specific: product brand/model, color code (e.g., Pantone #), size, and specification section reference. Include approved color samples and material samples on a key sheet." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Failing to cross-reference schedule entries to detailed specification sections, creating ambiguity about prep, application, and durability" correction="Every schedule entry must link to a specification section. E.g., 'Boysen Permacoat, Color #B150, per Section 2.0.5 Paint Systems,' ensures builders read the full spec." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Inconsistent finishes across similar rooms or units, requiring field changes and change orders" correction="Standardize finishes for like spaces (e.g., all bedrooms in residential units use the same paint/floor). Document custom finishes separately with cost tracking." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Omitting finish schedules for door and window hardware, leading to color/style mismatches" correction="Include hardware finish in door and window schedules (e.g., 'Brass handles, stainless hinges, brushed stainless push plates per Section 8.7'). Consistency requires specificity." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Not accounting for finish transitions where different materials meet (e.g., tile to wood, paint to wallpaper)", "Failing to specify grout color for tile finishes, assuming default (results in color mismatch and rework)", "Omitting baseboard and trim heights in finish schedules (75mm, 100mm, or custom)", "Not specifying ceiling finish details (grid type, tile size, NRC rating, paint sheen)", "Creating schedules without a key/legend sheet showing actual material and color samples for field reference"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Interior Finishes: **lea-matl-007-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-02-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-04-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Fastener Systems
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Classify fastener systems (nails, screws, bolts, anchors, rivets, welding, adhesives) by material, load capacity, substrate compatibility, and installation method, and select the appropriate fastener for a given structural or non-structural connection.
## Core Concept

Fasteners are classified by type (nails, screws, bolts, rivets) and material grade. Nails are categorized by length and diameter. Common nails have a larger diameter and are used for general construction and framing. Finishing nails have a smaller diameter and smoother shaft, minimizing surface damage, suitable for trim and cabinetry. Roofing nails include a neoprene washer to prevent leakage. Nail sizes are measured in penny weight, abbreviated 'd' (penny), historically based on the weight of 100 nails. A 16d common nail is 3.5 inches long; a 10d common nail is 3 inches long. Penny weight does not scale linearly; reference tables are essential.

Screws are classified by drive type (Phillips, slotted, square/Robertson, hex head), material (steel, stainless, brass), and application. Wood screws have a coarse thread and sharp point for timber; self-tapping screws (or sheet metal screws) have finer threads and cut their own thread pilot in metal. Lag screws (or lag bolts) are heavy-duty fasteners with a hex head, used for timber-to-timber or timber-to-concrete applications. Machine screws are precision fasteners with consistent thread pitch, used with nuts for metal assembly.

Bolts are classified by head shape and material grade. Hex bolts are the most common. Carriage bolts have a rounded head and a square neck underneath to prevent rotation during installation. Anchor bolts are embedded in concrete and used to secure machinery or structural members. Expansion bolts (toggle bolts, wedge anchors) are used to attach to existing concrete without drilling all the way through. ASTM A307 grade bolts have a minimum tensile strength of 60,000 psi and are used for general-purpose applications. ASTM A325 bolts are high-strength structural bolts with 120,000 psi tensile strength, used in structural steel connections. ASTM A490 bolts provide 150,000 psi tensile strength for ultra-high-stress applications.

Rivets are historical fasteners largely replaced by bolts and welds. They are driven hot, then cooled to create a permanent joint. Riveted connections cannot be disassembled, making them unsuitable for modern construction requiring serviceability.

Pull-out strength (or withdrawal strength) depends on fastener diameter, material, and embedment depth. Wood-to-wood connections: pull-out strength ≈ 25 to 50 lbf per inch of embedment for common nails; lag screws provide 300 to 500 lbf per inch. Concrete anchors vary by type: wedge anchors provide 1,000 to 2,000 lbf per inch of embedment.


<ArticleMedia id="media-fastener-comparison-chart" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison chart of fastener systems: nails, screws, bolts, anchors, rivets, welding, and adhesives with load capacity, substrate compatibility, and installation method"
  caption="Future chart: fastener system comparison — load capacity, substrate, and installation method"
  suggestedAsset="Fastener selection matrix with application illustrations"
  placementIntent="Helps learners select appropriate fasteners by connection requirements" />

## Key Provisions

| Property | Value | Standard | LEA Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Common Nail Size (16d) | 3.5 inches long | ASTM F1667 | Standard framing fastener; penny weight guides sizing |
| Finishing Nail Size (16d) | 3-1/4 to 3-1/2 inches long | ASTM F1667 | Trim and cabinetry; smaller diameter than common |
| Roofing Nail | 1.75 to 2 inches + neoprene washer | ASTM F1667 | Leak prevention; washer diameter ≥ 0.5 inches |
| Penny Weight (d) | 1d through 60d scale | ASTM F1667 | Non-linear relationship; reference tables required |
| Wood Screw Pull-Out Strength | 25-50 lbf per inch embedment | NDS / ASTM D1761 | Depends on wood density and fastener diameter |
| Lag Screw Pull-Out Strength | 300-500 lbf per inch | NDS / ASTM D1761 | Heavy-duty timber fastening |
| ASTM A307 Bolt Tensile Strength | 55-60 ksi (Grade A/B) | ASTM A307 | General-purpose low-strength bolts |
| ASTM A325 Bolt Tensile Strength | 120 ksi (≤1" dia.); 105 ksi (1-1.5" dia.) | ASTM A325 | Standard structural bolt for steel connections |
| ASTM F3125 Grade A490 Tensile Strength | 150-170 ksi | ASTM F3125 (A490 superseded) | Ultra-high-stress applications only |
| Expansion Anchor Pull-Out | 1,000-2,000 lbf per inch (concrete dependent) | ASTM E488 | Depends on concrete compressive strength |

## Philippine Construction Context

Philippine construction standards adopt ASTM fastener classifications, though many informal projects use non-standard fasteners. Common wire nails (CWN) are widely available through hardware stores but rarely meet ASTM specifications for uniformity. Filipino contractors often specify "20 inches" for roofing when 1.75-inch roofing nails are required, leading to fastener failure and roof leaks during monsoon rains. Lag screws and expansion anchors are less commonly used in informal residential construction, resulting in inadequate fastening of structural members to concrete foundations. Stainless steel fasteners, essential for typhoon and coastal corrosion resistance, are often substituted with carbon steel due to cost, leading to premature rust. Quality assurance is weak; ASTM A325 bolts may be mislabeled as A490, creating structural reliability issues.


<ArticleMedia id="media-fastener-load-chart" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison chart of fastener load capacities: nails, screws, bolts, anchors, rivets, and adhesives in shear and tension with substrate compatibility"
  caption="Future chart: fastener load capacity comparison — shear, tension, and substrate compatibility"
  suggestedAsset="Reference chart or infographic of fastener load capacities"
  placementIntent="Provides reference for fastener selection based on load requirements" />
## How It's Tested

**Exam Pattern 1: Nail Sizing.** A framing plan specifies "16d common nails." What is the length and intended application? Answer: 3.5 inches long; general framing and structural connections.

**Exam Pattern 2: Bolt Grade Selection.** A structural steel connection in a commercial building requires a tensile strength of 100,000 psi minimum. Which ASTM bolt grade is appropriate? Answer: ASTM A325 (120,000 psi); A307 (60,000 psi) is insufficient.

**Exam Pattern 3: Pull-Out Calculation.** A wooden roof rafter is fastened to a timber plate with a 10-inch embedment using 0.25-inch diameter lag screws. Assume lag screw pull-out strength is 400 lbf per inch. What is the total pull-out capacity? Answer: 10 inches × 400 lbf/inch = 4,000 lbf.

**Exam Pattern 4: Fastener Material Specification.** A coastal resort in the Philippines specifies carbon steel bolts for exterior connections. What is the risk? Answer: Carbon steel corrodes rapidly in salt spray; stainless steel (duplex or super-duplex) or hot-dip galvanized fasteners are mandatory for coastal applications.

<Tip>Memory aid: "Penny weight guides nail size (16d = 3.5 in common, 2.5 in finishing). A307 = 60k, A325 = 120k, A490 = 150k (bolt tensile grades). Wood-to-wood pull-out ≈ 25-50 lbf/in (nails) or 300-500 lbf/in (lags)."</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Assuming all nail sizes sclea linearly with penny weight (e.g., 20d is 4 inches because 16d is 3.5 inches)." correction="Penny weight is non-linear and historically based on nail weight. Use ASTM F1667 reference tables; 20d common is 4 inches, but 10d is 3 inches, not 2.5 inches." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Specifying carbon steel fasteners for a typhoon-exposed building, assuming corrosion is only an aesthetic concern." correction="Corrosion reduces fastener cross-sectional area and pull-out strength, leading to structural failure during wind or seismic events. Use stainless steel or hot-dip galvanized fasteners in coastal environments." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Using wood screws instead of lag screws to attach a heavy timber beam to a concrete foundation, assuming screw type has no structural impact." correction="Wood screws in concrete provide minimal pull-out strength and may strip out. Lag screws (or wedge anchors) are designed for timber-to-concrete and provide 300-500 lbf per inch of embedment." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing ASTM A325 (120 ksi structural) with A307 (60 ksi general-purpose); using the wrong grade leads to undersized bolts", "Calculating pull-out strength without considering embedment depth (the depth the fastener is driven into the material)", "Omitting neoprene washers on roofing nails, allowing water infiltration and fastener corrosion"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Hardware, Joints, and Fasteners: **lea-matl-008-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-008-02-core-concept**, **lea-matl-008-04-core-concept**, **lea-matl-008-05-core-concept**.

rows.title: Wall finishes range from paint systems
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Classify wall finishes (paint, wallpaper, gypsum board, plywood paneling, tile, stone cladding, fabric, metal panel, glass) by aesthetic effect, durability, installation method, and fire-resistance rating for interior wall applications.
## Core Concept

Wall finishes range from paint systems (latex, enamel, epoxy) to ceramic tile, wallpaper, natural stone veneer, wood paneling, and fiber cement board. Paint is the dominant finish globally and locally in the Philippines. Paint films must bond to properly prepared substrates and maintain adhesion through environmental cycling (humidity, temperature, UV).

Paint performance depends on film thickness and substrate preparation. Dry film thickness (DFT) is measured in micrometers (µm) and ranges from 50µm for primer to 75-150µm for topcoats. Surface preparation—sanding, priming, caulking—is non-negotiable; 90 percent of paint failures stem from substrate defects, not paint itself. Moisture in concrete or gypsum causes blistering and delamination within months.

The ASTM D3359 cross-hatch adhesion test quantifies bond strength. The test cuts a lattice pattern through the film to the substrate, applies tape, and measures adhesion loss on a 0-5 scale (5B = no loss, best; 0B = complete loss, worst). A rating of 5B (no adhesion loss) indicates excellent performance. A rating of 0B (complete adhesion loss) indicates a failed system. For interior drywall, ratings of 3 or better are typical; for concrete, ratings of 4 or better are expected if substrate is properly prepared.

In the Philippines, Boysen (Pacific Paint), Davies, and Island Paints dominate the market. Boysen's Permacoat (acrylic latex) and Acrytex (enamel/acrylic hybrid) are industry standards. Davies Paints are recognized for color range and premium positioning. These brands publish drying time, coverage rate (8-12 m²/L typical), and VOC limits that must match local air-quality requirements.

Wallpaper, while aesthetic, demands smooth drywall surfaces (sandpaper grit 220+) and proper adhesive formulation. Ceramic tile on walls follows the same adhesion principles as floor tile but with relaxed slip-resistance requirements. Natural stone veneer (marble, granite) requires moisture barriers on substrate to prevent salt efflorescence and spalling in tropical climates. Hardiflex (fiber cement board) offers moisture and fire resistance for wet rooms and exterior walls, avoiding traditional gypsum drywall susceptibility to mold.


<ArticleMedia id="media-wall-finish-comparison" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Comparison chart of wall finishes: paint, wallpaper, gypsum board, plywood paneling, tile, stone cladding, fabric, metal panel, and glass with aesthetic, durability, and fire-resistance ratings"
  caption="Future chart: wall finish comparison — aesthetic effect, durability, installation method, and fire rating"
  suggestedAsset="Material selection matrix with finish application photos"
  placementIntent="Provides comprehensive reference for wall finish selection" />

## Key Provisions

| Property | Specification | Standard | LEA Relevance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dry Film Thickness (DFT) Primer | 30-50µm | SSPC-PA 2, ASTM D7091 | Ensures adequate substrate seal |
| Dry Film Thickness (DFT) Topcoat | 75-150µm | SSPC-PA 2, ASTM D7091 | Provides color and durability |
| Paint Coverage Rate | 8-12 m²/L (typical) | Manufacturer specs | Affects project cost and timeline |
| Adhesion Rating (Cross-Hatch) | ≥3 on 0-5 scale | ASTM D3359 | Failure criterion for bond strength |
| Surface Preparation (Gypsum) | Sandpaper grit 220+; dust-free | ASTM D3276 | Removes contaminants, promotes adhesion |
| Moisture in Concrete | <3% CM (calcium chloride method) | ASTM F2170 | Prevents blistering and delamination |
| Prime and Paint Drying Time | 2-4 hours per coat (latex at 23°C, <50% RH) | Manufacturer specs | Determines recoat timing |
| VOC Limit (Interior Paint) | <300 g/L (low-VOC) | ASTM D3960, EPA guidelines | Air quality compliance |
| Substrate Temperature | 10°C minimum; avoid rain, <85% RH | ASTM D3276 | Ensures proper curing and adhesion |
| Hardiflex Moisture Resistance | >3mm water head per ASTM E96 | Manufacturer specs | Wet-room suitability |

## Philippine Construction Context

The Philippines' high humidity (60-95% year-round) and seasonal rain create moisture challenges for interior finishes. Boysen and Davies paint systems are formulated with fungicides to resist mold in damp conditions, a critical specification often overlooked. Construction timelines frequently push application in marginal conditions (high humidity, rain-threatening); insisting on ASTM D3276 conditions (23°C, <50% RH) delays projects but prevents future delamination.

Gypsum drywall, the standard substrate, absorbs moisture rapidly. Hardiflex fiber cement board offers mold resistance (e.g., HardiFlex NexGen with MoldBlock Technology) for kitchens, bathrooms, and ground-floor walls in flood-prone areas. Hardiflex costs 20-30% more than drywall but eliminates replacement risk in moisture-heavy zones.

Stone veneer (marble, granite imported or quarried locally) requires moisture barriers and proper flashing to prevent salt efflorescence, visible as white crystalline deposits. Wallpaper, while aesthetically popular in residential projects, must be paired with fungicide-treated primers in high-humidity zones.

Boysen brands like KNOxOUT (marketed as air-purifying with claimed NOx-reducing properties via titanium dioxide) appeal to premium projects seeking air-quality claims, though durability remains tied to substrate preparation.


<ArticleMedia id="media-wall-finish-assembly" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Cross-section of wall finish assemblies: paint on gypsum board, tile on cement board, stone cladding with anchors, and metal panel with sub-girt system"
  caption="Future diagram: wall finish assembly cross-sections — paint, tile, stone, and metal panel"
  suggestedAsset="Cross-section detail drawings of wall finish installations"
  placementIntent="Visualizes installation methods for different wall finishes" />
## How It's Tested

**Question Type 1 (Surface Preparation):** A painter applies latex topcoat to gypsum drywall sanded with 120-grit paper and not wiped. What will likely occur within 6-12 months? Students must recognize that inadequate surface prep (grit <220) and dust contamination cause delamination (ASTM D3276 violations).

**Question Type 2 (Moisture Management):** A ground-floor bathroom in Cavite shows paint blistering 4 months after application. Concrete substrate moisture test shows 5% CM. What is the root cause and solution? Answer: moisture >3% CM per ASTM F2170 causes vapor-induced blistering. Require moisture barrier or defer painting until concrete cures.

**Question Type 3 (Adhesion Testing):** A project specification requires ASTM D3359 adhesion rating of 4 or better. A site test shows rating 2. Is the coating acceptable and why? Answer: No. Rating 2 indicates 5-15% adhesion loss, unacceptable per spec and likely to fail during service life.

**Question Type 4 (Material Selection):** Specify a finish system for a high-humidity kitchen in Metro Manila. Options: latex paint, enamel, or wallpaper. Which offers best moisture resistance? Answer: Enamel or latex with fungicide primer (Boysen formulations); wallpaper is unsuitable without mold-resistant base primer.

<Tip>Memory aid: Surface prep is 90% of paint success. If sanding isn't done to 220-grit and dust-free, the best paint will fail. Humidity >50% and temperature <10°C during application = delay the work. ASTM D3359 rating 3 is acceptable minimum; rating 5 is complete failure.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Sanding drywall with 120-grit paper and skipping dust removal before priming" correction="Use 220-grit or higher per ASTM D3276 and wipe surfaces dust-free. Dust prevents adhesion and causes delamination within 12 months." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Applying paint to gypsum drywall without primer in high-humidity bathrooms" correction="Prime with fungicide-treated primer (e.g., Boysen fungicide-rich primers) before topcoat. Unprimed drywall absorbs moisture and promotes mold." />

is optional for topcoat adhesion\", \"Mixing incompatible binders (latex over enamel without sanding and primer)\", \"Failing to caulk gaps, joints, and penetrations before finish coat\", \"Applying topcoat before primer cure time (typically 2-4 hours per coat)\", \"Using VOC-high paints without confirming local air-quality compliance\"]}"
- Text: (none detected)

## Related Articles

See also within Interior Finishes: **lea-matl-007-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-04-core-concept**, **lea-matl-007-05-core-concept**.
