rows.title: In a reinforced concrete section under bending
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Explain how a reinforced concrete section resists bending through the tension-compression couple
- Define the Whitney stress block and its parameters (a = β₁c)
- State the assumed ultimate concrete strain (ε_u = 0.003)
- Distinguish between under-reinforced and over-reinforced sections
- Identify why under-reinforced design (ductile failure) is preferred

A reinforced concrete section can fail in three modes depending on the ratio of tensile reinforcement: balanced (steel and concrete reach their respective ultimate strains simultaneously), underreinforced (steel yields before concrete crushes, allowing warning), and overreinforced (concrete crushes before steel yields, sudden failure with no warning). Understanding these concepts is fundamental to designing safe, ductile structures. The distinctions are based on comparing steel strain and concrete strain at failure using ε_u = 0.003 for concrete and the yield strain of steel (≈ 0.0021 for Grade 60).

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-006-03-core-concept" type="image" caption="Reinforced Concrete Beam — Flexural Behavior Under Bending" description="Cross-section and strain/stress diagram of an RC beam under positive bending: (1) Cross-section showing tension steel (As) at bottom, compression zone at top; (2) Strain distribution (linear, assumed plane sections remain plane); (3) Stress distribution — rectangular stress block (Whitney) for concrete compression, steel stress at yield in tension; (4) Neutral axis depth c, effective depth d, and internal couple jd." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

In a reinforced concrete section under bending, the concrete carries compression in the top fiber while the reinforcing steel carries tension in the bottom. As load increases, both materials strain. The section fails when one material reaches its ultimate strain first.

**Concrete Ultimate Strain:** ε_u = 0.003 (3 parts per thousand). Concrete cannot strain beyond this before crushing. This value is fixed by the material behavior and is used in all reinforced concrete design.

**Steel Yield Strain (Grade 60):** ε_y = 414 MPa / 200,000 MPa = 0.00207 ≈ 0.0021 (about 2.1 parts per thousand). Steel yields and enters the plastic region at this strain. For Grade 40, ε_y = 275 / 200,000 = 0.00138.

**Balanced Section:** A section is balanced when the steel reaches its yield strain _exactly_ as the concrete reaches its crushing strain (simultaneously). The strain distribution is: concrete top fiber ε_c = 0.003; steel at bottom ε_s = 0.0021 (for Grade 60). At this point, both materials are at their limits; further loading causes failure with no additional capacity. The balanced reinforcement ratio (ρ_b) is a specific value calculated for each concrete and steel grade combination.

**Underreinforced Section:** A section with less reinforcement than balanced. When load is applied, the _steel yields first_ (reaches ε_y ≈ 0.0021) while the concrete is still in the elastic range (ε_c < 0.003). The steel develops plastic strain (large deformation) before the concrete crushes, providing visible warning and large deformations (ductility). After steel yields, the concrete continues to strain elastically until it reaches 0.003, at which point the concrete crushes. Failure is _ductile_: warning precedes collapse.

**Overreinforced Section:** A section with more reinforcement than balanced. The concrete reaches its crushing strain (0.003) _before_ the steel reaches its yield strain. The steel remains elastic (ε_s < ε_y) when the concrete suddenly crushes. There is no plastic deformation, no visible warning, and no ductility. Failure is _brittle_: collapse occurs suddenly without warning. Overreinforced sections are _undesirable_ in building design and are avoided in seismic regions.

**Design Philosophy:** Most building codes require structures to be underreinforced or balanced at critical sections to ensure ductility. Ductile failure modes (like underreinforced) allow structures to deform and absorb energy (important in earthquakes) without sudden collapse. Brittle failure (overreinforced) is dangerous and typically not permitted in seismic design or where code requires ductile behavior.

**Strain Comparison (Key):**
- Concrete crushing strain: ε_c = 0.003
- Grade 60 steel yield strain: ε_s = 0.0021
- Grade 40 steel yield strain: ε_s = 0.00138

If the actual steel strain in the section is less than the yield strain at failure, the section is overreinforced (concrete crushes first). If the actual steel strain exceeds or equals the yield strain, the section is balanced or underreinforced (steel reaches capacity).

**Strength Reduction Factors (Reference Only; See LEA-STRC-005-02):**
Design strength = φ × nominal strength. For flexure, φ = 0.90 (for underreinforced, ductile sections). For spirally reinforced columns, φ = 0.75 (higher safety margin due to ductility). For tied columns, φ = 0.70. These factors are covered in LEA-STRC-005-02 and are referenced here for context.

## Key Provisions

| Section Type | Steel Strain at Failure | Concrete Strain at Failure | Failure Mode | Design Suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Underreinforced** | ε_s > ε_y (0.0021 for Gr. 60) | ε_c < 0.003 | Ductile; steel yields first, warning | Preferred; φ = 0.90 |
| **Balanced** | ε_s = ε_y (0.0021 for Gr. 60) | ε_c = 0.003 | Transition; steel and concrete reach limits simultaneously | Acceptable; limit case |
| **Overreinforced** | ε_s < ε_y (0.0021 for Gr. 60) | ε_c = 0.003 | Brittle; concrete crushes first, no warning | Undesirable; avoided |

**Steel Strain Equations (Simplified Linear Distribution):**
In the standard strain-compatibility approach, if the neutral axis is at depth _c_ from the top fiber, the steel strain at depth _d_ is:

ε_s = ε_c × (_d_ − _c_) / _c_

where ε_c is the concrete strain at the top (typically 0.003 at ultimate), _d_ is the distance from compression fiber to steel, and _c_ is the neutral axis depth.

For a balanced section, ε_c = 0.003 and ε_s = 0.0021, so:
0.0021 = 0.003 × (_d_ − _c_) / _c_

This gives the balanced neutral axis position.

**Ductility Index (Simplified):**
- Underreinforced: ductility index > 1.0 (steel deformation > yield)
- Balanced: ductility index ≈ 1.0 (edge case)
- Overreinforced: ductility index < 1.0 (no plastic deformation)

## Philippine Practice Context

The PNSC and earthquake-resistant design codes in the Philippines require structures to be designed for ductility, especially in seismic zones. This means underreinforced or balanced sections are preferred; overreinforced sections are avoided or subject to stricter controls. In practice, designers calculate the reinforcement ratio and compare it to the balanced ratio to classify the section. For high-rise buildings and critical structures in Manila and other seismic regions, ductility design is mandatory. The φ factor (0.90 for underreinforced beams) reflects the higher safety and predictability of ductile failure. Tied columns (φ = 0.70) and spiral columns (φ = 0.75) have different φ factors because spirals provide superior ductility.

## How It's Tested

1. **Flexural Testing to Failure (ASTM C78 / ASTM C293):** A reinforced concrete beam specimen is loaded in four-point bending until failure. Deflection is measured continuously. Underreinforced beams show large deflection before sudden failure; overreinforced beams fail suddenly with little warning deflection. The load-deflection curve reveals the failure mode.

2. **Strain Gauge Monitoring:** Strain gauges placed on the longitudinal reinforcement and on the concrete surface record strain development. The engineer can observe whether steel yields first (underreinforced) or concrete crushes first (overreinforced) by comparing measured strains to the theoretical strain limits (0.0021 and 0.003).

3. **Neutral Axis Measurement:** After failure, the depth of the compression zone (neutral axis position) can be measured in the failed section. This confirms whether the neutral axis position was consistent with balanced, underreinforced, or overreinforced behavior.

<Tip>Memorize the strain hierarchy: Concrete crushing (0.003) vs. Grade 60 yield (0.0021). If actual steel strain < 0.0021 at failure, the section is overreinforced (bad). If actual steel strain > 0.0021, it is underreinforced or balanced (good). This distinction is the foundation of ductile design.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Concrete Materials** (lea-strc-006-01) for f'c and material properties, **Deformed Bars** (lea-strc-006-02) for the tension reinforcement, and **Stress-Strain** (lea-strc-003-01) for the material behavior underlying flexural theory.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Using 0.003 as the steel crushing strain instead of the concrete crushing strain. The strain 0.003 (3 parts per thousand) is specific to concrete, not steel. Steel at 0.003 strain is well into the plastic range and has long since yielded (at ≈ 0.0021). This confusion breaks strain-compatibility analysis.", "Confusing yield strain with ultimate strain. Steel yield strain ≈ 0.0021; steel ultimate strain is much higher (≈ 0.10 or 10% strain). The balanced section calculation uses _yield_ strain, not ultimate strain. Using the wrong value miscalculates the balanced point.", "Assuming overreinforced sections have no strength advantage. While overreinforced sections are less ductile, they do carry higher loads before failure. However, the lack of warning (brittle failure) makes them unacceptable in code-compliant design, especially in seismic regions.", "Forgetting that ductility (underreinforced sections) is a design requirement, not an option. Code requires ductile behavior to absorb energy and provide warning. Overreinforced design is a violation and may not be approved by authorities." ]} />

rows.title: EN 15978 Standard divides building lifecycle into six
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA ## Learning Goal Identify VOC (volatile organic compound) limits for interior finishes, recycled content requirements, regional sourcing criteria, and certified wood requirements under BERDE and LEED green building rating systems. ## Core Concept EN 15978 Standard divides building lifecycle into six modules: Product stage (A1-A3: extraction, processing, manufacturing; A4-A5: transport and construction), Use stage (B1-B7: operation, maintenance, replacement, repair, refurbishment, operational energy, water), End-of-life stage (C1-C4: deconstruction, transport, waste processing, disposal), and Module D (benefits beyond system boundary: reuse, recycling credits). Embodied carbon measures A1-A3 (cradle-to-gate) material production emissions; operational carbon measures B1-B7 energy consumption. Carbon sequestration in timber results from photosynthetic CO2 uptake during tree growth. Harvested timber retains this stored carbon for the product's service life (typically 50+ years for structural members). When timber is burned or decomposed at end-of-life, stored carbon is released; this is carbon-neutral relative to growth sequestration only if the forest is replanted and regrows. Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) per ISO 14025 provide standardized quantification of material environmental impacts, including embodied carbon (kg CO2e per functional unit), water consumption, eutrophication potential, and other metrics. EPDs enable comparison of equivalent materials and verification of embodied carbon claims. ## Key Provisions Product Stage (Raw Materials)A1Extraction and processing of raw materials (e.g., mining ore, harvesting timber, quarrying stone)Iron ore extraction; tree harvesting; limestone quarrying Product Stage (Manufacturing)A2Processing of secondary materials and manufacturing of products from processed materials (e.g., steelmaking, concrete production, lumber milling)Steel smelting via EAF; concrete batch plant production; lumber kiln drying Product Stage (Manufacturing)A3Packaging and all processes up to delivery from the manufacturer gateProduct bagging; palleting; factory loading onto truck Construction StageA4Transport from manufacturer to project site, typically including distance >150 km assumed at 100 kg CO2e per tonne-km by truckDelivery of concrete, steel, timber from plant to construction site Construction StageA5Installation of products in the building; labor, equipment, and waste associated with assembly on-siteConcrete placement labor; steel bolting/welding; timber framing labor and formwork Use StageB1Use and occupation of the building, excluding operational energy and waterMonitoring, maintenance planning, data collection Use StageB2Maintenance of materials and components to preserve function (scheduled replacement and repair)Painting, caulking, membrane repair, fastener replacement Use StageB3Repair of materials and components due to damage or wear beyond design intentionConcrete crack injection, structural member strengthening Use StageB4Replacement of materials and components due to wear exceeding design lifeRoof membrane (25-year service life); HVAC systems (15-20 years) Use StageB5Refurbishment of the building for significant upgrades maintaining occupancy (major systems renovation)Window replacement; MEP system upgrade; facade refurbishment Use StageB6Operational energy: heating, cooling, lighting, plug loads, and renewable energy productionAnnual electricity and fossil fuel consumption Use StageB7Operational water: water use and treatment including wastewater managementPotable and reclaimed water consumption; wastewater treatment End-of-Life StageC1Deconstruction/demolition of the building including selective dismantling and material separationStructural demolition; material segregation for recycle/reuse End-of-Life StageC2Transport from building site to waste treatment or final disposal facilitiesConcrete to crusher; wood to mulch facility; metals to scrap yard End-of-Life StageC3Waste processing for recycling, energy recovery, or disposal (landfill emissions and methane)Concrete crushing to aggregate; wood energy recovery; landfill gas End-of-Life StageC4Disposal of processed residues and final waste to landfill including emissions (methane, leachate)Non-recyclable/non-recoverable waste in permanent landfill Beyond System BoundaryDBenefits and loads beyond the system boundary: potential for reuse, recovery, or recycling in future cycles (cradle-to-cradle credit)Recycling credits for metals, concrete, gypsum reprocessing potential; timber reuse credit Embodied carbon (Module A1-A3: cradle-to-gate) represents 15-30 percent of total lifecycle carbon for most buildings, with operational carbon (B6-B7: energy and water use) dominating 70-85 percent over a 50-year building life. However, embodied carbon increasingly drives decarbonization targets in net-zero buildings, where operational emissions are near zero via renewable energy and efficiency measures. Operational carbon depends on building location (climate), occupancy patterns, energy source (grid mix), and operational efficiency (HVAC, lighting, water systems). A building in a fossil-fuel-dependent grid (Philippines relies 40-45 percent on coal) has higher operational carbon per kWh than a building in a renewable-energy region. Efficiency measures (passive design, natural ventilation, daylighting) reduce B6 and B7 emissions. Carbon sequestration in timber: A 1 m³ of softwood timber represents approximately 500 kg of dry wood, storing approximately 230 kg of CO2 (from photosynthesis during growth). This sequestered carbon persists in-use for 50+ years, representing a carbon credit or offset during service life. Harvesting and processing (A1-A3) generates approximately 0.15 kg CO2e per kg of timber; biogenic carbon storage (Module D) is approximately -0.46 kg CO2e per kg. Net embodied carbon = +0.15 - 0.46 = -0.31 kg CO2e per kg (negative because sequestration exceeds production emissions). Environmental Product Declarations (EPD ISO 14025) provide data for three typical scenarios: A1-A3 (cradle-to-gate, most common for comparison), A1-A5 (including construction), and sometimes full A1-C4 lifecycle. EPDs enable like-for-like comparison: two equivalent steel products can be compared by A1-A3 embodied carbon per kilogram, normalizing for differences in transport distance and energy sources. ## Philippine Construction Context The Green Building Code of the Philippines (published 2015, updated provisions ongoing) incorporates embodied carbon evaluation in Section 7 (Sustainable Material Selection). BERDE Version 5 allocates 8-9 percent of points to Materials and Resources, including embodied carbon reduction and local sourcing. Projects documenting 15-20 percent embodied carbon reduction compared to baseline material specifications may qualify for additional environmental credits. RA 9729 (Climate Change Act of 2009) establishes the Philippine Climate Change Commission to coordinate government climate response, including mainstreaming of low-carbon materials in building codes and public works specifications. DPWH has initiated pilot projects evaluating embodied carbon in material selection for major infrastructure projects. Philippine electricity grid composition (2023): approximately 40-45 percent coal, 20-25 percent natural gas, 20-25 percent renewable (hydro, wind, solar, geothermal), and 5 percent other. This coal-heavy mix results in higher operational carbon per kWh compared to grid-decarbonized countries (Denmark 50+ percent renewable, Costa Rica 95+ percent). Embodied carbon therefore becomes a larger percentage of total lifecycle carbon in Philippine buildings. Timber-producing regions in Mindanao, Palawan, and Visayas provide sustainably harvested tropical hardwoods and plantation-grown softwoods meeting Philippine Sustainable Forestry standards. Using locally harvested timber (lauan, teak, mahogany in sustainable operations) reduces A4 transport embodied carbon and supports rural livelihoods. However, wild-harvested timber from unmanaged forests creates deforestation risk and should be avoided; certification (FSC, PEFC) is necessary to ensure sustainability. ## How It's Tested LEA candidates must identify LCA phases by module number (A1-A5, B1-B7, C1-C4, D) and describe what each module includes (e.g., A1-A3 is cradle-to-gate production; B6-B7 is operational energy and water; C1-C4 is end-of-life). Questions present a building scenario and ask candidates to calculate embodied carbon reduction from material substitution (e.g., 20 percent fly ash concrete replaces virgin cement), accounting for both reduced production (A1-A3) and potential B4 (replacement) stage implications. A second test approach asks candidates to interpret EPD data for two equivalent materials and select the lower-embodied-carbon option, accounting for variations in A1-A3 values based on manufacturing location and renewable energy use. Candidates must recognize that embodied carbon A1-A3 values vary by manufacturer and location, and cannot assume all steel (or concrete, or timber) has identical values. Calculation questions may involve total lifecycle carbon: a building's operational carbon is estimated from climate zone heating/cooling degree-days and energy efficiency (kWh/m²/year). Embodied carbon A1-C4 is calculated from material quantities and EPD values. Candidates must compare the two and recognize that embodied carbon typically represents 15-30 percent of total lifecycle carbon unless operational efficiency is very high. When evaluating EPD data, note the system boundary: A1-A3 (cradle-to-gate) enables material comparison but excludes transport and installation. Full A1-C4 lifecycle assessments are more comprehensive but vary based on assumed service lives and end-of-life scenarios. Always confirm which modules are included in the EPD you are using. For timber, always consider sequestration credit (Module D): timber's negative embodied carbon (stored carbon) is a significant advantage over mineral materials when carbon accounting includes sequestration. ## Common Mistakes Candidates often treat embodied carbon (A1-A3, product production) as equivleant to operational carbon (B6-B7, energy consumption). Operational carbon is typically 3-5 times larger than embodied carbon over a 50-year building life. For decarbonization strategy, focusing on operational efficiency (HVAC, envelope, renewable energy) has immediate large impact, while embodied carbon reduction affects only 15-30 percent of total emissions. Candidates sometimes claim that all timber has negative embodied carbon without accounting for forest sustainability and regrowth. Carbon sequestration is only climate-beneficial if the forest is replanted and regrows after harvest. Deforestation (permanent forest conversion to other use) means carbon storage is temporary; the forest does not regrow to re-sequester the carbon. Candidates must verify FSC or PEFC certification to ensure sustainable harvest before claiming carbon credit. Module D assigns credits for future reuse and recycling potential, but actual recycling depends on market demand and facility availability. Candidates sometimes use overly optimistic Module D credits without verifying that recycling infrastructure exists. In the Philippines, recycling rates are low (less than 5% for C&D waste); assuming all segregated material will be recycled may overstate lifecycle carbon credits by 10-30 percent.
  • Assuming A1-A3 embodied carbon values are identical for all producers of a material; actual values vary by location, energy source (renewable vs coal-powered production), and process efficiency
  • Forgetting to account for transport distance (A4) in embodied carbon; importing materials increases A4 emissions significantly versus locally sourced materials
  • Confusing service life with building design life; replacing components (B4 module) during occupancy adds embodied carbon not accounted for in A1-C4 baseline LCA
  • Using single-year operational carbon (B6-B7) without accounting for climate variation, occupancy changes, or future energy grid decarbonization over 50-year building life
  • Applying international EPD data without adjusting for Philippine electricity grid composition (40-45% coal) and transport distances from manufacturing hubs to remote regions
  • Assuming Module D (recycling credits) equal 100% of material value; recycling efficiency losses and contamination typically reduce Module D credits to 30-80% of theoretical potential
    •  ## Related Articles See also within Sustainable and Green Materials: **lea-matl-005-05-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-07-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-08-core-concept**, **lea-matl-005-09-core-concept**. > **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Precast Concrete
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define precast concrete and distinguish it from cast-in-place
- Identify advantages of precast construction: quality control, speed, reduced formwork
- Describe typical precast elements: beams, columns, slabs, wall panels
- Explain connection requirements for precast systems in seismic zones

Precast concrete members are manufactured off-site in controlled conditions and transported to the construction site for assembly. Construction joints are planned weak points where different concrete pours meet and must be designed to transfer force and resist shear. Composite members combine precast and cast-in-place concrete, leveraging the efficiency of precasting with site-specific design. Understanding these concepts is essential for modern construction and ensures proper force transfer at joints.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-006-05-core-concept" type="image" caption="Precast Concrete Systems — Beam, Column, Slab, and Wall Components" description="Diagram showing typical precast concrete components: (1) Precast beam with shear keys and connection pockets; (2) Precast column with corbel for beam support; (3) Hollow-core slab unit with prestressed strands; (4) Precast wall panel with insulation layer. Connection details shown at beam-column joint and slab-to-beam interface. Comparison of precast vs cast-in-place advantages chart." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

**Precast Concrete** is concrete that is cast and cured at a facility (precasting plant) separate from the final structure's location. After reaching design strength, the member is transported to the construction site and placed in position. Precast members offer significant advantages: quality control in a factory environment, reusable forms, parallel production while site work proceeds, and controlled curing conditions. Common precast products include I-beams, double-T slabs, hollow-core slabs, columns, wall panels, and entire room modules.

**Advantages of Precast:**
- Factory quality control: consistent strength, dimensional accuracy, and durability.
- Faster on-site assembly: less weather delay and shorter construction schedule.
- Reduced site labor: assembly is straightforward, reducing unskilled labor needs.
- Reusable forms: long-term cost efficiency for repeated production.
- Controlled curing: especially important in tropical climates where rapid drying and temperature swings are challenges.

**Disadvantages and Limitations:**
- Transportation cost and logistical complexity for large or heavy members.
- Connections between precast members must be robust to achieve monolithic behavior (if desired) or properly isolated (if differential movement is expected).
- Limited on-site modifications or adjustments after member delivery.
- Joint design and quality are critical; poor jointing can compromise structural integrity.

**Construction Joints** are intentional, planned discontinuities in concrete where two concrete pours meet. Construction joints are _not_ failures; they are designed weak points that simplify construction scheduling and allow concrete to be placed in stages. Unlike control joints (which relieve internal stresses) or isolation joints (which allow differential movement), construction joints must _transfer shear and other forces_ across the discontinuity.

**Key Characteristics of Construction Joints:**
- Location: typically horizontal (in slabs) or vertical (in walls and columns) based on construction convenience and structural requirements.
- Preparation: the existing concrete surface is cleaned (usually sandblasted or scarified) to expose aggregate and improve mechanical bond with new concrete.
- Shear Transfer: shear forces are transferred by:
  1. Mechanical interlock (roughened surface creates friction and aggregate interlocking).
  2. Shear reinforcement (reinforcing bars crossing the joint) if required by design.
  3. Dowel bars (hooked bars embedded in the old concrete and extending into the new pour) in some applications (e.g., pavements).
- Surface Treatment: the interface must be clean, moist (but not saturated), and free of laitance (soft, weak cement paste layer) to ensure good bonding.

**Construction Joint Location Rules:**
The PNSC Chapter 7 specifies where construction joints are _permitted_ and where they must be avoided. Detailed location rules are owned by Article LEA-STRC-007-06 (detailing requirements). In general:
- Horizontal joints in slabs and beams: typically placed near the center of the span (point of lowest shear).
- Vertical joints in walls and columns: typically placed at mid-height or at floor levels.
- Avoid joints at points of maximum stress or critical sections.

**Composite Concrete Members** are structural elements combining precast and cast-in-place (CIP) concrete. The two materials must act together (composite action) to achieve the combined strength. Common examples:
- Precast hollow-core slab with cast-in-place concrete topping and concrete ribs connecting the topping to the cores.
- Precast beam or I-joist with cast-in-place concrete slab poured over the top.
- Precast walls with cast-in-place concrete shear walls or connections at floor levels.

**Achieving Composite Action:**
For composite behavior, the two concrete elements must be:
1. Mechanically bonded: roughened interface, clean surface, and mechanical friction.
2. Reinforced through the interface: shear reinforcement (dowels or hooked bars) crossing from precast to CIP concrete.
3. Tested or verified: composite sections must be analyzed as a unit, not as separate elements.

**Failure Modes at Joints:**
If a construction joint or precast-CIP interface is poorly designed or executed, failure can occur by:
- Horizontal shear: if shear reinforcement is insufficient, the two concrete elements slide past each other.
- Loss of composite action: if the interface is smooth or unbonded, the section cannot transfer moment or shear as intended.
- Water infiltration and corrosion: if the joint is not properly sealed, water reaches reinforcement and causes accelerated corrosion (critical in coastal Philippines).

**Quality Assurance for Precast and Joints:**
- Precasting plants are typically certified or accredited to ensure consistent quality.
- Construction joint surfaces are inspected before placing new concrete.
- Composite member connections are verified by analysis and testing (especially important in seismic design).
- Durability: all joints and interfaces are sealed or grouted to prevent water infiltration.

## Key Provisions

| Element | Key Parameter | Standard Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Precast Member** | Strength at removal (transfer) | Typically f'c ≥ 70–80% of design strength |
| **Construction Joint** | Surface preparation | Sandblasted, scarified, or wire-brushed |
| **Construction Joint** | Concrete surface condition | Clean, moist (not saturated), laitance removed |
| **Shear Transfer** | Minimum shear friction coefficient μ | 1.4 (concrete-to-concrete, clean) |
| **Composite Member** | Interface reinforcement | Minimum spacing per design (LEA-STRC-007-04) |
| **Composite Member** | Test requirement | Verification of composite action under load |

**Precast Strength at Removal:**
- Precast members can be removed from forms when concrete reaches sufficient strength to support self-weight plus lifting/handling stresses.
- Minimum strength at release: typically 50–70% of design f'c, or 10–14 MPa, whichever is higher.
- For pre-tensioned members, stress transfer occurs at 60–75% of design f'c (different from removal strength).
- Testing: cube or cylinder samples cured with the member verify release strength has been met.

**Construction Joint Shear Friction Formula (Simplified):**
The shear capacity of a construction joint is determined by the frictional resistance:

V_c = μ × A_c × f'_c

where:
- μ = shear friction coefficient (typically 1.4 for clean concrete-to-concrete interface)
- A_c = area of concrete in shear
- f'_c = strength of concrete

This formula is referenced here; full derivation and application are in Chapter 11 (Shear) and will be covered in LEA-STRC-008-XX (Shear Design).

## Philippine Practice Context

Precasting is widely used in the Philippines for housing projects, commercial buildings, and infrastructure. Manila's rapid urban development relies heavily on precast I-beams, double-T slabs, and columns to accelerate construction. Coastal projects use precast and careful joint design to minimize water infiltration and durability issues related to tropical humidity and salt spray. The PNSC Chapter 7 specifies construction joint detailing for the Philippine environment; engineers must verify that joint preparation and grouting are done correctly on-site. Quality control of precasting plants (inspection and testing) is critical to ensure consistent member quality. Construction scheduling often depends on proper sequencing of precast delivery, positioning, and topping concrete placement for composite action.

## How It's Tested

1. **Strength at Removal (ASTM C39 / Field Testing):** Sample cylinders cured with the precast member (same temperature, humidity, and curing method) are tested at the same age as removal. If strength is adequate (typically ≥ 10 MPa or 70% design f'c, whichever is higher), the member is allowed to be removed from forms and lifted.

2. **Shear Transfer Across Joints (Push-off Test / ASTM C944):** A sample specimen with a construction joint interface is prepared with both old and new concrete. The specimen is loaded in shear across the joint until failure. The maximum shear stress before slip is recorded and compared to design expectations. This test verifies that the joint preparation method provides adequate shear transfer.

3. **Composite Action Verification (Load Testing):** A composite slab or beam (precast + CIP topping) is loaded to service levels or failure. Deflection and strain are measured at the interface. If the two materials deflect together (not separately), composite action is confirmed. If they slip or deflect independently, the design must be reconsidered.

4. **Durability and Joint Sealing (Visual Inspection):** After construction, joints are inspected for water infiltration, cracks, and sealant condition. In coastal areas, joint quality is critical; testing may include salt spray exposure or chloride penetration testing.

<Tip>Construction joints are planned weak points, not failures. They are designed to handle predictable stresses by mechanical bonding, surface roughness, and shear reinforcement. The key to success: clean the old surface (sandblast or scarify), reinforce across the joint, and keep the interface moist during new concrete placement. This is a critical supervision point for site engineers.</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Prestressing** (lea-strc-006-04) for how prestress is commonly combined with precast, **Concrete Materials** (lea-strc-006-01) for the material properties, and **Construction Joints** (lea-strc-007-06) for how precast connections differ from cast-in-place joints.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={[ "Treating construction joints as errors or defects that should be hidden. Construction joints are intentional, designed features. They simplify scheduling and allow staged construction. Poor joints result from inadequate preparation and reinforcement, not from the joint concept itself.", "Placing construction joints without shear reinforcement (dowels or hooked bars) crossing the interface. Shear forces must be transferred; rough surface alone is insufficient in high-shear regions. Dowels are required by code at many construction joint locations.", "Neglecting surface preparation: not sandblasting or scarifying the old concrete surface before placing new concrete. The interface bond depends on mechanical interlocking with exposed aggregate; a smooth surface (laitance) will not develop adequate friction and composite action will be lost.", "Forgetting that precast members and composite structures must be tested to verify composite action and strength. Design calculations assume the two materials work together; testing confirms this assumption. Inadequate testing can lead to serviceability or strength failures." ]} />

rows.title: Bearing wall system relies on walls to resist both
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal
By the end of this article, you will be able to:

- Define a bearing wall system and explain its load path
- Identify which structural elements resist gravity loads and which resist lateral loads in a bearing wall system
- Describe the height and slenderness limitations of bearing wall construction
- Compare bearing wall systems to moment frames and shear wall systems

Structural systems classify buildings into two primary categories: bearing wall systems (where walls carry gravity loads) and frame systems (where skeletal frameworks carry loads). This distinction determines load paths, member sizing, and lateral bracing strategies.

## Core Concept
<ArticleMedia id="media-lea-strc-002-01-core-concept" type="image" caption="Bearing Wall System vs Frame System — Load Path Comparison" description="Comparative cross-section diagram showing: (1) Bearing wall system — gravity loads flow through walls directly to foundation, lateral loads resisted by wall in-plane shear; (2) Frame system — gravity loads flow through beams→columns→foundation, lateral loads resisted by frame bending or separate shear walls. Load path arrows in contrasting colors for gravity (blue) and lateral (red)." suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" status="placeholder" />

A **bearing wall system** relies on walls to resist both gravity and lateral loads. The walls transfer vertical loads directly to the foundation through compression, while also functioning as shear walls for lateral resistance. Bearing walls in masonry or reinforced concrete are common in low-to-mid-rise construction because they are economical and inherently stiff.

A **frame system** uses a skeletal arrangement of columns and beams connected by rigid or pinned joints. The frame carries gravity loads through bending in the beams and axial compression in the columns. Lateral loads are resisted through frame bending (moment-resisting frames) or by separate shear walls and diaphragms. Frame systems allow more open floor plans and are preferred for mid-to-high-rise buildings.

**Key distinction:** In bearing walls, the gravity and lateral load paths are integrated into the same structural element. In frames, they are often separated—gravity is handled by the frame skeleton, and lateral is handled by shear walls or frame rigidity.

The NSCP Section 202 defines these system types to guide member design, component selection, and response modification factors for seismic analysis. Choice of system affects not only structural efficiency but also constructability, fire rating, and architectural flexibility.

## Key Provisions

| Aspect | Bearing Wall System | Frame System |
|--------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Primary load path** | Walls carry gravity directly to foundation | Columns/beams distribute loads to foundation |
| **Lateral resistance** | Walls act as shear walls | Shear walls, diaphragms, or frame moment resistance |
| **Typical materials** | Masonry, reinforced concrete, light-gauge steel studs | Steel, reinforced concrete, wood |
| **Typical height range** | 1–6 stories (economical) | 5+ stories (more efficient at height) |
| **Architectural flexibility** | Limited (walls are structural) | High (columns can be spaced widely) |
| **Seismic response** | Stiffer, lower displacement | More flexible, higher displacement if not braced |
| **Cost typical applications** | Residential, low-rise commercial | Commercial, office, tall buildings |

## Philippine Practice Context

Bearing wall systems dominate residential and mixed-use construction in the Philippines due to material availability, labor skills, and lower initial cost. Concrete shear walls are standard for multi-unit residential blocks. Frame systems (steel or RC moment-resisting frames) are used in commercial office towers and buildings in Seismic Zone 2, where R factors reward rigid lateral systems.

## How It's Tested

**Remember-level:** Identify whether a given structural system is bearing wall or frame based on a building description.

**Understand-level:** Explain why a bearing wall system is economical for low-rise buildings but frame systems are preferred for mid-to-high-rise.

**Apply-level:** Given a building in Seismic Zone 2 with 10 stories, justify why a frame system with moment-resisting capability would be chosen over a bearing wall approach.

<Tip>**Memory aid:** Bearing walls **bear** loads directly; frames **defer** loads to a skeleton. Think "walls work, frames relax."</Tip>

## Related Articles

See also: **Shear Walls** (lea-strc-002-02) for lateral-force-resisting variants, **Bearing Walls** (lea-strc-002-04) for the wall elements themselves, and **Moment-Resisting Frames** (lea-strc-002-03) for an alternative lateral system.

## Common Mistakes

<Warn>These are frequently tested traps. Memorize them to avoid losing easy points on exam day.</Warn>

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Confusing bearing wall with any wall that touches a load—bearing walls must carry superimposed loads, not just their own weight (thresholds defined in LEA-STRC-002-04)","Thinking frame systems cannot have shear walls—frames require lateral bracing (shear walls, diaphragms, or moment connections)","Assuming bearing walls are always masonry—RC shear wall systems are bearing systems, and light-gauge stud walls can be bearing if they carry required loads"]} />

rows.title: Change Orders Types Authority Limits and the Documentation Process
rows.content:
## Change Orders — Types, Authority Limits, and the Documentation Process ## Learning Goal After reading this article, you should be able to: - Define a Change Order and distinguish it from other contract modifications (Change Directive, Field Order). - Identify the types of changes: owner-initiated, field-discovered, deficiency, regulatory, and force majeure. - Explain the Architect's authority limits for issuing Change Orders and when Owner authorization is required. - Describe the Change Order documentation process and how cost and schedule adjustments are documented and approved. Change orders formalize modifications to the scope of work, establishing new contract terms when conditions require deviation from the original design or scope. ### Definition and Necessity of Change Orders A change order is a formal modification to the original contract scope of work. Change orders address unanticipated site conditions, design modifications requested by the owner, errors discovered in contract documents, regulatory requirement changes, and other circumstances requiring work outside the original contract scope. Without a change order process, disputes arise regarding what work is included in the contract price and what constitutes extra work. The change order serves as a formal contract amendment documenting the modification, specifying what additional or revised work is required, establishing responsibility for cost and schedule impacts, and recording the agreement of all parties to the modification. This formal documentation prevents future disputes over whether specific work was authorized and what the contractor's compensation should be for the modified scope. ### Types of Changes and Their Causes Changes fall into several categories. _Owner-initiated changes_ occur when the owner requests design modifications, additional scope, or specification changes. These changes increase the contract scope beyond the original documents. _Field-discovered changes_ arise from unforeseen site conditions like subsurface obstacles, underground utilities, or structural deficiencies not apparent from initial documents. _Deficiency changes_ address errors in the contract documents, such as conflicting specifications or impossible design requirements requiring clarification. _Regulatory changes_ result from code changes or new requirements imposed by authorities having jurisdiction during construction. _Force majeure changes_ may arise from extraordinary circumstances like natural disasters, though these are often addressed by contract provisions rather than formal change orders. ### The Change Order Documentation Process When a change is identified, the architect documents the proposed modification in detail. The change order proposal includes a clear description of the work to be added, deleted, or modified, specifications and standards to be applied, drawings or sketches showing the change, and a cost estimate for the additional work. The architect requests the contractor's proposal regarding cost, schedule impact, and resource allocation for the change. The contractor provides a proposal including the cost of performing the changed work, any schedule delay caused by the change, and modifications to resource allocation if required. The contractor's proposal may include overhead and profit calculations. The architect evaluates the contractor's proposal against industry standards and similar completed work to assess reasonableness. ### Cost Adjustments and Schedule Impacts Change orders must address both cost and schedule implications. An addition to the scope increases the contract price; a deletion reduces it. Deductions may be based on a reduction in material quantities, labor hours eliminated, or scope of equipment rental reduced. The change order must specify exactly how the contract price is adjusted and the basis for the adjustment. Schedule impacts are equally important. Many changes delay the project schedule. The change order should quantify delay impact and establish a revised substantial completion date. If a change is directed by the owner and causes delay, the contractor may be entitled to a time extension allowing extended performance without liquidated damages. The change order documents this time adjustment formally. ### Types of Change Order Provisions Change orders may be _additive_, increasing both cost and scope. They may be _deductive_, reducing cost and scope. _Directive changes_ are owner directives requiring specific modifications, sometimes issued before the cost and schedule impacts are fully determined, with final pricing determined later. _Constructive changes_ arise when the architect's direction or the owner's actions effectively require modified work even though no formal change order has been issued—these create disputes requiring careful documentation. A _force account change_ is performed on a time-and-materials basis with the contractor billing for actual labor, materials, and equipment time with overhead and profit markups applied. This approach is used when the scope change cannot be estimated precisely before work begins and the actual cost will be determined by what is ultimately performed. ### Documentation Requirements and Record-Keeping Complete documentation of all changes is essential. The architect maintains a change order log tracking all proposed and approved modifications. Each change order should be numbered sequentially and cross-referenced to the contract documents and project records. Copies are distributed to the contractor, owner, and all relevant parties. The contractor maintains daily logs documenting all work performed on changed scope, materials incorporated, equipment utilized, and schedule impacts. These records support the contractor's cost documentation if disputes later arise regarding what work was actually performed or what scope modifications occurred. The architect's inspection records should similarly document observation of the changed work as it is performed. ### Cumulative Impact and Pricing Over a project's duration, multiple changes accumulate, potentially creating significant pricing and scheduling impacts. Some contracts include provisions addressing cumulative change impact, requiring the architect to re-evaluate overhead, profit, and resource allocation as the total modified scope increases. A contractor whose original contract work was substantially modified by multiple changes may have justification for additional compensation reflecting the increased complexity and resource impact of extensive modifications. Disputes frequently arise regarding whether the contractor is entitled to overhead and profit adjustments when multiple changes substantially alter the original contract conditions. Clear change order language addressing pricing methodology for cumulative changes prevents these disputes. RA 9266 governs architectural practice and contract requirements. Agreements must specify scope, compensation, termination, and dispute resolution per SPP Document 201.
  1. Proposal — Scope definition and fee negotiation
  2. Contract Execution — Signing of UAP Doc 301
  3. Service Delivery — Performance of defined phases
  4. Payment Processing — Progress billing and certificates
  5. Close-out — Final certificate, retention release
 Under UAP Doc 301, basic services = all 6 phases. Additional services (feasibility, supervision) are separately compensated. Verify exclusions.

rows.title: Earthwork volume
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

Calculate roofing material quantities — area coverage per sheet, side lap and end lap allowances, ridge length, fascia/gutter lengths, fastener count — for corrugated GI sheets and other roofing systems on sloped roofs.
## Core Concept

Earthwork volume is calculated from cross-sectional areas at measured stations (e.g., every 10 or 20 meters along a road centerline). The trapezoidal formula is: _V = (L/2) × (A₁ + A₂)_ for a single section, where L is the distance between cross-sections and A₁, A₂ are the areas. For multiple sections at regular intervals: _V = (L/2) × [(A₁ + Aₙ) + 2(A₂ + A₃ + ... + Aₙ₋₁)]_.

The prismoidal formula is more accurate, particularly for parabolic or irregular sections: _V = (L/3) × [(A₁ + Aₙ) + 4(even-numbered areas) + 2(odd-numbered areas)]_. The prismoidal method typically yields 2–8% lower volumes than the trapezoidal method for the same data, particularly on undulating terrain.

In the Philippines, standard practice uses the trapezoidal method for preliminary estimates and the prismoidal method for final billing and payment. The formula constants (L/2 vs. L/3) reflect the different integration approaches.


<ArticleMedia id="media-roofing-quantity-diagram" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Diagram showing corrugated GI sheet coverage calculation with side lap, end lap, and slope allowance on a roof plan"
  caption="Future diagram: roofing quantity estimation — GI sheet coverage, laps, and slope allowance"
  suggestedAsset="Roof plan with sheet layout and lap allowance callouts"
  placementIntent="Visualizes roofing material quantity estimation" />

## Key Provisions

| Formula | Application | Accuracy | LEA Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trapezoidal: V = (L/2)(A₁ + A₂) | Single section, two cross-areas | Lower | Basic calculation |
| Trapezoidal: V = (L/2)[(A₁ + Aₙ) + 2(sum of middle areas)] | Multiple sections, regular intervals | Moderate | Standard site use |
| Prismoidal: V = (L/3)[(A₁ + Aₙ) + 4(even) + 2(odd)] | Multiple sections, higher precision | High | Final billing |
| Cut volume | Excavation of existing material | Positive | Cost driver |
| Fill volume | Placement of new material | Positive | Material sourcing |
| Section interval (L) | Distance between stations (10–30 m) | Standard | Per project specs |
| Shrinkage factor | 1.1–1.3 (volume increase after excavation) | 10–30% | Adjustment for loose soil |
| Swell/compaction | Site-dependent; clay swells more | Varies | Material behavior |
| DPWH Blue Book | Item specifications, earthwork method | Standard | Governs public works |

## Worked Examples

<Example>
**Scenario 1: Road section with two cross-sections 20 meters apart; Cut area A₁ = 50 m², Cut area A₂ = 60 m²**

**Step 1: Apply trapezoidal formula for single interval**

V = (L/2) × (A₁ + A₂) = (20/2) × (50 + 60) = 10 × 110 = 1,100 m³

**Answer: 1,100 m³ cut volume**
</Example>

<Example>
**Scenario 2: Road grading with 5 cross-sections at 15 m intervals; Areas: A₁ = 40 m², A₂ = 52 m², A₃ = 58 m², A₄ = 45 m², A₅ = 35 m²**

**Step 1: Apply trapezoidal formula for multiple sections**

V = (L/2) × [(A₁ + A₅) + 2(A₂ + A₃ + A₄)]

V = (15/2) × [(40 + 35) + 2(52 + 58 + 45)]

V = 7.5 × [75 + 2(155)]

V = 7.5 × [75 + 310]

V = 7.5 × 385 = 2,887.5 m³

**Step 2: Apply prismoidal formula for verification (higher accuracy)**

V = (L/3) × [(A₁ + A₅) + 4(A₂ + A₄) + 2(A₃)]

V = (15/3) × [(40 + 35) + 4(52 + 45) + 2(58)]

V = 5 × [75 + 4(97) + 116]

V = 5 × [75 + 388 + 116]

V = 5 × 579 = 2,895 m³

**Comparison**: Trapezoidal = 2,887.5 m³; Prismoidal = 2,895 m³ (differ by ~0.3%, both reasonable)

**Answer: ~2,890 m³ (trapezoidal for simplicity, prismoidal for accuracy)**
</Example>


<ArticleMedia id="media-roofing-estimation-example" layout="single" type="image" status="placeholder"
  alt="Step-by-step roofing estimation example showing roof area, GI sheet coverage with end and side laps, ridge length, and fastener count"
  caption="Future diagram: roofing estimation worked example — sheet coverage, laps, ridge, and fasteners"
  suggestedAsset="Step-by-step illustrated calculation example"
  placementIntent="Provides practical example of roofing material estimation" />
## Quick Reference: Earthwork Formula Table

| Method | Formula | Suitable For | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trapezoidal (1 section) | V = (L/2)(A₁ + A₂) | Two adjacent cross-sections | Simple, common |
| Trapezoidal (n sections) | V = (L/2)[(A₁ + Aₙ) + 2Σmiddle] | Multiple regular sections | Industry standard |
| Prismoidal | V = (L/3)[(A₁ + Aₙ) + 4(even) + 2(odd)] | High-precision estimates | Better accuracy 2–8% lower |
| Average end area | V = L × avg(A₁, A₂) | Simplified approximation | Quick estimates |

## Philippine Construction Context

In the Philippines, earthwork is a major cost component for road construction, building sites, and land development. The DPWH Blue Book specifies the trapezoidal method for progress billing and the prismoidal method for final payment on significant projects (Item 202, Earthwork). Large projects (highways, reclamation) use prismoidal exclusively for precision.

Standard cross-section intervals are 20 meters for highways and 10–15 meters for complex terrain (mountainous, undulating). Surveyors measure areas at each station using theodolites and GPS. Cut and fill are tracked separately: cut is the excavated material, and fill is the imported or reused material for embankments.

Climate: Philippines' rainy season affects excavation costs (increased equipment wear, slower work) and soil conditions (saturated clay swells more). Material sourcing from borrow pits or quarries involves haul distances that impact costs significantly.

## How It's Tested

On the LEA, earthwork volume questions focus on:

1. **Two-section volume**: Given L and two cross-sectional areas, calculate volume using V = (L/2)(A₁ + A₂).

2. **Multiple sections (trapezoidal)**: Given multiple area measurements at regular intervals, apply the standard trapezoidal formula.

3. **Multiple sections (prismoidal)**: Apply the prismoidal formula with careful attention to even/odd area numbering.

4. **Cut vs. fill**: Identify and sum cut areas separately from fill areas.

5. **Shrinkage/swell adjustment**: Apply a swell factor (1.1–1.3) if loose excavated soil volume is needed.

6. **Cost estimation**: Volume × unit cost per m³ = earthwork cost.

<Tip>
**Memory aid**: Trapezoidal = (L/2) × [first + last + 2(middles)]. Prismoidal = (L/3) × [first + last + 4(even stations) + 2(odd stations, excluding first and last)]. When in doubt, use trapezoidal; it's simpler and acceptable for most LEA-level problems.
</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Confusing the trapezoidal formula constant L/2 with L/3 (prismoidal)" correction="Trapezoidal uses L/2. Prismoidal uses L/3. If you can't remember which, stick with trapezoidal for simplicity." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Forgetting to divide the first and last terms by 2 in the trapezoidal formula" correction="The formula is (L/2) × [(A₁ + Aₙ) + 2(sum of middle areas)]. The first and last are NOT doubled; only the middle areas are." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Using incorrect numbering for even/odd stations in the prismoidal formula" correction="Stations are numbered 1, 2, 3, ..., n. Even stations: 2, 4, 6, ... Odd stations: 3, 5, 7, ... (exclude 1 and n)." />

<WikiMistakeCard mistake="Not separating cut and fill volumes" correction="Cut and fill are tracked independently. Do not mix them in one calculation." />

<WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Applying a swell factor without being asked (swell only applies if loose excavated volume is the deliverable)", "Using area measurements in the wrong units (ensure all areas are in m²)", "Forgetting that L is the interval between sections, not the total length", "Confusing prismoidal accuracy (typically 2–8% lower than trapezoidal) as a defect rather than expected behavior"]} />

## Related Articles

See also within Estimating Quantities and Material Computation: **lea-matl-010-01-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-02-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-03-core-concept**, **lea-matl-010-04-core-concept**.

> **Overview:** See **overview-building-materials** for the full curriculum structure and study strategy. See **mastery-building-materials** for connections across topics.

rows.title: Section 2 of the Code
rows.content:
## What You Need to Know for the LEA
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

- Define the fiduciary nature of the architect-client relationship and the architect's duty of unquestioned loyalty.
- Identify disclosure obligations: conflicts of interest, third-party compensation, and material relationships.
- Explain the prohibition on accepting compensation from third parties without client knowledge and consent.
- Apply fiduciary duty principles to LEA scenarios involving conflicts of interest, client trust, and ethical obligations.

The architect-client relationship rests on good faith and the architect's unquestioned loyalty to the client. The architect must disclose all conflicts of interest, refuse compensation from third parties without client consent, and prioritize client welfare even when this conflicts with fee maximization.

## Core Concept

Section 2 of the Code establishes that the architect-client relationship is "depended upon good faith" and that the architect's position "carries with it certain moral obligations to his Client and to himself." This creates a **fiduciary relationship** — the architect is a trusted adviser who places the client's interests above the architect's own profit.

<LawCallout code="ra9266" section="Section 2 (a-j)" title="Client Obligations — The Fiduciary Standard">
Section 2 of the Code establishes the architect's fiduciary duty to the client. Key subsections: (b) ascertain scope and fees at inception; (c) advise against impractical projects; (f) charge fair fees per Basic Minimum Fee standards; (g) cannot undertake fixed-sum construction of own designs; (h) shall not accept returns from any source other than the client; (i) disclose conflicts of interest; (j) include arbitration clause in agreements.
</LawCallout>

<ArticleMedia id="media-eth004-client-duties" layout="single" variant="contained" type="image" status="placeholder" aspectRatio="16:9" title="Duties to the Client — Fiduciary Obligations" alt="Hub-and-spoke diagram centered on Fiduciary Duty to Client with six spokes: Absolute loyalty Section 2-h, Conflict disclosure Section 2-i, No third-party compensation Section 2-h, Confidentiality, Truthful advice Section 2-c, Fair fees Section 2-f. Each spoke includes key code reference and an exam-relevant note." placementIntent="ethics-framework" suggestedSearchQuery="architect fiduciary duties to client Code of Ethics Section 2 loyalty confidentiality" suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image" alt="Hub-and-spoke diagram of fiduciary obligations to clients" caption="Future diagram: hub-and-spoke diagram of fiduciary obligations to clients" />

The obligation has six interconnected dimensions:

1. **Absolute loyalty** — defined in §2-h as receiving compensation "solely through his professional fee charged directly to the Client" with "no other returns in whatever form from any interested source other than the Client."

2. **Conflict of interest disclosure** — Section 2-i requires: "If the Architect has any business interest which will relate to, or affect the interest of his Client, he should inform his Client of such condition or situation."

3. **No money from third parties** — Section 2-h is unambiguous: the architect "shall not accept nor ask for any other returns in whatever form from any interested source other than the Client."

4. **Confidentiality** — Implied from the fiduciary duty; the architect cannot disclose the client's budget, timeline, negotiating position, or proprietary information.

5. **Truthful advice** — Section 2-c requires: "The Architect shall advise a Client against proceeding with any project whose practicability may be questionable due to financial, legal or arresting or exigent conditions, even if such advice may mean the loss of a prospective commission to the Architect."

6. **Fair and transparent fees** — Section 2-f requires fees "commensurate with the work involved and with his professional standing and experience based upon the Basic Minimum Fee prescribed under the 'Standards of Professional Practice.'"

## Key Provisions

| Provision | Source | LEA Relevance |
|-----------|--------|---------------|
| Good faith relationship | Code §2 Statement | Foundation: architect is fiduciary |
| Loyalty to client | Code §2-h | Cannot accept payments from suppliers/contractors |
| Disclose conflicts of interest | Code §2-i | Must inform client of any business interest affecting advice |
| No compensation except from client | Code §2-h | All third-party compensation violates duty |
| Advise against impractical projects | Code §2-c | Must risk commission loss to protect client |
| Fair, professional fees | Code §2-f | Must comply with Basic Minimum Fee standard |
| Cannot undertake fixed-sum construction | Code §2-g | Architect cannot be contractor for own designs under fixed-sum |
| Disclose financial interests | Code §2-i | "Tend to weaken... standing" test applies broadly |
| Maintain confidentiality | Code §2 (implied) | Client information is privileged |
| Include arbitration clause | Code §2-j | Disputes resolved through arbitration, not litigation |

## Philippine Practice Context

Under RA 9266 §33, the architect retains copyright in all drawings and specifications prepared, but the client receives a right to use these documents for the commissioned project only. This ownership distinction reinforces the fiduciary relationship: the architect owns the intellectual property but serves the client's interests. The architect cannot reuse design solutions or documents from one client's project for another client without explicit consent.

The PRBoA has consistently disciplined architects who accepted contractor payments, discounts, or commissions without client knowledge. In one case, an architect received 5% from a preferred contractor in exchange for steering contracts; this resulted in suspension. The Board views such arrangements as inherent conflicts that distort professional judgment.

Architects employed by government agencies face heightened scrutiny: their loyalty obligation extends to the public (as taxpayers), not just to the government entity as contracting party.

<Warn>
  **Common Exam Trap:** The LEA frequently tests whether "small" gifts or discounts are acceptable if disclosed. The answer is NO under §2-h — ANY compensation from third parties is prohibited unless it is a market discount credited to the client under §4-b. Verbal disclosure to the client does not make it permissible; the architect must refuse or pass the benefit to the client.
</Warn>

## How It's Tested

**Pattern 1: Undisclosed Compensation**
A contractor offers architect 8% commission on project costs. Architect accepts. Violation: §2-h (undisclosed compensation violates sole-source requirement).

**Pattern 2: Conflict of Interest Concealment**
Architect is part-owner of a building supply company and specifies that company's materials. Client not informed. Violation: §2-i (undisclosed conflict of interest).

**Pattern 3: Impractical Project Advice**
Client requests design the architect knows is financially unfeasible. Architect proceeds to avoid losing the commission. Violation: §2-c (duty to advise against impractical projects).

**Pattern 4: Fixed-Sum Construction Contract**
Architect designs building, then agrees to construct it for fixed lump sum. Violation: §2-g (architect "shall not undertake, under a fixed contract sum agreement, the construction of any project based on plans prepared by him").

<ExamTip>
  **LEA Watch:** Apply the "FAIR" test for client obligation questions: (F)iduciary duty to act in client's best interest; (A)dvise truthfully even at cost to yourself; (I)nterested parties must be disclosed; (R)eceived only from client — no third-party compensation. Anything that weakens the architect's standing as "unprejudiced and honest adviser" violates §2-i.
</ExamTip>

<Tip>**Memory Aid: "FAIR"—Fiduciary, Advised truthfully, Interested parties disclosed, Received only from client.** If a question involves third-party compensation, conflicts of interest, or impractical project advice, apply the FAIR test. Anything that weakens the architect's standing as "unprejudiced and honest adviser" violates §2-i.</Tip>

## Common Mistakes

<WikiMistakeList
  mistakes={[
    "Believing 'small' supplier discounts or commissions are acceptable without disclosure — §2-h prohibits ANY compensation 'in whatever form from any interested source other than the Client' except market discounts credited to client per §4-b",
    "Confusing 'market discount' with 'commission' — market discounts must be credited to the client and are the only permissible third-party benefit",
    "Assuming conflicts of interest can be concealed if they 'don't affect this specific project' — §2-i requires disclosure of ANY business interest that 'affect[s] the interest of his Client' or 'weaken[s]... standing as unprejudiced adviser'",
    "Thinking architect can advise client truthfully and still accept contractor/supplier payment — the two are incompatible under §2-h and §2-i",
    "Accepting fixed-sum construction contracts thinking §2-g only applies if architect designed the building — §2-g explicitly prohibits this 'under a fixed contract sum agreement... based on plans prepared by him'",
    "Overlooking confidentiality as part of client obligation — fiduciary duty includes protecting client information from competitors and third parties",
  ]}
/>

---
